blocks.h: HOLD HER UNDER UNTIL SHE LOVES YOU
Roya Publication No. 112
by Chew Z
SYNOPSIS

Naples sits between two volcanoes, and the one under its western half is waking. Every month the ground beneath the old town of Pozzuoli rises a little higher, and every month three million people decide, once again, not to be afraid.

Domenica Esposito has never had to decide. Left as a baby on the steps of a church in 1992, she was taken before anyone could write her name down, and she has no papers, no number and no face in any computer. She was born without fear. Not with a little, or with less than most: with none. Two small almond-shaped parts deep in her brain, the parts that tell the rest of us to be afraid, have been stone since she was a child.

A secret order raised her. The Held are forty respectable, frightened people, a notary, a banker, a priest, a pharmacist, who meet on Sunday mornings above a pharmacy by the sea. For three hundred and seventy years they have found children like Domenica and kept them on the only leash such a child can wear. Every Sunday, in a cave where volcanic gas lies on the floor like an invisible lake, an old man named Ferrante holds her face down in the poison until her body screams, and then lifts her out into the air. She calls it love. On the other six days she goes wherever the Held send her, and does whatever no one else can.
Then a doctor gives her a single breath from a mask, and she recognises the feeling.
A NOTE FROM THE AUTHOR

This book contains killing, torture, the suffocation of children and adults, and harm to children described in its aftermath. Its language is foul. It is the darkest thing Roya has published, and I would rather you knew that before the first page than after it.

This book began with a question I could not put down. What would a person be capable of if they had never once been afraid? Not brave, because bravery is having fear and going anyway. Just without it, the way some people are born without the sense of smell.

The answer starts with a real woman, known in the scientific papers only as S.M. A rare inherited illness, Urbach-Wiethe disease, turned the two fear centres of her brain to calcium when she was a child. When a man held a knife to her throat in a park, she was calm, and the next night she walked through the same park. Then, in 2013, researchers in Iowa asked her to breathe one lungful of air heavy with carbon dioxide, and she panicked for the first time since childhood. Fear of not being able to breathe comes up another road. Domenica was built in that gap.

The Cave of the Dog is real too: a short passage near Agnano where volcanic gas pools on the floor, and where guides once held dogs down for paying travellers. The ground under Pozzuoli really is rising. The foundling wheel, the skulls of the Fontanelle and the city’s plagues, massacres and uprisings are history. The Held, the Foundation, the Book of Choosing and every person in this story are invented. So are the evacuation, the swarm of December 2026 and everything that happens in it.
What I hope the book leaves you with is a single question: whether what you would call your own goodness comes from somewhere in you, or from the heavy air round your feet.
Chew Z
I. THE WHEEL
1. Nothing in the Room Was Frightening
You do not breathe until you are lifted.
The man with the cleaver had been cutting onions before I came in.

There was a crescent of white onion stuck to the flat of the blade, and the whole kitchen smelled of it, sweet and sharp, laid over a deeper smell of meat that had been cooking in tomato since noon. It was a Saturday. On a Saturday in Naples every second kitchen has a ragù [rah-GOO] on the stove. That is beef and pork, sometimes a rind of something, sunk in tomato and left on the lowest flame for six hours. Whoever walks past gives it a stir, so that on Sunday the family can eat it and say it was worth the gas. In this city you can find a building by the smell of its Saturday. I found this one that way. The address was only there to confirm it.
There were three people in the kitchen.

The first sat at the table with his right hand flat on the oilcloth and his fingers spread, the way a child presses a hand onto paper so someone can trace around it. He was fifty-one and heavy. He wore a vest that had been white on Monday, and he had a gold chain buried in the hair of his chest like a wire in a hedge. He was the debt.

The second stood over him with the cleaver. Twenty-five, gym arms, a phone in his back pocket with the screen cracked in a star. He worked for a lending app. Those are the new moneylenders. You borrow with one tap of your thumb, at interest that would make a priest cross himself. When you cannot pay, the app sends a boy. This was the boy. He was not the debt. He was a coincidence, and I don’t like coincidences. They are untidy.

The third was the wife. She stood by the stove holding a wooden spoon upright, like a candle in a procession. She was the client. Two weeks before, she had folded six fifty-euro notes very small and pushed them into the little wooden house of a skull. Then she had asked, so quietly that the man taking her request had to bend down to hear, for her husband to stop.
And then there was the heavy air.
I should tell you about the heavy air now, at the start, because you will need it. You have never seen it, and I have never seen anything else.

When a person is afraid, I see the fear come off them. It is like the shimmer over a road in August: colourless, faintly bending the light behind it. It is heavy, so it does not rise. It sinks. It pours off a frightened body and settles on the floor, and it fills a room from the bottom up, the way water fills a bath. I have never needed anyone to tell me how afraid they are. I look at their legs.
In that kitchen the heavy air stood at the knee.

The husband sat in it to his waist. The boy with the cleaver stood in it to his shins, and it was rising, because I had just walked in and he did not know who I was. The wife stood in the deepest of it. It came up to her chest. She had been standing in it, I think, for about twenty years, and she had stopped noticing, the way you stop noticing the sea when you live beside it.
Some people live in it up to the neck. You know some of them. You may be one.
I have none of my own. Not a drop. I walk through rooms and my shoes come out dry.

The door had been on the latch. In the Sanità [sah-nee-TAH] the doors are always on the latch, because there is nothing to steal but each other. The Sanità is a quarter of the city built in a ditch. It is a long, deep valley just outside where the old walls stood. The Greeks buried their dead there, and then the Romans, and then the Christians, who dug catacombs into the soft yellow rock, underground tunnels of graves, and painted saints on the walls of the graves. Later the living moved in on top of the dead and built palaces, and the palaces fell on hard times and filled up with families. Two hundred years ago the French kings who ruled Naples built a bridge clean over the whole valley, so the royal carriage could go from the city to the palace on the hill without passing through the Sanità at all. The Sanità has lived under that bridge ever since. It has laundry for flags and a shrine on every corner. Its boys are good with motorbikes and knives. Its grandmothers can tell you which saint to ask for what, and how much the saint will cost.
I went in. I went past the three of them to the stove, took the wooden spoon out of the wife’s hand, dipped it, blew on it and tasted.
“Too much salt,” I said.

All three of them turned and looked at me. Nobody had noticed me until then. That happens. People notice a body by the fear that comes off it, the way a dog notices a smell, and I don’t give them any.
“Who the fuck are you?” said the boy.
“You can save it with a potato,” I said to the wife. “Peel one, cut it in half, put it in for twenty minutes, take it out. It drinks the salt.”
The boy pointed the cleaver at me.
I’ll tell you what I saw, because seeing is what I do instead of the other thing.

It was a cheap cleaver, six euros at most, from the shop on the Via Foria [VEE-ah FOH-ryah], the long loud road below the Sanità, that sells everything in plastic boxes. There was a chip in the blade near the heel. There was the crescent of onion. His hand was wet on the handle, and his thumb was on the wrong side of it, on top, where it would slip if he ever had to put any weight behind a blow. He had never had to. The cleaver was for frightening people, and up to now it had always been enough.

Here is what happens when you point a blade at a person. The blade is a question. It asks: are you afraid? Everyone answers. Their body answers before they do. Breath goes up into the chest. The hands come up. The weight goes onto the back foot. The eyes go wide, to let in more light, because the old animal in them wants to see where the danger is going to come from. This all happens in less than a second, and nobody chooses it. It is the oldest conversation in the world.

I don’t answer. I don’t have the part that answers. I’ll tell you later what it is and where it should be. For now, imagine shouting into a well and hearing nothing come back. Not even your own voice.

The heavy air came up to the boy’s thighs. He had never pointed a knife at someone who did not answer. He did not know what to do next. There is no next, in that conversation, if the other person doesn’t speak.

I took the cleaver out of his hand the way you take a fork from a toddler: by the handle, without hurrying, while looking at something else. I was looking at the wife’s forearm. There were four oval bruises on the inside of it, in a row, going yellow at the edges. They were the right size and the right spacing for a man’s fingers.
“Go home,” I told the boy.
“He owes four thousand—”
“Tell them he’s dead.”
“He’s not dead.”
“Tell them anyway. You’ll be right by the morning.”

He looked at me then, properly, for the first time. I watched him understand that he was in a room with something he did not have a word for. The heavy air rose to his belt. He backed into the doorframe, then turned and went out and down the stairs. He had to wade out through his own fear, like a man wading out of the sea against the pull of it. Long after I could no longer see him I could hear him taking the stairs two at a time.
I was wearing yellow dishwashing gloves. I always do. Nobody remembers a woman in yellow dishwashing gloves. They think she has come to clean.
She has.

I sat down at the table across from the husband. His hand was still flat on the oilcloth. Nobody had told him he could move it, so he hadn’t. The oilcloth had a pattern of lemons and green leaves. There was a ring on it from a wine glass and a small burn from a cigarette.
“What do you want?” he said. His voice was high. The heavy air was at his chest now. He was sitting in it like a man in a bath that is slowly filling, who can’t find the tap.
“Nothing,” I said, which was true. I have never wanted anything from any of them.
I’ll tell you the next part in the order it happened, because order is the only decency I have.
It took one breath. One of mine. He had time for about half of one of his.

The cleaver went into the side of his neck, just under the ear, where the big blood vessel runs up to the head like a pipe up the outside of a wall. A cleaver is not a good knife for this, because it is made for bone and not for anything clever. But it is heavy, and heaviness forgives a great deal.
First there was the sound, a wet, flat sound, like a fish dropped on a marble counter.

Then the blood. It came out in pulses, keeping time with his heart, which was going very fast because he was so frightened. Fear is a pump. It pushed the blood out of him in long bright ropes across the lemons on the oilcloth, onto the tiles, and in one long arc up the front of the cooker, where it ran down into the gas ring and hissed. Then it slowed, because the heart was running out of what it pumps. Then it stopped.
His hand stayed flat on the table the whole time. He had been told to keep it flat, and he did. I want you to remember that. Obedience is a strange thing. It outlives the man.

When it was done, the heavy air in the room went down the way a bath goes down when you pull the plug. Not all of it. The wife’s never goes all the way. But it went down to her waist, and then to her hips, and she put a hand on the edge of the cooker to steady herself, and she breathed in, deep, as if she had been under water.
I put the cleaver on the floor by the door, where a frightened boy would drop it running. His fingerprints were on the handle and mine were in a pair of gloves from the shop on the Via Foria.
“A boy from the lending app was here,” I said to her. “You saw him. You’ll say what you saw.”
“Thank you,” she said.
“Don’t,” I said. “You paid.”

I took the gloves off at the bottom of the stairs, turned them inside out one into the other, and dropped them in a bin three streets away, among the vegetable peelings outside a greengrocer’s. Then I walked out of the Sanità the long way, up and over, under the bridge. It was after eleven. There were boys on scooters going nowhere fast, three to a seat. An old woman was changing the candle in a shrine to the Madonna, set into a wall behind a little glass door. She had plastic roses, a photograph of a young man in a football shirt, and a small brass heart. I went down past the museum to the old straight street the Greeks laid out, the one we call Spaccanapoli [spahk-kah-NAH-poh-lee], Split-Naples, because from the hill above it cuts the old city in two like a knife through a loaf. In a bar on that street there is a shrine to a dead footballer with one of his real hairs in a glass case. People stop and pray to it. I stopped and looked at the hair. It was a good hair, black and curled. Then I went on to the station for the last train west.
I want to be clear about one thing from the start, because later people are going to call it something else and they’ll be wrong.

It wasn’t courage. Courage is when you have fear and you go anyway. Courage is expensive, and it is beautiful, and I have seen it in other people and admired it the way you admire a language you don’t speak. I don’t have any fear to go in spite of. I just go.
Nothing in the room was frightening. It never is.
Tomorrow was Sunday. On Sundays I go under.
My name is Domenica [doh-MEH-nee-kah]. In Italian that means Sunday.
They named me for the day they own me.
2. Esposito
Everyone who is afraid owes something to someone who is not.

My other name is Esposito [es-POH-zee-toh]. It means exposed, as in put out, set down, left. If you look in the telephone book of Naples, back when there were telephone books, you would find more Espositos than any other name, page after page of us. The reason is a hole in a wall.

The hole was in the church of the Annunziata [ah-noon-TSYAH-tah], in the old city, near the port. For five hundred years it held the ruota [RWOH-tah], the wheel. It was a wooden drum set into the wall, open on one side like a cupboard, that turned on a pin. A woman who could not keep her baby came to the wall at night, put the baby in the open side of the drum, turned the drum, and rang a small bell. On the other side of the wall a nun heard the bell, turned the drum the rest of the way, and took the baby out. Neither woman ever saw the other’s face. That was the point of the wheel. It was a machine for letting go without being seen.

The nuns wrote each baby down in a book, and every one got the same surname: Esposito, the left one, the put-out one. In this city, the name goes, you are either somebody’s child or you are the Madonna’s. The Espositos were the Madonna’s. Some grew up and married and had children, and gave the name on to them, and that is how half the city came to carry it. Most people named Esposito today come from parents who were wanted, and from grandparents who were wanted. Somewhere far back, though, there was always a bell at night.
The wheel was closed in 1875. You can still see the hole where it was. It’s bricked up now, with a little grille, and tourists take photographs of it.

I was left there in 1992, one hundred and seventeen years after it closed. Not in the wheel, which is bricked up, but on the steps under it, in a wooden crate that had held fennel. It was April and it was raining. Someone had wrapped me in a man’s shirt and put a plastic bag over the top of the crate to keep the rain off, which I have always thought was kind. They left no note. The building remembered what it was for, I suppose, even after all that time. People went on leaving babies at that door for years after the wheel was gone.
I don’t know who left me. I have never wondered. I’m told this is unusual.
What happened next is the important part, and it is very simple. Before anybody wrote me down, I was taken.

In Italy you exist when the town hall writes you down. A child is born and her name goes into the register of the comune [koh-MOO-neh], the town she belongs to. She gets a number for taxes and a number for the doctor, and later a card with her face on it. All the rest of her life is built on top of that first line, the way a building is built on top of its first course of stones.
I don’t have a first line.

The woman who found me on the steps was not a nun. She was a nurse from the hospital round the corner, coming off a night shift. She was a member of an order I will tell you about, and she knew what to look for. She did not take me to the police or to the nuns. She took me home. She waited, and watched me, and on the third day she made a telephone call. Nobody ever wrote down that a baby had been found at the Annunziata in April 1992. Nobody had to look for me, because nobody knew I existed.

So I have no papers. No card with my face, no number for the doctor, no number for taxes, no bank account, no telephone contract in my name, no name in any computer anywhere in the world. When the police stop a car I am in, I am a cousin. When a hospital wants a name, I borrow one. When I die there will be a body, but in every way that the state can measure, there will have been no person.
The most fearless thing about me is that I am not anywhere.
I live in Pozzuoli [pot-TSWOH-lee]. To understand Pozzuoli you have to understand the ground.
Naples sits between two volcanoes. The famous one is Vesuvius, to the east, the one that buried Pompeii, with a little cloud tied to its top like a flag. It isn’t the one I mean.

The one I mean is to the west, and you can’t see it, because you are standing in it. It’s called the Campi Flegrei [KAHM-pee fleh-GREH-ee], the Burning Fields. Long ago it was a mountain. It blew itself apart and fell in, and left a bowl in the earth twelve kilometres across. Scientists call that a caldera [kahl-DEH-rah], the old Italian word for a cooking pot. Half the pot is under the sea. On the other half live five hundred thousand people, in Pozzuoli, in Bagnoli [bahn-YOH-lee], in the west end of Naples. They go to school and to Mass in a cooking pot, and the stove underneath is still on. The drains smell of rotten eggs. At the Solfatara [sol-fah-TAH-rah], the sulphur place, the ground hisses through yellow-crusted holes.

And the ground moves. Not all at once, the way it does in an earthquake, but slowly, over years, like the flank of a sleeping animal breathing in. People here call it bradisismo [brah-dee-SEEZ-moh], slow earthquake. Since 2005 the whole town of Pozzuoli has been lifted about a metre and a half, every house and church and harbour wall, the way you’d lift a tray. The old harbour steps now climb out of the water to nothing. When the lifting goes fast, the earthquakes come in swarms, hundreds in a night, like a pot rattling its lid. Last year they were stronger than any since the instruments were put in.
Men from the government handed out leaflets about where to go when the time comes. Nobody goes. That’s Naples. I’ll come back to that.

I live in the Rione Terra [ree-OH-neh TEHR-rah]. It’s the oldest part of Pozzuoli, a high square block of rock over the harbour, where the Romans had a town and a temple. Later the temple became a cathedral, and the town on top of it became a maze of tall, narrow houses joined by bridges and stairs. In 1970 the ground went up very fast, and the government emptied the Rione Terra in a single day. Three thousand people were put on trucks with whatever they could carry, and they never came back. For fifty years the place stood empty. Laundry poles stuck out of the windows with nothing on them, and kitchen tables sat with their chairs pushed back. Little by little they have been rebuilding it, as museums and expensive rooms for visitors, but there are parts of it no one has touched. In one of those, at the top of a stair whose bottom flight has fallen away, I live.

I have no lease. A person with no name cannot sign one. The people who raised me arranged it with whoever needed arranging. I have a bed, a stove, a table, a chair, a moka [MOH-kah], the little eight-sided coffee pot that every Italian kitchen has, a window that looks over the harbour, and electricity that comes off a cable belonging to the cathedral. I sleep exactly over the point where the ground rises fastest. The scientists put their instruments on the rock under my building because it moves more than anywhere else in Italy.
I find that funny. You probably don’t.

That Saturday, after the Sanità, I got home a little after one in the morning. I washed my hands and face and the back of my neck, and made coffee in the moka. I like coffee at night. It doesn’t keep me awake. Nothing keeps me awake.
At twenty past one the swarm started.

First there was a sound like a lorry going past in the street below, though no lorry can get up to the Rione Terra. Then the moka walked across the stove. It went about four centimetres on its own, rattling, and tipped over and spilled the coffee into the flame, which hissed and went out. The cup on the table shivered against the saucer. A little plaster sifted down from the ceiling like flour from a sieve. Then it stopped. Ninety seconds later it came again, smaller. Then again. By two o’clock there had been forty of them. The next morning the observatory would put the biggest at magnitude three point nine, on the scale they use to measure the strength of an earthquake, and the depth at two and a half kilometres, which is not deep at all. It means the thing that was moving was just under my bed, about as far down as a long walk to the shops.
I went to the window.

Below me, in the lower town, the lights were coming on one after another, the way they do in a theatre when the show is over. Doors opened. People came out into the streets in their pyjamas and slippers. Women carried babies wrapped in blankets and men carried television sets, which I have never understood. Somebody had a birdcage with a canary in it. Car engines started all along the seafront, because the cars were where people slept now on bad nights, with the seats pushed back and the doors unlocked so they could get out fast.
And the heavy air came up out of them.

It came out of every door and every window, out of every body. It ran down the stairs and the steps and the steep lanes, just as water runs downhill, and it gathered in the streets and the squares. By two o’clock it was ankle-deep along the whole of the seafront. In the square in front of the town hall, where people had crowded together because it was open ground and nothing could fall on them, it was up to their knees. Under the streetlights it shimmered. Some of the children were standing in it to the waist, because children are short and also because they catch it from their mothers.
The whole of Pozzuoli was standing in a lake of fear. It was perfectly still, and colourless, and nobody could see it but me.
I watched for a while. It’s beautiful, if you can see it, the way flood water is beautiful from a hill.
Then I wiped up the coffee and went back to bed.

Three million people live between these two volcanoes, and half a million of them inside the government’s red zone, the ground that goes first. When it shakes they go out in their pyjamas. In the morning they sweep up the plaster and have a coffee.

Outsiders call it courage, or stupidity. It’s neither. It’s a bargain. The city has made an arrangement with the fire under it, the same arrangement it has made with its saints, its moneylenders and its government. We know what you can do to us. We will be polite. We will not ask too much. In return, not today. Then every morning that the bargain holds, the city wakes up and is grateful and doesn’t look down.
It’s a whole city that has agreed not to look at its fear. It stands in the heavy air up to its ankles every day of its life and calls it the floor.
I was raised by the people who keep the city’s other bargains. I’ll take you to them next.
3. The Held
God gave breath first. Fear is God taking it back. Whoever gives it back is God.
They met on Sunday mornings, after Mass, in Chiaia [KYAH-yah].

Chiaia is the other end of the city from the Sanità in every way that matters: palaces along the sea, shoes and watches that cost a Sanità family’s year, small dogs in little coats. The heavy air there is a thin film at the ankles. People in Chiaia are afraid of the right things in the right amounts.

On a narrow street climbing from the seafront there is a pharmacy that has stood since 1788, with wooden shelves to the ceiling and two hundred jars of painted pottery labelled in Latin. Some of them are poisons. One of them, if you know which, still holds a little of what its label says.

Above the pharmacy is the Fondazione Respiro [fon-dah-TSYOH-neh reh-SPEE-roh], the Breath Foundation. The brass plate says it’s a charity, and it is, in every way that can be checked. It buys inhalers for children with asthma and holds a fish dinner every December where rich people write cheques. A tax inspector once went through its accounts for three months and found them perfectly clean. Behind reception there are glass offices with grey carpet.

Behind the glass offices there is a door that looks like a cupboard. Behind the cupboard is a room that is kept, by a machine humming in the wall, at exactly fourteen degrees, with the air neither too wet nor too dry. In that room there are shelves, and on the shelves are skulls.

There are sixty-one of them. Each one sits in a little house of its own, made of wood or tin or carved stone, with a tiny roof and a little door. Some have lace curtains. Some have a candle stub in front, and some have a coin or two, or a folded note.

In the Sanità there’s a cave called the Fontanelle [fon-tah-NEL-leh], the little fountains, a quarry as big as a cathedral with no windows. For three hundred years, whenever the city had more dead than its graveyards could hold, the dead went there. Then the women of the Sanità began going down into the dark to adopt a skull, a stranger’s, nobody’s. They polished it, built it a little house, and asked it for favours: a husband, a son home from the war, a lottery number. They called them the capuzzelle [kah-poot-TSEL-leh], the little heads. The souls were stuck halfway to heaven and needed prayers to get out. You gave prayers; they gave favours. A bargain, like everything here. One skull, Donna Concetta [DON-nah kon-CHET-tah], was said to sweat.
In 1969 the archbishop closed the cave and called it superstition. The women went home.
Not all of them. Sixty-one are on the shelves in Chiaia, in a room at fourteen degrees.
The Held took them a long time ago, and some of them are the skulls of Keepers. I’ll explain what a Keeper is. Not yet.

On Sunday mornings forty people come up the stairs past the brass plate. They’re not who you’re imagining. There are no robes, no hoods, no Latin, no candles in a circle. There’s a notary, a woman with grey hair cut very short who witnesses wills and property sales. There’s an adoption lawyer, a geneticist from the hospital laboratory, a banker who manages the money of old families, a priest from a church in the Vomero [VOH-meh-roh], the respectable quarter on the hill, an assistant to a member of parliament, a man who owns three car dealerships, a woman who runs a private clinic, and the pharmacist from downstairs, who has thin white hands and keeps a cough sweet in his cheek at all times. Doctors, accountants, a judge. People you would trust with your house keys. People who are trusted.
Every one of them is afraid of something. That’s how they came to be here. That’s what holds them.

I could tell you what each one is afraid of by looking at their legs. The notary stands in it to the ankle, an old fear, small and steady, about something she signed thirty years ago. The banker is shin-deep; he is afraid of being poor, which he never will be. The geneticist is at the knee, and it rises on Sundays when she comes up the stairs, because she knows better than any of them what we are and where we come from. The priest wades in it to the thigh. I have never asked him why. I don’t need to know the shape of a fear to know its depth.

They sit on grey chairs in the biggest of the glass offices, with their coats on their knees and their phones turned off. At the front there’s a desk, and behind the desk there’s an empty chair, until he comes.
And on Sundays, a client.

A client is someone from outside. Nobody knows how they find their way up the stairs. Somebody tells somebody who tells somebody. One of the forty knows a woman whose sister cleans for a family whose son is in trouble. The client is always very frightened. That’s the first condition. The Held have no use for anyone who is angry, or greedy, or simply wicked. Those people go to the Camorra [kah-MOR-rah], the old criminal clans of Naples, which have a price list. The Held want people who are drowning.

That Sunday the client was a man of about sixty, in a good coat that had once been very good. He sat on a grey chair at the front with his hat on his knees, turning it round and round by the brim. The heavy air was up to his chest. He kept swallowing.

He’d been a builder. He had built, he said, a block of flats in Bagnoli in 1998. He had saved money on the concrete. He didn’t explain how, and he didn’t need to. Everyone in the room knew what it means to save money on concrete in a place where the ground moves. Last year an engineer from the government had come to inspect the building after the swarms, a young engineer, very serious, with a beard. The engineer had taken samples. The engineer’s report was due at the end of the month. If the report said what the samples said, the building would be emptied, and there would be questions, and then there would be a court, and he was sixty-one, and his wife was ill.
“I’m not a bad man,” he said.
Nobody answered. In the room of the Held nobody ever tells a client what they are.

He took an envelope out of his coat and stood up. He didn’t know where to put it. The pharmacist got up, took him by the elbow very gently, led him through the cupboard door into the cold room of the skulls, and showed him the little house of a skull with a tin roof and a scrap of lace for a curtain. The man pushed the envelope inside. He touched the top of the skull, quickly, the way you touch a hot pan. Then he came back and sat down and put his hat on his knees again.
Then Ferrante [fer-RAHN-teh] came.

I’ll describe him properly later. Today I’ll tell you only what the room saw: an old man, very upright, in a grey suit and a dark blue tie, with white hair combed straight back. He had a long, mild face like a horse’s, and big hands, a workman’s hands, which he kept folded in front of him. He came in from the back, from the cold room. He always comes from there, as if he had been talking to the skulls. When he came in, the heavy air in the room went down. Not a lot. A few centimetres. You could see the forty of them breathe out.
He didn’t sit. He stood behind the desk and looked at the builder for a long moment, kindly, with his head a little on one side.
“The engineer,” he said. “Yes.”
That was all. He didn’t ask anything. He didn’t discuss. He has decided hundreds of debts in that room, and I have never heard him use more than eleven words on one.

The builder began to cry. The heavy air went down to his waist. You’d think a man would be horrified to hear his wish granted like that, in one word, by a stranger. He wasn’t. He was relieved. That is the thing I most want you to understand about the Held, and about fear: the frightened do not want to be saved. They want someone else to decide.
Ferrante raised one big hand, and the room stood. Forty chairs scraped. They said the creed together, quietly, the way you say a prayer you learned before you could read.
God gave breath first.
Fear is God taking it back.
Whoever gives it back is God.
Then the rules. The children of the Held learn seven, and the members say five aloud. The other two are not for saying.
One. You do not breathe until you are lifted.
Two. The hand on your neck is the only hand.
Three. What happens under stays under.
Four. The Keeper is never wrong about air.
Five. Everyone who is afraid owes something to someone who is not.
When they say the fifth rule, the forty of them don’t look at Ferrante. They look at me.

I always stand at the back by the window, with my coat on. I don’t sit on the chairs. They have never asked me to, and I have never wanted to. When the fifth rule is said, forty frightened, respectable faces turn round and look at the woman by the window. I see in them what you’d see in a family looking at the big dog that lives in their yard. The dog guards them, and once, years ago, she bit the postman so badly that they had to pay for a hospital. They love her for it. They’re proud of her. They don’t want to be alone in a room with her.
The builder looked too. He didn’t know who I was, or what I was for. But he looked at me, and he understood something, and the heavy air came up again past his waist. I watched it climb.
Afterwards, when they had gone down the stairs and out into the bright cold of a Sunday morning in March, Ferrante put on his coat and his hat and a grey scarf, and came to stand by me at the window.
“You smell of onions,” he said.
“Somebody’s Saturday.”
“Was it good?”
“Too much salt.”
He nodded, as though this was what he’d expected, and touched my elbow with two fingers to turn me towards the stairs.
“Come,” he said. “The dog’s waiting.”
4. Sunday
Sunday is not a day. It is a depth.

Ferrante drives a white van, nearly thirty years old, with a dent in the back door and a statue of Padre Pio [PAH-dreh PEE-oh] stuck to the dashboard with a pad of grey glue. Padre Pio was a monk from the south who had the wounds of Christ in his hands, and Neapolitans put him on their dashboards the way other people put on a seatbelt. The van smells of fennel, always. I don’t know why. I have never seen fennel in it.
We drove west out of Chiaia along the sea, and then through the hill.

West of the city there is a ridge called Posillipo [poh-ZEEL-lee-poh], which comes down to the water. Its name is Greek and means the rest from pain, because the rich Romans built their summer houses on it and came to forget. The Romans also cut a tunnel straight through the bottom of it, seven hundred metres long, so carts could go west without climbing. Their tunnel is closed now. Next to it there are new ones for cars, lit orange inside, and you go into the hill in Naples and come out of it into the Burning Fields.

You know when you’ve arrived, because the light changes. The sky’s the same, but the ground is different: lower, flatter, scabbed with old craters that have become fields and suburbs and car parks. The air has a faint taste of matches.

Agnano [ahn-YAH-noh] is one of the craters. Once it held a lake, round and blue, six kilometres around, with the spa baths on its southern shore where the hot springs came out. People came from all over Europe for the waters. In 1870 the lake was drained, because it had gone bad, standing water full of fever, and the men of the new Italy wanted the land. Now the lake bed is a racecourse, and on Sunday afternoons you can hear the crowd from the road, and the voice on the loudspeaker calling the horses home. The old spa is still there, half rebuilt, half falling down. Behind it, at the foot of a slope of scrub and broken stone, there is a gate, and behind the gate there is a hole in the hill.
The Grotta del Cane [GROT-tah del KAH-neh]. The Cave of the Dog.

It isn’t much to look at. It’s a doorway cut into the rock, about as high as a man’s chest, opening on a passage that runs straight back into the dark for nine metres and then stops. Someone dug it, a long time ago, Romans or someone before them, maybe as part of the baths. The walls are warm. At the bottom of the passage, in the floor, is the reason for everything: a crack where the volcano breathes out.

What it breathes out is carbon dioxide. That’s the gas you breathe out yourself, every time, the used-up part of the air. You can’t see it and it has hardly any smell. But it is heavier than ordinary air, half as heavy again, and so it does what heavy things do. It sinks. It flows out of the crack in the floor, lies down in the bottom of the passage, and fills it like an invisible pool. The pool is about as deep as your shin. Above it, the air is fine. A grown man can walk into the cave and stand in it and breathe as easily as in his kitchen.
A dog can’t, because a dog’s head is down where the pool is.

For hundreds of years, that was the show. Rich travellers came to Naples on what they called the Grand Tour, which was how young English and German and French gentlemen finished their education: they looked at ruins, drank too much, and caught diseases. A man would be waiting for them at the cave, with a dog on a rope. For a coin he would take the dog into the passage and hold it down by the neck. The travellers stood above it, breathing easily, and watched. The dog would struggle, then shake, then roll its eyes and go limp. Then the man would carry it out and throw it into the cold lake, and it would come up coughing and paddle to the shore, alive. The travellers would clap. Goethe [GUR-tuh] came, the great German poet, in 1787. Alexandre Dumas [ah-lek-SAHN-druh dew-MAH] came, the man who wrote The Three Musketeers. Mark Twain came in 1867 and wrote, joking, that he had been keen to see a dog die. One dog, it was said, did this every day for years and learned its part so well that it would faint as soon as it saw a tourist coming.
When the lake was drained, the show stopped. There was nowhere to throw the dog.
The Held came before the tourists, and they stayed after.

Ferrante parked by the old spa. There’s a tap on the outside wall there, for the gardeners. He took two steel buckets from the back of the van, filled them both at the tap, and carried them up the slope one in each hand, at eighty-nine years old, without spilling. He always carries them himself. I have offered, once, when I was ten. He looked at me as if I had offered to say his prayers for him.
“The lake was drained in 1870,” he said, as he says every Sunday, in the same voice. “So we carry the lake.”
The gate has a padlock. He has the key. The ground is volcanic dust and broken pumice, a light grey stone full of holes like bread, which floats if you throw it into water.
And the dog was there.

It’s yellow, the yellow of old straw, short-haired, the size of a big fox, with a tail that curls up over its back and a torn left ear. It lives at the cave. Nobody feeds it that I’ve ever seen. It’s always there on Sundays, lying in the sun at the mouth of the passage, and it gets up when we come and wags the back half of its body and puts its nose into Ferrante’s hand. Then it looks at me. It has brown eyes with gold in them.
It’s the same dog I met when I was six. I’m thirty-four. It’s not an old dog. It has never been an old dog.
I don’t think about that. You can.

At the mouth of the passage Ferrante set the buckets down and took a candle from his coat pocket, a stub of white church candle, and lit it with a match. He bent down, slowly, his knees cracking, and set it on the floor just inside the entrance, and we watched it.

The flame stood up straight and yellow for a breath. Then it leaned. Then it went small and blue, and lay down on its side like a tired animal, and went out. A little thread of grey smoke went up from the wick and hung there, just above the floor, at the top of the pool. It lay flat on the invisible surface like smoke on a lake at dawn, showing where the air ended and the other thing began.
“Good,” said Ferrante. “It’s high today.”

I took off my coat and folded it and gave it to him. I took off my shoes. The stone was warm under my feet, warm like a bed someone has just got out of. I walked into the passage, five metres in, to where the roof comes down low and you have to stoop. I knelt down in the dust with my back to the entrance and my face to the dark.

The yellow dog came in after me and lay down beside me, on its side, its whole body under the surface of the pool, as if the gas were grass. It put its head on its paws and watched me with its gold-brown eyes, and breathed slowly in the stuff that kills dogs, and didn’t die.
Ferrante came and stood behind me, upright, his head in the good air, his big hand open.

I want to describe this properly, because it is the best thing in my life, and I’ve thought about how to tell it so that you will understand. I’m going to try to make it short, because it is short. You’ll feel the sentences go. That’s right. That’s what it’s like.

His hand came down onto the back of my neck. It was warm and dry and heavy. It covered my neck from one side to the other, the thumb under one ear and the fingers under the other, and it pressed, and my face went down.

I didn’t hold my breath. You are not allowed to. The First Rule is that you do not breathe until you’re lifted. The children of the Held learn early that this doesn’t mean you hold your breath. It means you keep breathing, in and out, normally, the whole time, and you don’t try to come up for air until the hand lifts you. You breathe what’s there.
What’s there is not air.

The first breath tastes sour. It tastes of a battery on the tongue and a fizzy drink gone wrong. The gas mixes with the wet of your mouth and eyes and turns a little bit to acid, so your eyes sting. They water. Your nose burns.
The second breath goes deep and finds nothing in it.
The third.
The body knows. Not you. The body.

It is an alarm. Somewhere far down, low, at the back of the head where the neck joins it, something old wakes up. It is older than thought, older than speech, as old as fish. It has one job. It measures the gas in the blood, and when there is too much it presses one button.
The button is now.
My heart goes.
It is the only time my heart runs. It runs. It runs like a horse with a fire in the stable. It hammers on the bone of my chest from the inside like a fist on a door.
My lungs pull. They pull like hands. Air air air. Bigger breaths, faster. Each one worse. The more you breathe, the more you drown.
Everything in me wants up.
The hand stays.

Light. Light at the edges of the eyes, little lights, then a ring of it. Then the dark goes long. A tunnel. Someone is in it with me. Someone beside me in the dark. I can feel them, a warmth on the left side, close. Close as a mouth. I can’t see them.
Time goes thin. Stretches. A second is a room.
The dog’s eye. Gold.
Under me the stone hums.
Up.
Up.
Up up up up

This is the thing I want you to understand. For six days of every week there is nothing in me. No alarm. No weather. I walk through rooms full of heavy air and my shoes come out dry. I have watched men die and felt what you feel watching a kettle. The world goes past me like a film with the sound off.

And then on Sunday, under his hand, for forty seconds or fifty or sixty-two, there is everything. There is the whole bottom of the sea. There is all of it, all the fear in the world, all at once, coming up through the floor of me. I’m terrified, utterly, purely, the way you were terrified as a baby when you woke up in the dark and didn’t know yet that there were such things as mornings. I’m all the way alive.

And then the hand lifts, and then he pulls me up by the back of the neck into the good air above the pool like a cat lifting a kitten, and in the same movement the whole bucket of cold water comes down over my head, cold from the tap, cold like the lake that isn’t there, and it goes into my mouth and my nose and my eyes and down my back inside my shirt, and I’m on my knees in the light at the top of the cave with my head up, dripping, and I breathe in.
I breathe in.

That first breath is called the gift. That’s the Held’s word for it. You cannot imagine it. You’ve breathed every second of your life and never once had a breath like that one: so cold and clean and full that it goes all the way down to the soles of your feet and comes back up as light. Every cell in the body opens its mouth and drinks. The heart, which was running, stops running and stands still, shaking, the way a horse stands after a race. The tears run down, and it isn’t crying. It’s only the body letting go.
He kept his hand on my neck. Not pressing now. Holding.
“There,” he said. “There. There. Good girl.”
I leaned back against his legs, and he put his other hand on top of my wet head, and I closed my eyes.
“I love you,” I said.
“I know,” he said. “I love you too.”

I’ll be honest with you, because there is no point in any of this if I’m not. I meant it. I meant it completely, with my whole body, the way you mean it the first time, and I’d meant it every Sunday since I was six years old. That hand was the only thing in the world that had ever made me feel anything, and the feeling was so enormous that I had never once in twenty-eight years asked what it was made of. Why would you? You don’t take apart the only light in the house to see how it works.

He did it three times that Sunday. Forty-one seconds, then fifty-three, then sixty-eight. He counts aloud, softly, in a voice like a man reading to a child. Afterwards he writes the numbers down in a book with brown ink.
The yellow dog got up off the floor of the cave, shook itself, and walked out into the sunshine. It lay down again by the gate and closed its eyes.
Driving back through the tunnel in the orange light, Ferrante took a paper bag of sugared almonds from the glove box and gave it to me, the way he used to when I was small.
I ate them all. I was starving. I always am, after.
You’ll want to call it something. People always do. You’ll call it cruelty, or brainwashing, or abuse, and you’ll feel better for having a word. Go on. I’ll wait.

Here is what I’d ask you, though, while you’re feeling better. In your whole life, has anything ever made you feel as much as that? Anything? And if it had, and if it came only on Sundays, and only from one hand — what would you have done for that hand on the other six days?
You know what I’d do. You’ve seen it. You’ll see more.
5. The Portfolio
A fearless child is a fire. A fire is a gift to a house with a stove. To any other house it is the end.
On Wednesday he showed me the portfolio.

He did it in his office at the Foundation, the small glass room at the end, which has no plants and nothing on the walls except a framed print of an old engraving: the Cave of the Dog in 1706, with three men in wigs and a dog being dragged into the dark on a rope. He had a laptop on the desk. He doesn’t like computers. He uses them the way he handles a dead bird, carefully and as little as possible. He turned it to face me.
“You’ve met them,” he said. “Not all of them. You’ve seen them come on Sundays. I think it’s time you knew what they’re for.”
There were four faces on the screen.
I’ll give them to you as he gave them to me, by what they do, because that’s how he talks about them, and because names are the first thing the Held change.
The first was a man of about forty with a shaved head, a broken nose and very light eyes. Under his face was a word: the Soldier.

“Found in Salerno [sah-LEHR-noh], down the coast,” said Ferrante. “Nineteen eighty-six. The geneticist before this one found him. He went into the army at eighteen and into the parachute regiment at twenty. Then into the ninth, the Col Moschin [kol mos-KEEN].” That’s the oldest of the Italian special-forces units, named after a mountain in the north where its first men attacked up a cliff in the First World War. “Afghanistan four times, Iraq twice. He has medals he can’t wear because he isn’t allowed to say what he did to earn them. Now he’s at Lago Patria [LAH-goh PAH-tree-ah].”

Lago Patria is north of the city, on a lagoon by the sea. NATO has a headquarters there, a big one, low and white and fenced, behind which generals from twenty countries plan for wars that haven’t started yet.
“What does he do there?”

“He’s useful,” said Ferrante. “He’s in the rooms where the plans are made. And when a plan needs a man to walk into somewhere nobody would walk into, it’s him they ask. He’s never once said no. He’s never once come back hurt. They think he’s lucky.”
The second was a man in his thirties in a dark blue suit, very thin, with glasses. The Trader.

“Milan. He bets other people’s money on whether things go up or down. Every trader alive is afraid every second of being wrong, and the fear keeps them careful.” He tapped the screen. “He isn’t careful. He bets everything, every time. When he’s wrong, he doesn’t sweat and he doesn’t sell. He waits. In nine years he’s made the Foundation more money than it made in the century before.”
The third was a young woman with her hair shaved on one side, laughing at someone off the edge of the photograph. The Founder.

“San Giovanni [sahn joh-VAHN-nee].” That’s the old factory district on the east side, where the university has built a technology campus in glass and red brick. “She started a company at twenty-two. It should have died ten times. Each time she did what a frightened person wouldn’t: borrowed more, hired more, promised what she didn’t have yet. Now it’s worth more than the whole of the Sanità.”
The fourth was a woman of fifty with grey eyes and a hard, plain face. The Surgeon.

“Rome. She operates on the hearts of newborn babies. Hearts the size of a walnut. Her hands don’t shake. When something goes wrong on the table, when the others freeze, she doesn’t. She goes in.” He closed the laptop gently. “Children live because of her who would have died anywhere else.”
I sat and looked at the lid of the closed laptop.
“I’ve seen them,” I said. “On Sundays.”
“Yes.”
“They don’t stand in anything.”
He knew about the heavy air. He’s the only one I’ve ever told. He has never doubted it, not for a moment. He just nodded, as if I’d said they all had brown eyes.
“No,” he said. “They don’t. They’re like you.”
Then he explained it to me properly, the way he does, slowly and plainly, like a man drawing a map on a napkin.

“There’s a word the doctors use,” he said. “Fearless dominance. It’s a measurement. They give people questions to answer, and from the answers they put a number on how calm a person stays when there’s danger, how bold they are, how easy among strangers. Everybody has some. Most people have a little. A few have a lot.”
“And the ones with a lot?”

“Are found in three places.” He held up a big finger for each one. “Among leaders. Among heroes, the man who goes back into the burning house for the child, the woman who stands in front of the soldier’s gun. And among the worst people alive, the ones who can hurt others and feel nothing. It’s the same trait. What it becomes depends on what it is pointed at.”

In 2012, he said, psychologists in America had rated the American presidents for it, and the ones with the most were, more often than not, the ones history called great. Then he added, as his own opinion and not the study’s, that they were also the ones most willing to send other men to die.

There’s a man in America who climbs sheer rock a kilometre high without a rope. In 2016 scientists put him in a scanner that photographs the brain at work and showed him pictures meant to frighten anyone. In other people a small part deep in the brain lit up like a struck match. In him, it barely glowed.

“He’s not like you,” said Ferrante. “His is turned down. Very far down, but it’s there. Most people have their fear turned down a little, or turned up. We find the ones in whom it was never turned on at all.”
“And you put them in chairs.”

“We put them where fear would have stopped anyone else. And they do the thing that fear would have stopped. And the world is changed, a little, every time, in the direction we’ve chosen.” He folded his big hands. “That’s the whole of it. That’s all the Held have ever done. For three hundred and seventy years. In different chairs.”
“And the leash.”

“Is Sunday.” He said it simply. “A fire is a gift to a house with a stove. To any other house it’s the end. If you’d been left loose, Domenica, without the cave, without the hand, what do you think you’d have become?”
I thought about it honestly. I always think honestly with him.
“Anything,” I said.
“Yes,” he said. “Anything. That is the most frightening word there is.”
“Why wasn’t I placed?”
He smiled. It is a lovely smile, sad and kind, the smile of a man in a painting of a saint.
“They are placed,” he said. “You’re kept.”
Then he gave me the debt.

There was a journalist. He was forty-four and worked for one of the newspapers in Rome, the kind of journalist who spends a year on a single story and doesn’t care that nobody reads past the second paragraph. Somebody had told him something. He had become curious about a children’s charity in Naples whose name kept coming up in adoption records, which is a strange thing for a breathing charity. Twenty-three adoptions in thirty years had passed through one lawyer’s office, and every one of the children was a foundling or a hospital case. He had written to the lawyer and to the notary. He had found a woman who’d been a nurse at the Annunziata hospital, and she had talked to him, a little.
He had been planning to talk to the geneticist next week.
“He’s afraid,” said Ferrante, “every day now, of what he’s found. He sleeps with the lamp on. Isn’t that sad.”
“Yes,” I said.
“Don’t let him be afraid for long,” said Ferrante. “He hasn’t done anything wrong.”

I’ll tell you how I do it, because it shows something. That’s the reason I’m telling you any of this. You asked, back at the start, without knowing you’d asked, what a person without fear can do. This is one of the answers. It’s a small one, but it’s real.

The journalist had a flat in the Vomero, on top of the hill, all wide streets and doormen and geraniums. You get up there by funicular, a little railway pulled straight up the hillside on a cable. His building’s owner was a man who comes up the stairs past the brass plate on Sunday mornings. A key arrived for me in an envelope.

I went in at seven o’clock in the evening, when he was at the library. I looked at everything once, slowly: his kitchen, his books, the photographs of his mother, the ashtray, the bottle of sleeping pills by the bed with eleven left in it, the lamp. Then I got into his wardrobe and closed the door.

It was an old wardrobe, dark wood, with a long mirror on the outside of the door and slats near the top to let the air move. It smelled of cedar and of camphor, the white balls people put in with their clothes against moths. There were five shirts on hangers, a winter coat, a suit in a plastic cover from the dry cleaner, and on the floor three pairs of shoes and a box of old letters. I stood among the shirts with my back to the wood, my arms at my sides, and looked out through the slats into the room.

He came home at twenty to eight. He ate pasta out of the pan, standing up. He telephoned his mother and told her he was fine, and that he had a cold, which was a lie; he said it to explain his voice, which was tight. He read his notes. He went to the window five times and looked down into the street. He checked the lock on the door twice. The heavy air in the flat came up to his knees and stayed there all evening, and at about midnight, when a motorbike stopped outside and its engine idled for a minute and then moved on, it went up to his waist.
He took two of the pills at half past twelve and went to bed with the lamp on.
I stood.

I want to tell you what that’s like, because you’d fidget. You’d shift your weight. Your heart would get loud and you’d be sure he could hear it. You’d need to swallow and be afraid of the sound of swallowing. Your nose would itch, your leg would cramp, and you’d think of a hundred ways it could go wrong. That would make your legs weak and your breath short, and then you’d make a noise. Fear is noisy. People think it is silent, but it isn’t. It creaks. It sweats and swallows and coughs and shifts.

My heart went at sixty-two beats a minute, and I know that because I counted it, for something to do. My breathing was slow and full and soundless. I stood with my weight on both feet, and when a leg grew tired I moved the weight onto the other by a centimetre at a time, over a minute, the way the ground of Pozzuoli goes up. I looked at his shirts. One was blue with a white collar, and a button was missing from its left cuff. I looked at his face, asleep in the lamplight, his mouth open. He had a small scar on his chin, white, the kind you get falling off a bicycle at eight years old. I didn’t think about anything at all. I was a piece of furniture in a wardrobe.
I stood for nine hours.
At four o’clock in the morning, which is the hour when sleep is deepest and the most people die, I opened the door of the wardrobe and came out.
There was a second pillow on the bed beside him, on the side where nobody slept. I picked it up.
In the Held, we don’t waste a death. We use the kind that teaches. The cave teaches that breath is a gift, so we take it back the way it was given.
I put the pillow over his face and leaned on it with both forearms and all of my weight.
He woke up.

I’ll tell you only this much, and you can take it as a gift, because it’s all I have to give him: he wasn’t afraid for long. He was afraid for about ninety seconds, which is the most anyone can be afraid. The heavy air came off him so fast and so thick that it filled the bed, then the room to the height of the mattress, then the windowsill, then my chest. For a moment I was standing in his fear up to my shoulders, a whole room drowned in it, the lamp shining through it the way a lamp shines through water. His hands came up and found my wrists and pulled. He was strong. People are, at the end. I didn’t move. His heels drummed on the mattress, and his whole body arched up off the bed like a bridge, and then it came down, slowly, the way the ground at Pozzuoli comes down, and was still.
When the heavy air drained out of the room it went out under the door and down the stairwell like water going down a drain. I could hear it, almost.

I put the pillow back on the other side of the bed, plumped it, and turned it so the side that had been on his face was underneath. I closed his mouth. I took his notebooks and his laptop and his phone, put them in a shopping bag, and left the sleeping pills where they were. Men of forty-four don’t die in their sleep very often. But they do, in a city this size, about once a week. The doctor writes heart, because heart is always partly true.
I turned off his lamp. He’d been afraid of the dark, and he wasn’t now.

Then I let myself out and walked down the hill. The funicular doesn’t run at that hour, so I took the long stairs that go down through the gardens, a thousand steps, with the whole bay below me going grey and then pink as the sun came up behind Vesuvius.
That was the journalist. I’ve told you all of it.
There are debts in the Register that I’ll tell you about the way I told you that one, and there are some I won’t tell you about at all. You’ll get used to that.
6. Two White Stones
The Keeper is never wrong about air.
The headaches started after the swarm.

They weren’t bad. I’d tell you if they were. They sat behind my eyes in the mornings like a thumb pressing, and went away by noon. I mentioned them to Ferrante the way you’d mention that the van was pulling to the left, and he went quiet and still, the way he does when he’s afraid. The heavy air came up round his good shoes, a centimetre of it, the first I’d seen on him in a year.
“You’ll have a scan,” he said.

A person with no name can’t have a scan. So I borrowed one. The notary has a daughter who is thirty-three and lives in London and is real on paper in every way that I am not. For one Tuesday morning in March I was her. I carried her card and her doctor’s number, and a letter from the clinic of the woman who comes up the stairs on Sundays.

The hospital was the Cardarelli [kar-dah-REL-lee], the biggest in the south of Italy: a city of tired yellow buildings on the hill above the Vomero, with its own streets and bus stops, and a chapel, and cats. I sat in a corridor for two hours under a sign that said not to use mobile telephones, among a hundred people who were using them. Everybody in that corridor was standing in heavy air to the shin. Hospitals are like that. A small girl with a bandage over one eye was sitting in it up to her shoulders, on her mother’s lap, quite still.

They put me into a machine like a white tunnel that knocks and hums while it takes photographs of the inside of your head in slices, like a loaf. I lay inside it for twenty-five minutes and nearly fell asleep. It’s the most restful place I’d ever been. Nobody can reach you in there.

Afterwards they took me to a small office with a window that looked at a wall, and a neurologist came in. He was a doctor of the brain, about forty-five, with a soft beard going grey and good shoes and a wedding ring he turned with his thumb. He sat down and looked at me, and then at the screen of his computer, and then back at me. There was something on his face I had seen before on the faces of people who find things: a coin in a field, a ring in the sand.
“You don’t have anything bad,” he said first. “I want to say that first. No tumour. No bleeding. Nothing growing. The headaches are probably tension. Or coffee. How much coffee do you drink?”
“Some.”
“Have less.” He turned the screen to face me. “But there’s something else. It’s not dangerous. I’ve only ever seen it in books.”

It was a grey picture of a brain, sliced flat across, as if someone had cut a head through at the level of the eyes and looked down at the cut face. It was like a walnut in its shell, in two halves, folded and grey and full of shapes. And deep inside, one on each side, roughly behind where the temples would be, there were two small white marks, each about the size and shape of an almond, as white as chalk, white as teeth.
“Those,” he said.
“What are they?”
“They’re you,” he said. “They should be grey, like the rest. They’re stone.”
He told me plainly, and I’ve kept his words as far as I can, because they were good ones.

There is a part of the brain, deep down, one on each side, called the amygdala [ah-MIG-dah-lah]. That’s the Greek word for an almond, because that’s the shape. It’s very old. Lizards have something like it, and so do birds. It works like a watchman. Everything you see and hear and smell passes by it first, before you even know you’ve seen it, and the watchman looks at each thing and asks one question: is this going to hurt me? If the answer is yes, the watchman pulls a cord, and the whole body goes off like a fire bell. The heart jumps. The breath goes high. The blood leaves the skin and goes to the legs, ready to run. The eyes open wide. You haven’t decided anything yet, and you’re already afraid. That’s what fear is, he said. Not a thought. A watchman pulling a cord.
“Yours are calcified,” he said. “Turned to calcium. Bone, more or less. Both of them. Completely.”
“Since when?”

“Probably since you were very small. It happens slowly, in childhood. There’s a disease. It’s very rare. It’s called Urbach-Wiethe [OOR-bahk VEE-teh], after the two doctors in Vienna who first wrote it down in 1929. One looked at skin and the other at throats. That’s how they found it. The skin and the voice.”
He asked if he could look at my eyelids. I let him. He bent close with a small light, and I could smell his coffee and his soap.

“Yes,” he said softly. “There. You see?” He gave me a little mirror from his drawer. Along the edge of each eyelid, where the lashes grow, there was a row of tiny pale bumps, like a string of very small pearls. I’d had them all my life. I thought everyone did.
“And your voice,” he said. “It’s always been like that?”
My voice is low and rough. It sounds like a woman who’s smoked for forty years and shouted in a market. I have never smoked. I have never shouted.
“Always,” I said.

“It’s the same thing,” he said. “There’s a gene. One single gene, called ECM1. It’s a recipe the body uses for building a kind of glue in the skin and the throat and other places. If you get a broken copy of it from your father and another broken copy from your mother, the glue is wrong, and it builds up where it shouldn’t: in the voice box, so the voice is hoarse; in the eyelids, as the little pearls; and sometimes, in some people, in the brain, in exactly those two places. Nobody quite knows why there. There have only been a few hundred cases ever written down. There’s a valley in South Africa where it’s less rare, because the families there are all descended from a few settlers who married each other, and so the broken copies stayed together. Other than that, it’s one in millions.”
“What does it do,” I said, “to have stones there?”
He looked at me for a long moment, turning his ring.

“There’s a woman in America,” he said. “The doctors call her S.M., so that nobody knows her name. She has what you have. They’ve studied her for more than thirty years, at a university in Iowa. They took her to a shop that sells snakes and she picked them up, big ones, and had to be stopped from touching the dangerous ones, because she wanted to. Curious. They took her to a haunted house, the kind with actors who jump out at you in masks. She frightened one of the actors by poking him in the head, to see what the mask was made of. She stands too close to strangers. She doesn’t see danger in faces.”
“Is that all?”

“No.” He hesitated. “She was walking through a park at night, once, alone, and a man pulled her onto a bench and held a knife to her throat. She wasn’t afraid. She told him calmly that if he was going to kill her, he’d have to get past God’s angels first. He let her go. She walked home. The next night she walked through the same park.”
I laughed.

It came out of me before I could stop it, low and rough, like a dog barking once. The neurologist jumped. The heavy air came up round his good shoes and lay there, a pale little pool on the hospital lino, not much, about to the ankle.

I’m sorry. I couldn’t help it. For thirty-four years I’d been a thing that nobody had a word for. The Held had a word, but it was their word. It was a word for what I was for, not what I was. And here, in a hospital office with a window looking at a wall, it turned out that I had a name with two surnames, like a firm of lawyers. I was in books. There was a woman in a place called Iowa who had walked through the same park the next night. I’d have liked to meet her. I think we’d have sat on a bench and said nothing at all, for hours, quite happily.
“I’m sorry,” said the neurologist. He’d misunderstood. He thought I was upset.
“No, it’s funny,” I said. “It’s very funny. Go on.”
He looked at me for a while longer. He’d stopped turning the ring.

“There’s one more thing they found,” he said. “With S.M. It was in 2013. It surprised everyone. It changed what people believed about fear.” He wet his lips. “There’s a test we can do. It’s safe. It takes a minute. You breathe in once, from a mask. We have the equipment here, for the lungs.” He was trying not to look eager, and he was looking eager. “Would you let me? It would mean a great deal. Not for a paper. Your name is safe. For me.”
He meant the notary’s daughter’s name. He didn’t know he was asking someone with no name at all.
“What do I breathe?” I said.
“Carbon dioxide,” he said. “A lot of it, all at once. Thirty-five parts in every hundred.”
I knew exactly what carbon dioxide was. I’d been breathing it every Sunday of my life.
“All right,” I said.
7. Thirty-Five Percent
The hand on your neck is the only hand.

He did it on the Thursday, in a room in the basement with no windows. It had a narrow bed, a machine with a screen that drew green lines, a steel cylinder of gas on a little trolley with a dial on top, and a mask. The mask was clear plastic, shaped to go over the nose and mouth, with a soft rubber edge. It was attached by a tube to a bag the size of a football.

Two other people were in the room: a nurse who stuck little cold pads to my chest to read my heart, and a young doctor with a clipboard to write things down. Both of them were standing in heavy air to the shin. People are always a little afraid of an experiment, even when it isn’t happening to them.

“It’s one breath,” said the neurologist. “Breathe out all the way first, empty, then put the mask on and breathe in as deep as you can, everything you have, and hold it for a moment, and then take the mask off and breathe normally. That’s all. Some people find it unpleasant. It only lasts a minute or two. You can stop whenever you want.”
He told me, while the nurse fixed the pads, what had happened in Iowa in 2013.

The scientists had thought they knew the answer before they started. They believed the watchman, the almond, was what made a person afraid of not breathing too. If you breathe in a lot of carbon dioxide, your blood turns a little bit sour, a little bit acid, and they thought that was something the almond felt and raised the alarm for. So they expected S.M. to breathe in the gas and feel nothing, the way she felt nothing with a knife at her throat. They tested her, and two other women who had the same stones, and twelve ordinary people.

“Before the test,” he said, “the ordinary people were nervous. Their hearts went up while they waited. They sweated. The three women weren’t nervous at all. They sat there. They didn’t know what nervous was.”
“And then?”

“And then all three of them panicked,” he said. “Worse than the ordinary people. Much worse. S.M. tried to tear the mask off. She said afterwards she’d felt panic, mostly, because she didn’t know what the hell was happening. It was the first time she’d been afraid since she was a child. One of the other women called it fear. She’d never used the word before about herself. All three of them had never had a panic attack in their lives. They didn’t know what it was.”
He looked at me with his soft, grey-bearded, curious face.

“There are two roads into fear,” he said. “That’s what they think now. One comes in from outside, through the eyes and the ears, past the watchman. The snake, the knife, the man in the mask. Yours is closed. The other comes up from inside the body, from the blood and the lungs, down at the back of the brain, where the oldest parts are. That’s the road for I can’t breathe. It doesn’t go past the watchman at all. And it looks as if the watchman, when it’s working, holds that second road a little bit shut, to keep us calm. So when the watchman’s gone…”
“The road’s wide open,” I said.
“Yes.”
“Louder than for anyone else.”
“Yes.” He held up the mask. “We’ll see.”

I lay back on the narrow bed. The nurse turned the dial on the cylinder, and the bag filled up and went tight and round. I breathed out, all the way, until my lungs were flat and empty, and I put the mask over my nose and my mouth, and I breathed in.
It tasted of battery.
I knew it at once. I know that taste the way you know your mother’s kitchen. The cold sour sting on the tongue and in the nose. The eyes watering.
Then it went down. All the way down, everything I had, as deep as he’d told me.
And it came.

You know what it was. I’ve told you already. I’ve told you the best I can. The alarm at the back of the head, old as fish, pressing its one button: now. The heart breaking into a run. The chest heaving for air that isn’t there. The lights at the edges of the eyes. The tunnel. Someone close on the left, a warmth, near as a mouth. The terror, total and pure, the bottom of the sea coming up through the floor of me.
All of it, the same. The same.

But there was no cave. I was on my back on a narrow bed in a hospital basement in the Arenella [ah-reh-NEL-lah], the hospital’s neighbourhood, with a plastic mask on my face, and a nurse was holding my wrist, and a young man with a clipboard was writing down the green lines. There was no dust and no warm stone, no dog with gold in its eyes, no bucket of cold water, no candle lying down on its side. And there was no hand on my neck.
And it was the same.

That’s what broke. Do you see? I was so frightened that my body was trying to climb off the bed, and the nurse was saying calm, calm, it’ll pass, it’s passing. But under the fright, in the middle of it, very small and very clear, like a coin at the bottom of a deep well, there was a thought. The thought was this:
I know this.
I know this feeling.
This is what I feel for him.

For twenty-eight years I’d lived a week that had one day in it. Six days of nothing, and then the hand, and the dark, and the terror. Then the lift, and the gift, and the cold water, and his voice saying there, there, good girl. Then the great flooding wave that I had always, always called love. Because it was the only thing I’d ever felt, and because he called it that, and because when it came it came with his face.

And now it was coming up through me on a hospital bed with nobody’s hand anywhere near me. It came from a cylinder of gas with a dial on top. It was exactly the same shape. Exactly the same size. Not like it. The same. The heart was the same and the tunnel was the same and the warmth on the left was the same.
It had never been him.

It was the gas. It had always been the gas. The love was what drowning feels like, when the one thing standing between you and the drowning is the hand on the back of your neck. The heart running, the lungs begging, and then the lift, the gift, the breath, there, there. Twenty-eight years of my body learning, every Sunday, that the terror ends when he decides, and that when he decides, there’s light. A body only has to learn that so many times before it can no longer tell the difference between the man and the air.
He hadn’t made me love him. He’d made me suffocate, and then he’d stood there while I did, so that he’d be the first thing I saw when I could breathe.
I tore the mask off.

The nurse said something. The young doctor stood up. The green line on the screen was going up and down like a child’s drawing of mountains. I was sitting up on the bed with my knees drawn up and my arms around them, breathing in great rough sobs of good air, and the tears were running down my face. It wasn’t crying. It was only the body letting go. It always does that, after.
The neurologist came and crouched in front of me, close, his face level with mine, kind and worried and fascinated all at once.
“It’s passing,” he said. “It’s all right. You’re all right. That was very strong. That’s what happened to them too. You’re all right now.”
I looked at him. The heavy air was up round his knees. He was afraid for me. That was decent of him.
“Can I ask you something?” I said. My voice was rougher than ever.
“Of course.”
“Is love supposed to feel like this?”
He didn’t understand. How could he? He looked at me with his mouth a little open, and then he did what doctors do when they hear something they don’t know how to answer: he wrote it down.

I signed nothing. I said thank you. I put on my coat, and walked up out of the basement and out of the Cardarelli and down the hill, past the cats and the bus stops and the chapel. I walked all the way, eighteen kilometres, through the tunnel in the hill and out into the Burning Fields, and it was dark by the time I reached Pozzuoli.
I didn’t go home. I went down to the harbour, to the seawall below the Rione Terra, and sat on it with my legs hanging over the black water.

Behind me in the dark, in a fenced-off square below the street, there are three tall marble columns standing up out of a sunken floor. They’re all that’s left of a Roman market hall, a round building where two thousand years ago people bought fish and meat and wine, with a fountain in the middle. For a long time people called it the Temple of Serapis [seh-RAH-pis], after an Egyptian god whose statue was found there, and the name has stuck.

If you look at those columns in daylight, about halfway up, there’s a wide band where the marble is full of small round holes, thousands of them, as if somebody had stood there for a year with a drill. The holes were made by a kind of shellfish that lives in the sea and bores into stone to make its home. It can only live underwater.

So for some long stretch of years, that floor where the Romans bought their fish went down, slowly, under the sea, deep enough for the water to cover the columns halfway up. The shellfish came and drilled their houses in the stone. Then the ground came back up, slowly, and lifted the whole market out of the sea again into the air, with the holes in it, and the shellfish died in their houses. Two hundred years ago a Scottish scientist put a picture of those three columns at the front of one of the most important books ever written about the earth. They were the proof that the ground is not solid, not fixed. It breathes. It goes under and comes back up, and the stone remembers.
I sat on the seawall all night and looked at the black water.

The Held say that fear is God taking breath back. They say that whoever gives it back is God. I’d always thought that was just something they said, the way people say God willing. But they meant it exactly. They had built a god out of a hole in the ground and an old man’s hand, and they’d built it inside me.

I didn’t feel betrayed. I want to be careful here, because you’ll want me to feel that, and I didn’t. I don’t have the part for it, I think. I didn’t feel angry, and I didn’t feel sad. I felt what you’d feel if you’d lived your whole life in a house and then, one night, gone down to the cellar and found the wires. Oh. So that’s what the light was.

But something did happen, sitting there. It was small. I’ll tell you exactly what it was, because I’ve never had a thing like it before or since, and because everything that comes after in this story grows out of it, the way a whole tree grows out of a seed you could lose under a fingernail.
It was a question. Just one.

For twenty-eight years I’d done what the hand wanted. I’d gone into rooms and come out of them, and stood in wardrobes, and walked down a thousand steps at dawn. I’d never once asked why, any more than the cleaver asks why it is lifted. I’d never had a reason to ask. I’d had the hand.

Now I sat on the seawall above the breathing ground, with the stones in my head and the Roman columns behind me in the dark, and the sea going in and out below my feet, and for the first time in my life I asked myself something.
Have I ever chosen anything?
