The tide went out. The fishing boats came in. A little after five the sky went grey over Vesuvius, and then pink. The first swarm of the morning came through the ground under the harbour, three small shocks, and the water in the harbour shivered like the skin of a horse.
I didn’t know the answer. That was new too.

On Sunday I went to the cave as usual. I knelt down on the warm stone with the yellow dog beside me, and his hand came down on my neck, warm and heavy, and my face went down into the dark. I breathed what was there, and I was lifted, and I was given the gift, and he said there, there, good girl.
And I said, “I love you.”
I said it well. I said it exactly as I’d said it every Sunday for twenty-eight years. I don’t think anyone alive could have heard a difference.
That is something a person with no fear can do. I’m telling you now, early, so that later you can’t say I didn’t.
THE BOOK OF CHOOSING · I — 1656
Here the Keepers write down how each child was chosen,
each in his own hand, so that the one who comes after will
know that it has been done before, and that it was
necessary.
Centuries ago I chose a child.

It was the summer of the Year of Our Lord 1656, in the city of Naples, which then was one of the largest cities in Christendom, the Christian world, and belonged to the King of Spain. He ruled it from Madrid through a viceroy, a governor in his place, who lived in the great palace by the sea and was afraid of the people. He was right to be.

The plague came in the spring on a ship, or with soldiers. Nobody agrees. At first the viceroy said it was not the plague. He said it was a fever, nothing, that the doctors who said otherwise were making trouble, and he had one of them thrown in prison for saying the word. Then the people began to die in the streets, so many and so fast that there was no more saying what it was. Then the people, who needed someone to blame, decided that there were poisoners going about the city at night, men who smeared the doors and the holy-water stoups, the stone basins of blessed water by church doors, with a powder that brought the sickness. They found some, or said they did, and tore them to pieces in the squares. And still the plague came on.
I was a physician. I want you to understand what that meant, in that year. It meant that I knew nothing, and was paid for it.

We did not know what the plague was. We thought it was the air, a bad air that rose out of the earth, the dead, and the poor. We wore long coats of waxed cloth to the ground, and gloves, and over our faces a mask of leather with glass eyes and a long beak like a bird’s, and in the beak we packed herbs, rose petals and cloves and camphor, against the bad air. We walked through the city like great black herons. Children ran from us. They were right to.

By June the dead were five hundred a day. By July they were five thousand. They lay in the streets where they fell, in their own black blood, their armpits and groins swollen up in great purple lumps the size of eggs, the size of apples. The houses stank. The churches stank. The sea stank, because the dead were thrown into it from the harbour walls by the boatload, and the sea gave them back on the beaches. There were not enough priests to bury them and not enough ground to bury them in. So the carts came round, and the corpse-carriers, who were the lowest men in the city, convicts, beggars, men with nothing left to lose, threw the dead into the carts with long hooks and drove them out of the city and tipped them into the old quarries in the hill outside the walls. Into the Fontanelle, among others. Into the dark under the hill. By the end of it, the people of my city who had died were as many as the people who lived. Half the city, gone in a summer.
That is where I found him, in the Sanità, on a corpse cart.

He was about nine. He was one of the children of the wheel, an Esposito, from the Annunziata; I knew it by the little lead medal they hung on a cord round every foundling’s neck, to know them by. The nuns were dead or fled. The children of the wheel had been turned out into the streets, and most of them were dead too. This one had found work on the carts. They paid him in bread.
He was sitting on top of the dead.

He was sitting on top of the pile of the dead in the cart, cross-legged, as you might sit on a haystack, eating his bread, and he was singing. It was a song of the street, a rude one, about a priest and a washerwoman. When the cart stopped he slid down and took hold of a dead woman by her ankles, and pulled her to the edge, and the men with the hooks did the rest. Then he climbed back up and went on eating his bread.

Everyone else in that street had a cloth over their face and was walking fast, close to the wall, looking down. Grown men were weeping in doorways. A woman in a window was screaming a name over and over, one name, as if it were the only word left in the world. And this boy sat in the sun on the dead and ate and sang.
I stopped. I am a man of science, or I was. I stopped, and through the glass eyes of my bird’s mask I watched him.

I bought him from the carters for a coin. They were glad to see him go. He made them nervous, they said. He did not keep his distance from the bodies, and he did not say his prayers, and he laughed when the swollen ones burst.
I took him home. I washed him. I tested him.
I put a knife to his throat, a good knife, and pressed until the skin dented. He did not draw back. He looked down along his nose at the blade with great interest and asked if he could hold it.

I held a candle near his hand. He watched the flame. He did not pull his hand away until it burned, and then he pulled it back the way you pull your hand from a wet wall: without hurry, surprised, curious. He had no fear of the fire before it touched him. Only after.

I shut him in a room for a night with a man who was dying of the plague, raving, black-faced, bleeding from the mouth. In the morning I opened the door. The man was dead, and the boy was asleep on the floor beside him with his head on the dead man’s arm.
And then I found out what he was for.

I was a physician to the rich. The rich, in that summer, did what the rich do: they fled. They went up to their villas in the hills and shut the gates. Some of them did not go fast enough. The sickness went with them and they lay dying in their great empty houses on the hill, and their servants ran away, and their sons and nephews and cousins waited at the bottom of the hill, outside the gates, too afraid to go in.

Some of the dying had made their wills. And some of the dying, as they lay there with their swollen groins and their black tongues, alone, abandoned, were beginning to talk of changing them, of leaving it all to the Church, or to the one servant who stayed, or to a woman nobody knew about.
I knew the nephews. The nephews knew me.

Nobody would go into those houses. Not the priests, not the servants, not the soldiers, not I. Only one person in all of Naples would walk up that hill, past the shut gate, into the empty house that stank of the dead, and climb the stairs, and go into the room where the old man lay muttering about his will, and take the pillow from under his head.
He did it without any hesitation at all. With curiosity. He watched them as they died, the way a boy watches a beetle on its back.
The nephews paid me in gold. I gave the boy bread and a bed and a new shirt, and he was very pleased with the shirt.
That autumn, as the plague began to slacken, I saw the boy look at me.

It was in my own kitchen, at night. I was tired and had drunk too much wine and fallen asleep in my chair by the fire. I woke up and he was sitting on the floor in front of me, cross-legged, as he had sat on the dead in the cart. He was looking at me with the same face. Interested. Not wicked, not cruel. Interested, the way he had looked at the knife, and at the fire, and at the old men on the hill.
I understood then what I had brought into my house.

I had made a door. I had opened a door in the world through which this child walked to do the thing that nobody else could do. But a door opens both ways, and a boy with no fear has no reason to stop at the threshold of any room. Not even mine.

Every lock on earth is made of fear. The law is fear, and the Church is fear, and the King’s soldiers, and the gallows, and God’s own hell. They are all of them a single key that turns in a single lock that is in every one of us. In this boy, there was no lock. There was nothing in him that any key could turn.
I did not sleep that night. I sat up and thought.

As a student, years before the plague, I had gone out with the other young doctors to the lake at Agnano, to see a thing every visitor to Naples was taken to see: the dog in the cave. I had watched the dog go stiff and roll its eyes in the poisoned air. I had watched it thrown into the lake and come up coughing. I had written down in my notebook, in my student’s Latin, that the bad air in the cave appeared to strike at life itself without any wound. The animal went down in terror though nothing touched it.
Though nothing touched it.

In the morning I took the boy to Agnano. It was a long morning’s walk, west, through the old Roman tunnel under the hill. The lake was very blue and still, with the reeds standing up at the edges and the steam coming off the hot springs on the shore. The keeper of the cave was dead of the plague, and his dog was gone, and there was no one there at all.
I took the boy into the passage, five steps. I told him to kneel. He knelt, smiling. He thought it was a game.
I put my hand on the back of his neck and pushed his face down into the bad air, and I held it there.
And I saw it. I saw it go into him.

He struggled. He had never struggled in his life, and he struggled. He fought, he bucked like a calf under my hand, he clawed at the stone, and his eyes, when I could see them, were wide, wide, white all the way round. He was making a sound I had never heard from him, a high thin sound like a kettle. He was afraid. For the first time in his life, and perhaps, I thought, the first time in all the history of his soul, he was afraid.

I counted. I did not know how long was too long. I counted to forty, my heart going nearly as fast as his. Then I lifted him out by the neck into the good air and carried him out of the cave into the light, and threw him, as I had seen the dog thrown, into the cold blue lake.
He came up coughing and choking and spitting, and thrashed in the reeds, and found his feet, and stood up to his waist in the water, and breathed.
And he looked at me.

I have spent my whole life since then looking for a word for the way he looked at me. He looked at me the way a man in a painting looks at the face of God when the heavens open. The way the drowning look at the rope.
I waded in and took him in my arms, wet as he was, and held him, and said into his wet hair the first thing that came into my head, which was:
“There. There. Good boy. I love you.”
And he said, through his chattering teeth, “I love you.”

That was the first Sunday. I had not planned it as a Sunday. It was a Thursday, in fact. But we went back on the Sunday after, after Mass, and on the Sunday after that, and I have kept every Sunday since.

On the walk home, that first night, he walked so close to me that his shoulder bumped my hip with every step. He held on to my coat. I had found the lock. It was not in his heart, where the rest of us keep ours. It was in his lungs.
I wrote the words down that night, and they have not been changed since: God gave breath first. Fear is God taking it back. Whoever gives it back is God.
I learned two things in the year that followed, and I set them down here for the one who comes after.

The first is that he learned to cry. He did not cry on that first Sunday, only coughed and shook. On the second Sunday, when I lifted him out, he wept and clung to me, and I was moved almost past bearing. He learned to cry on the second Sunday. I wrote that in the margin of my book and underlined it, because I was so proud. I did not ask myself, then, where he had learned. I think now I should have.
The second is that he was not the only one.

There was a girl in the next street to the one where I had found him, in the Sanità. She was about eleven, a washerwoman’s daughter. People told me about her: how she had gone into the plague houses for loot when the families were dead, how she had cut the rings off swollen fingers with a kitchen knife, and how she had laughed at the poisoner they tore apart in the square. I went to look at her. She stood in the door of her dead mother’s house, in the stench, with a pile of stolen silver behind her, and looked back at me without blinking. The same look. The same nothing behind it.
I thought for a long time about what a city would be if there were two of them in it. If one of them were held, and one of them were loose.
Then I sent my boy.
He came back in the morning and ate his bread and asked for more. He had a little cut on his hand, from her teeth.
I opened my book, the one in which I had begun to write down his Sundays, the seconds of each one, and next to the girl’s name I drew a small circle.
That is how it began. With the plague, and greed, and a hole in the ground. With one held and one not held, and a circle.
Whoever comes after me will understand why.
II. THE CAVE
8. Before Words
Do not choose a child who weeps at the wheel. Choose the one who is quiet in the rain.
I was six the first time.

That’s late. I know that now. Some of the others went under at four. Ferrante waited for me because, he told me afterwards, I had to be old enough to remember it and young enough not to have words for it yet. Words get in the way, he said. A child with words will try to explain a thing to herself, and a thing that has been explained can be argued with. He wanted the cave to go into me underneath the words, where nothing argues.

He got what he wanted. I’m going to try now to put words on it for the first time, thirty-four years old, sitting in my kitchen in the Rione Terra, with the ground going up under my chair at one and a half centimetres a month. Forgive me if they come out wrong. They’ve never been used.

I grew up with the nurse who found me on the steps. She had a flat in the Sanità, on the fourth floor of a palace that had once belonged to a duke and now belonged to eleven families and a great many pigeons. There was a courtyard with a dry fountain in it, a staircase wide enough for a carriage, and a smell of drains and frying. Her flat was two rooms. I slept on a folding bed in the kitchen under a picture of Saint Lucy, who holds her own eyes on a plate.

The nurse fed me, washed me and taught me to say please. She didn’t love me, and she didn’t pretend to. I think she was afraid of me. Even then, as far back as I can remember, she stood in the heavy air at the ankles when she bent over my bed at night. She’d watched me put my hand flat on the hot iron at two, to see. She’d watched me walk off the edge of the kitchen table at three, straight out into the air, because I wanted to know where the floor went. She’d watched me stand at the open window on the fourth floor with my toes over the sill and look down at the courtyard, not leaning back, not leaning forward, just interested. She’d pulled me in by my dress so hard that it tore, and slapped me. I didn’t cry. I asked her why her hand was shaking.

She kept a little book in the kitchen drawer, with a pencil tied to it by a string. Once a month a man came and read it. I know now what it was. It was the first page of my Register. She was writing down what I didn’t do.

The man who came once a month was tall and old even then, with white hair combed straight back. He brought sugared almonds. He sat on the nurse’s one good chair with his big hands on his knees and looked at me, for a long time, in the kindest way anyone has ever looked at me. Then he went away again.
On the morning of my sixth birthday he came on a Sunday, in a white van that smelled of fennel.

I remember the drive. Most of it. The tunnel under the hill with the orange lights going over the windscreen one after another, like the beads of a rosary going through fingers. Coming out the other side into a light that was the same light and wasn’t. Padre Pio on the dashboard with his gloves on, to hide the holes in his hands. The bag of almonds in my lap. The racecourse, empty and green, where the lake had been. The old spa with its broken windows and a fig tree growing out of the roof.
The tap on the wall. The two steel buckets filling, loud, then quieter, then quiet.
“The lake was drained in 1870,” he said, “so we carry the lake.”

I didn’t know what a lake was. I’d never been out of the Sanità. I’d seen the sea from the top of the steps below Capodimonte [kah-poh-dee-MON-teh], the hill and palace above the Sanità, as a blue line between buildings, but I didn’t know it was water. I thought it was the edge of the world, painted.
The gate. The key. The dust, grey and light, puffing up round my sandals. And the dog.

It was lying in the sun at the mouth of the cave, yellow as straw, with its torn left ear. It got up when we came and wagged the back half of its body and put its nose into Ferrante’s hand. Then it came to me and pushed its nose into my hand too, cold and wet, and looked up at me with gold in its brown eyes.

It was the first animal I’d ever touched that didn’t move away from me. The pigeons in the courtyard moved away from me. The cats moved away from me. Dogs in the street put their tails down and showed their teeth when I came near, or crossed the road. I didn’t know why. I know now. Animals can smell fear, and they can smell the lack of it, and the lack of it is worse. A person with no fear is a person with nothing that stops her. Animals know what that means.
This dog didn’t move away. It leaned its whole weight against my legs.
Ferrante lit the candle and put it on the floor, and we watched it lie down and go out. The thread of grey smoke lay flat on top of the nothing.
“What’s that?” I said.
“That,” he said, “is God’s breath, going back to Him.”

I didn’t understand, and I didn’t need to. He took my shoes off for me, one and then the other, and put them side by side by the gate. He took me by the hand and walked me into the dark. The stone was warm under my feet like an animal’s back. Five metres in, where the roof came down, he showed me how to kneel. He knelt himself first, slowly, his knees cracking, to show me: back straight, then forward, hands flat on the warm ground on either side, head bowed.
“Like that,” he said. “Like saying prayers.”
I knelt like that. He got up. The dog lay down beside me in the dark.
He put his hand on the back of my neck.
I’ve told you what happens. I’ve told you twice. I won’t tell you a third time. I’ll tell you what was different the first time, because there was one thing.
The first time, I didn’t know it would end.

When you’re six and you’re terrified for the first time in your life, you don’t know there’s an after. You don’t know the thing has edges. I didn’t know the word afraid. I’d never needed it. I’d watched other people be it, the way you’d watch other people speak Chinese. So when it came up through me in the dark, all of it at once, the whole bottom of the sea, I didn’t think I am afraid. I didn’t think anything. I was it. There wasn’t a me that was having it. There was only it.

I think that’s what Ferrante meant about words. If I’d had the word, I’d have had somewhere to stand while it happened. I didn’t. It went right through me, into the floor of everything, and it built a room there, and it moved in.
Then the hand lifted. The water came down, cold, and I was in the light at the top of the cave, choking.
And there was his face.

He was kneeling in front of me now, in the good air, his face level with mine, very close, with his big hands holding my face on both sides. Behind him the doorway of the cave was a square of white sunlight, so bright I couldn’t look at it, so his face was all there was. A long mild face, like a horse. Kind eyes, wet. White hair.
The most beautiful thing I had ever seen. The only thing.
“There,” he said. “There. Good girl. There.”

I didn’t cry. I didn’t say anything. I couldn’t. I just looked at him and breathed, and breathed, and breathed, and every breath was the gift. And he was in every one of them, the way the sun is in every leaf.

He held me for a long time. Then he stood up, and took a book out of his coat pocket, and a fountain pen, and wrote in the book with brown ink. I watched him. I couldn’t read yet, but I could read numbers, because the nurse had taught me numbers so that I could count pills.
He’d written my name, Domenica, the first time I’d seen it written. Next to it he’d written 22.
Twenty-two seconds. That’s all it was. Twenty-two seconds of my life, and it’s the longest thing that ever happened to me.
Above my name on the page were other names, with other numbers. I couldn’t read them. One of them had a little circle drawn next to it, in the same brown ink, very neat. I pointed at it.
He closed the book. Not quickly. He closed it the way he does everything, gently, and put it back in his coat.
“Next Sunday,” he said.

On the way home, through the orange tunnel, I held on to the sleeve of his coat with both hands. I wouldn’t let go, not even to eat the almonds. He drove with one hand so I could keep hold of the other arm.

That was the first thing I ever wanted. I want you to understand that, because it’s what all of the rest of this is built on. Before that Sunday I had never wanted anything, not a toy, not a sweet, not my mother. Wanting is a kind of fear. It’s the fear of not having. I didn’t have it.
After that Sunday I wanted one thing. I wanted to go back.
9. The Rules of the Held
There is only ever one leash.
I never went to school.

A child with no papers can’t. A school wants a birth certificate and a doctor’s card and a tax number for the family, and it wants to know where you live. So the Held taught me at their kitchen tables instead, a different table every day of the week, all over the city. It was like being passed round a family at a wedding.

On Mondays the notary taught me letters and numbers, in a flat in Chiaia full of clocks. She stood in the heavy air to the ankle the whole time, small and steady, and she never once touched me, not even to move my hand on the pencil. On Tuesdays the pharmacist taught me chemistry in the back of his shop, among the painted jars: what kills, how fast, how much, and how a doctor would find it. I was a good pupil. On Wednesdays the priest taught me the catechism, the questions and answers of the faith that children learn by heart, and the saints, and Latin, in the sacristy, the room behind the altar where the priest keeps his robes, of his church in the Vomero, where it smelled of old incense and dust. He was in the heavy air to his thighs the whole time. He sweated. I liked the saints. They were the only people in the books who didn’t seem to be afraid of anything either, and everybody loved them for it. I couldn’t see why they got loved and I got watched. The priest said it was because they were afraid of God. I said, What does that feel like? He didn’t answer. He went and stood by the window.

On Thursdays the banker taught me money. On Fridays the geneticist taught me the body: bones, blood, the heart, the lungs. She drew it all on big sheets of paper with coloured pens, and every Friday she drew the brain last. She always drew two almonds deep inside it, and she always coloured them in white. She never said why. I thought it was just how brains were.
Saturdays I spent with the nurse, who taught me to cook. She was good. Her ragù was famous in the building. She showed me the potato trick for too much salt.
And Sundays.
On Sundays, in those years, I wasn’t the only child at the cave.

The Held keep more than one at a time. They find them where they can, one every few years, in the hospitals and at the baby hatches and in the files that the geneticist reads, and they forge them all, and they keep the best. There were six of us that I knew, in those first years. We didn’t go to the cave together, never more than two at a time, and we weren’t allowed to talk to each other much. But we saw each other, coming and going, at the gate, by the van. And because of what we were, we knew each other at once, the way a dog knows another dog across a whole square.

The one I remember best was a boy called Saverio [sah-VEH-ryoh]. That wasn’t his name later. He was twelve when I was six, tall and bony, with a shaved head and big ears and very light eyes, almost white. He’d been found in Salerno. He came on Sundays with a woman from the Held who drove a red car. He would come out of the cave dripping, and stand in the sun with his hands on his knees, breathing the gift, and then he would look at me, and I would look at him.
He was the first person I ever saw who stood in no heavy air.

Nothing. Dry to the soles of his shoes. Everyone else I’d ever looked at, every single person in my whole life, had a little of it round their feet, at least: the shimmer on the floor, the faint pool. Saverio had none. Standing next to him was like standing next to a mirror. I’d never seen myself before.

One Sunday when nobody was looking he took a knife out of his pocket, a little folding knife with a horn handle. He showed me how to throw it at the trunk of the fig tree that grew out of the roof of the old spa. He threw it nine times and it went in nine times. Then he gave it to me, and I threw it, and it bounced off and fell in the dust, and he laughed. Then I threw it again, and again, and I didn’t stop until it went in. It took me an hour. He sat and watched the whole time and didn’t get bored. Nobody else in the world would have sat and watched a six-year-old throw a knife at a tree for an hour. The woman with the red car would have stopped me. Ferrante would have stopped me. The nurse would have screamed. Saverio just watched, with his white eyes, interested.
When it went in he nodded. That was all. One nod.
Remember that nod. I’ll give it back to you later.

There was a girl a little older than me, with red shoes, who came for two years and then didn’t come any more. There was a little boy from the hospital in Caserta [kah-ZEHR-tah], north of the city, who came for one summer. There was a pair of twins from somewhere in the north, a boy and a girl, who came only twice and screamed so much the first time that Ferrante had to hold them both, one in each hand.
“Where’s the girl with the red shoes?” I asked him once, in the van.
“Placed,” he said.
“Where?”
“Where she’s needed.”
I didn’t ask again. I didn’t care very much. She’d never thrown a knife with me.
The members said the five rules at the gathering. The children learned seven. Ferrante taught them to me in the van, a rule a month, the way the nurse taught me my numbers.
Six. Sunday is not a day. It is a depth.

I liked that one. I didn’t understand it, and I liked it. I said it to myself on the other six days, in the notary’s flat full of clocks, in the pharmacy among the poisons: it is a depth. I’d whisper it under my breath like the priest whispered his prayers, and feel my heart, for a second, remember running.
The seventh rule I never heard properly.

I was nine. It was a Sunday in winter, and we were in the van, coming back through the tunnel. He’d been teaching me rule seven, and he’d said the first part of it. Then the van went over a metal plate in the road with a great bang, and there was a long scream of brakes from a lorry somewhere behind us in the tunnel, and a horn. Everybody in the tunnel braked at once, and the bang and the horns went on and on, echoing off the orange walls.
When it was quiet again he’d finished. I’d only heard There is only ever one. One what, I didn’t hear.
“One what?” I said.
He looked at me in the mirror for a long time.
“You’ll learn the rest,” he said, “when you need it.”

Saverio went into the army at eighteen. I was twelve. He came to the cave one last time in a uniform, with his hair even shorter, and stood in the sun after the gift with his hands on his knees. Then he looked across the dust at me, and I looked back at him across the dust, two dry people in a world full of water.
Then he got into the red car and was gone. I didn’t see him again for twenty-two years.
That was the year I paid my first debt. I’ll come to that. First I have to tell you about the dog.
10. The Dog
The dog was there before us. It will be there after. We do not ask it questions.
In the nurse’s kitchen drawer, under the little book with the pencil tied to it, there was a photograph.

I found it after she died. She died when I was nineteen, of a stroke, in the dry fountain in the courtyard. She’d gone down to get the post and fallen into the fountain, and no one found her for an hour. I went through her drawers before the Held came to clear the flat. There wasn’t much: rosaries, receipts, a hundred and forty euros in a biscuit tin, and a photograph from the instant camera she had, the kind that pushes out a square photograph with a white edge, which goes from grey to colour while you hold it in your hand.

It was the cave. Someone had taken it on my first Sunday, from the gate, and given it to her. In it a little girl in a yellow dress was standing at the mouth of the cave, barefoot, holding the hand of a tall old man with white hair, and beside the little girl was a yellow dog, its tail curled up over its back and its left ear torn.
On the back, in the nurse’s handwriting: D., the first Sunday. April 1998.
I took it to the cave the next Sunday. I knelt down in the dust at the gate, with the dog lying in the sun in front of me, and I held the photograph up next to it.

Same dog. The same torn ear, torn in the same place, in the same shape, like a bite taken out of a biscuit. The same white mark on its chest like a thumbprint. The same curl to its tail. The same gold in its eyes. It wasn’t a dog that looked like that dog. It was the dog. Thirteen years on, and it wasn’t one day older. There was no white round its muzzle. It didn’t stiffen in the back legs when it got up. It got up as it always did, in one fluid movement, like water standing up.

Dogs live for twelve years. Fourteen, if they’re lucky and small. In the old pictures of the Cave of the Dog, like the one Ferrante has framed on his office wall, there’s a dog: in the one from 1706, and in a painting from the eighteen-hundreds that hangs in a museum in the city, and in a print from a travel book that an Englishman wrote in 1820, the dog being dragged into the dark by a man in a hat. I’ve looked at them all. I’ve looked at them with a magnifying glass. In two of them you can see that the dog’s tail is curled up over its back. In one, the one from 1706, its left ear is torn.
I asked Ferrante about it once.
“The dog was there before us,” he said. “It will be there after us. We don’t ask it questions.”
So I don’t. You can.
I’ll tell you what I do know, because it’s the truest thing I know about the cave.

Every Sunday for twenty-eight years, that dog has lain down beside me in the gas while I went under. It never gets lifted. Nobody holds it down. It lies down in the poison by itself, on its side, with its whole head under, its nose in the place where the air ends, and it breathes there, slowly, with its gold eyes open, watching me. When I’m lifted it gets up, and shakes itself, and walks out into the sun, and lies down by the gate, and closes its eyes. It does this as if the gas were grass.

When I was small I thought it was there to keep me company. Then, when I was older, I thought it was there to show me what I was: an animal in a cave, held down, like the dogs of the Grand Tour. When I was older still, I thought it was there to remind Ferrante. That he wasn’t the first. That this hole in the ground was older than him and older than the Held, and had been killing dogs for the amusement of men since before anyone wrote it down.
Lately I’ve thought something else. I’ve thought it was the first child.

The first one who was ever held down in that cave and lifted out, by a guide in a hat, for a coin. Before the Held. Before any of it. A dog who learned, the way I learned, that the terror ends when the hand decides. Who learned it so well, as the story of the old show dog says, that it would faint at the sight of a tourist coming. And who then, somehow, at some point, stopped needing the hand. It went under by itself. It lay down in the poison as though it were home. It learned that the drowning was the only place it was ever all the way alive, and it moved in.
I don’t know if that’s true. I know that it’s what I’d do, if I were a dog. If I had nowhere else to go.

On the Sunday after the hospital, after the mask and the seawall and the question, I went to the cave early. I went before Ferrante, on the first bus to Agnano. I sat in the dust by the gate with the dog, because I wanted to be near the place without the hand for a while, to see what it was without him. He’d given me a key years ago, for emergencies. I’d never used it.
I unlocked the gate and went in a little way, standing, my head up in the good air. I didn’t kneel. I looked down at the floor of the passage, where the pool would be lying, invisible, on the dust.

There was something in the dust, half buried, just where the floor drops a little at the end of the passage. Something pink. I crouched, keeping my head high, reached down into the pool with my bare arm, feeling the warmth of it, and picked it up.
It was a hair clip, the kind little girls wear: a snap clip shaped like a strawberry, pink plastic with little green leaves and yellow dots for the seeds, about as long as my thumb.
I sat back on my heels in the good air and turned it over in my fingers.

It wasn’t old. It had no dust in its hinge. The pink wasn’t faded and the green leaves weren’t chipped. On the back, on the flat part, there was the ghost of a price sticker, a little white rectangle of glue where a label had been peeled off, still a bit sticky, with a little fluff caught in it. The plastic smelled of a shop. When I squeezed it, it snapped open and shut, bright and new.
Little girls lose hair clips all the time, in parks, on buses, in the sand.

Little girls don’t come to the Grotta del Cane. It’s been closed for a hundred and fifty years, behind a locked gate, at the back of a ruined spa, at the bottom of a slope of broken stone. Nobody comes here at all except the Held.
The dog came in and lay down at my feet, under the gas, on its side, and watched me with its gold eyes.

When Ferrante came up the slope at eleven o’clock with the two buckets, I was sitting on the wall by the gate in the sun, and the clip was in my coat pocket. I showed it to him, on the flat of my hand.
He looked at it for a long moment. The heavy air came up round his good shoes, a centimetre, two. Then it went down again. I watched it go.
“Old,” he said. “Someone’s child. A long time ago.”
He was lying. I don’t know how I knew. I’ve never been able to tell when people lie. People who lie are afraid, and everybody’s afraid all the time, so it all looks the same to me. But I knew.
I put it back in my pocket. I’ve still got it. It’s in the drawer of my kitchen table, next to the photograph of the dog.
Then I took off my shoes, and knelt down in the dark, and his hand came down on my neck.
11. Twelve
The first debt is not for the client. It is for the Keeper, to see what he has made.

The first man I killed was an accountant called nothing. I mean that I’ve forgotten his name. I’ve forgotten very little in my life, and his name is one of the things. I remember his tie, which was green with small yellow ducks on it. He wore it, I think, to be liked.
I was twelve. It was October 2004.

He did the books for the man who owns the car dealerships, the one who comes up the stairs past the brass plate on Sundays. The accountant had found something in the books that shouldn’t have been there. It wasn’t anything to do with the Held. It was ordinary, a few cars sold to the wrong people for cash. But he’d found it, and he’d made a copy, and he’d started asking for money every month to keep the copy in his drawer. The car dealer stood in the heavy air to his chest every Sunday for a year. He couldn’t sleep. His hair came out on his pillow.
Ferrante had decided the debt in four words: Yes. The child. Wednesday.

I want to tell you why he sent me, and not someone else, and not one of the older ones who’d been placed. It wasn’t for the client. The accountant could have been dealt with by anybody, a man from the Camorra, a car that didn’t stop at a crossing. Ferrante sent me because he wanted to see.
Every Keeper does it, I know now, with every child. The first debt is a test. Not of whether the child can do it. Of what the child is, afterwards.

The pharmacist made it up for me in the back of his shop, among the painted jars, on the Tuesday. He measured it on a little brass scale and folded it into a twist of paper the size of a sugar packet. He told me how much, and how quickly it worked, and what the doctor would think it was, and what the doctor would write. His hands shook doing it. He kept the cough sweet in his cheek the whole time, and it clicked against his teeth.
“You don’t have to,” he said, very quietly, when he gave it to me. He was standing in the heavy air to his waist.
I didn’t understand what he meant. He might as well have told me I didn’t have to breathe.

The accountant had his coffee every morning at nine in the same bar on the Via Toledo [toh-LEH-doh], the long straight shopping street that runs from the royal palace up through the middle of the city. It was a long bar, steel and mirrors, with a man in a white jacket working the big brass machine and a glass case of pastries. You stand to drink coffee in Naples. You don’t sit. You stand at the counter with your elbow on the steel, and you drink it in three mouthfuls, and you go.

I went in at five to nine in my school uniform. I didn’t go to school, but the Held had bought me a uniform so I’d look like a girl who did: a blue tunic, a white collar, a satchel. I bought a pastry, a sfogliatella [sfol-yah-TEL-lah], the shell-shaped one made of a hundred thin leaves of crisp pastry around a filling of sweet ricotta and orange peel, which shatters when you bite it and gets all down your front. I ate it at the end of the counter and watched the door.

He came in at nine exactly, in the duck tie. He ordered his coffee. While the man in the white jacket was making it he went to the toilet, as he did every morning; the car dealer had told us that. The coffee came out of the machine into its little thick white cup and was set down on its saucer on the steel counter in front of the empty space where he’d been standing, with a little spoon and a glass of water beside it.

I walked down the counter, past it, brushing the cup with my satchel. I stopped and said sorry to nobody, and moved the cup back where it had been, and walked on to the door. It took perhaps four seconds. Nobody in the bar looked at me. A girl in a school uniform with flakes of pastry down her front is the most invisible thing in Naples.

I didn’t leave. I’d been told to leave. I stood outside by the window, among the people going past, and watched him come back from the toilet, and pick up the cup, and drink his coffee in three mouthfuls, and put it down, and pay, and go out of the door right past me and turn left up the Via Toledo.

He walked eleven steps and stopped. He put his hand flat on his chest, on the ducks. He looked surprised. People always look surprised, I’ve learned. Then he sat down on the pavement, carefully, the way an old man sits on a low wall. Then he lay down on his side.

People stopped. A woman screamed. A man knelt by him and loosened the duck tie and shouted for an ambulance, and the heavy air came off the crowd and spread across the pavement, ankle-deep, knee-deep, shimmering in the October sun among their shoes. I stood at the edge of it with my satchel and watched him go grey and then blue round the mouth. It took about four minutes.

I wasn’t upset. I wasn’t pleased. I was interested, the way you’d be interested in a film you’d heard about. I watched carefully, because I’d been told how it would happen and I wanted to see if it was true, and it was all true, exactly as the pharmacist had said. I remember thinking how clever the pharmacist was. I remember the smell of the sea coming up the street from the harbour, and a pigeon walking about in the heavy air round everybody’s feet, quite unbothered, pecking at pastry crumbs.
When the ambulance came I went home on the bus.

That evening I told Ferrante, in his van, everything I’ve just told you, in the same voice. I told him about the ducks, and the eleven steps, and how he sat down like an old man on a low wall, and the pigeon. I told him that the pharmacist had been right about everything and that I’d like to learn more from him.
He listened without moving. When I’d finished he sat for a long time with his big hands on the steering wheel, looking out through the windscreen at nothing.
The heavy air was coming up off him. Up past his ankles, his shins. It filled the footwell of the van. It was the most I’d ever seen on him.
“You stayed,” he said. “You were told to leave.”
“I wanted to see.”
He nodded. Then he started the engine and drove me home, and he didn’t say anything else, and he didn’t give me any almonds.
From that week, the Sundays doubled.

Not more days. More times, and longer. Five times under every Sunday instead of three, and every time longer. Forty seconds. Fifty. Sixty. I’d come out of the cave grey and shaking and sick into the dust, and he’d lift me and pour the water and say there, there. But his voice was different. Tighter. And his hand stayed down on my neck a second longer, and then another second, every week, as if he were listening for something in me that wasn’t there yet.
I didn’t know what he was listening for. I learned.

It was on the third Sunday after the accountant. He lifted me out of the dark the second time that day, sixty-one seconds, and threw the water. I came up into the light with my chest heaving, and his face was in front of mine, and this time — I don’t know why — the gift came out of my eyes. The tears ran. I sobbed. My whole body shook with it, and I put my arms round his neck and held on, and cried into his coat like a little child.

I felt him go soft. All of him, at once. I felt it through his coat, his whole body letting go of something, like a man putting down a suitcase he’d carried a long way. The heavy air went down round his shoes like a tide going out.
“There,” he said, and his voice was his own again. “There. There. Good girl. Oh, good girl.”
He didn’t put me under a third time that day. He gave me the almonds in the van.

The next Sunday I cried again, after the first lift. And he didn’t put me under the second time. And the Sundays got shorter again, week by week, and kinder, and his hand on my neck was gentler, and he looked at me in the mirror on the drive home the way he’d looked at me when I was small.
I learned to cry.

I want to put that down plainly, without decorating it, the way I’ve put down everything else. I learned to cry on the third Sunday after the accountant, and after that I cried every Sunday of my life, at the right moment, after the lift, into his coat.

On the Sunday after the hospital, after the mask and the seawall, I went under three times. And each time, after the lift, I did something I’d never done before: I watched it. I watched myself cry the way I’d watched the accountant die, from the edge, interested, the way you’d watch a film you’d heard about.
The tears came each time in the same place. Two breaths after the water. Not one, not three. Two. Every time, like a clock.
I sat in the van afterwards with the almonds on my knee, not eating them, and thought about it all the way through the orange tunnel.
I wondered who had taught me.
Then I wondered whether anyone had.
12. Ferrante’s House
Chaste goddess, who silvers these sacred old trees…
He asked me to dinner on the Thursday.

He lives on the ridge of Posillipo, on the side that faces the sea, in a house built for a rich family a hundred and fifty years ago. It’s pink, or it was. Now it’s the colour of a shell that’s been on a beach a long time. It has green shutters with half their slats gone, an iron gate that doesn’t shut, and a garden that falls away below it in steps, terrace after terrace of lemon trees and old vines, all the way down to the rocks and the water. At night from his kitchen window you can see the whole bay. Naples is a horseshoe of lights on the right and Vesuvius a black shape against a lesser black, and straight out in front, the island of Capri [KAH-pree] low on the sea like a sleeping animal.

The house is full of books. They’re in every room, in shelves to the ceiling and in piles on the floor and on the stairs, one pile on each step, so that you climb up to bed through a library. Most of them are old. Many of them are about the lungs, about breath, about drowning, about saints, about the plague. He’s read every one.

He was cooking when I came, in an apron, with his shirtsleeves rolled up over his big forearms. The ragù had been on since noon. He makes it the old way, the way the nurse who kept him as a baby made it in the Sanità before the war: three kinds of meat tied with string, the tomato passed through a sieve by hand, a glass of red wine, and six hours on the lowest flame. The pot muttered to itself like an old woman in church. He’d made the pasta himself as well, long thick tubes, and laid them out to dry on a cloth over the back of a chair.
On an old record player in the corner of the kitchen there was music. A woman’s voice, alone, high and slow and very pure, rising and falling over a few soft strings.
“Bellini,” he said, when he saw me listening. “Norma.” Bellini was a composer from Sicily who wrote operas two hundred years ago and died young. “She’s a priestess, in Gaul, in the old days, when the

Romans ruled. She’s praying to the moon for peace. Casta diva [KAH-stah DEE-vah]. Chaste goddess.” He stirred the ragù. “She’s secretly in love with a Roman. She’s had his children. Nobody knows. She stands in front of her whole people under the moon and prays for peace, and the whole time she’s carrying the thing that will destroy her, inside her, and nobody can see it.”
“What happens to her?”
“She walks into the fire,” he said. “At the end. She chooses it.” He tasted the sauce, and closed his eyes for a moment. “It’s the most beautiful thing ever written.”

We ate at the kitchen table by the window. The bay was dark and full of lights. He poured me wine, which I don’t drink, and I held the glass. He asked about my week. He asked whether I’d been sleeping, and whether I’d eaten properly, and whether the headaches had gone. He cut bread for me from a big round loaf, holding it against his chest and drawing the knife towards himself, the old way, as women in the Sanità do. He watched me eat with the same face he’d had at the nurse’s flat when I was four, a face that seemed to have been waiting all its life to watch me eat.
I’d decided before I came that I would watch him. Not the way I watch a debt. The way you’d watch a machine that you’d always used and never opened, now that you’d seen the wires.
So I watched him, and here’s what I saw.

I saw that he loved me. I’m sorry if that’s not what you expected. It’s what was there. Everything about him at that table was love: the bread, the sauce, the way he leaned to fill my glass that I wasn’t drinking from, the way his eyes went to my plate and to my face and back. It wasn’t acted. I’ve seen acting all my life. The Held act all day long, and so do their clients, and so does everyone. This wasn’t that. It was the realest thing in the room. It was realer than the table.
And I saw that it didn’t make any difference.

That’s what I can’t explain to you properly, and I’ll try. You’d think, wouldn’t you, that if the man who drowned you every Sunday turned out to love you, it would make it better. Or worse. That it would mean something. I sat across from him and watched him love me, and understood all at once that his love and the cave weren’t two different things. They weren’t a kind man doing a cruel thing, or a cruel man pretending to be kind. They were the same thing, the way the flame and the heat are the same thing. He held me under because he loved me. That’s what the love was for, and what it was made of. If you love a fire, you build a stove round it.
After dinner he made coffee in a little copper pot, and we took it to the window, and stood looking at the bay.
“Tell me about the scars,” I said.

He’d rolled his sleeves down by then and buttoned his collar, as he always did. But I’d seen them all my life, when he bent over to lift me in the cave: two thin white lines on the back of his neck, side by side, very old, just under the hairline, like two strokes of a pen.
He touched them, with two fingers, without thinking.
“My Keeper had strong hands,” he said.
The heavy air didn’t move round his shoes. Not a centimetre. He said it as if he were telling me the time.
Then, because I’d asked, or because he’d been waiting years for someone to ask, he told me about the Four Days.
He didn’t tell it about himself. He told it about a boy.

In September 1943, he said, Naples was the most bombed city in Italy. The Americans and the British had been bombing it from the air for three years. The port was a field of sunk ships and the old city was full of holes like a bad tooth. Then Italy surrendered and changed sides, and overnight the Germans who’d been our friends became the people who owned us. They knew they’d have to leave, so they decided to leave nothing behind. They blew up the port and the water and the power, and they rounded up the city’s men to ship north to the camps.
And on the twenty-seventh of September, the city stood up.

Nobody organised it, he said. Nobody planned it. It started in a dozen places at once, in the Vomero and the Sanità and the old streets by the port: men with old rifles from the last war, women dropping furniture out of windows onto German trucks, priests hiding men in crypts. And the boys. The scugnizzi

[skoon-YEET-tsee], the street boys of Naples, boys of ten and eleven and twelve who lived in the ruins and sold black-market cigarettes to soldiers and slept in doorways. They ran at German tanks with bottles of petrol with a rag on fire. One of them, a boy called Gennarino [jen-nah-REE-noh], eleven years old, was killed throwing a grenade at a tank on the third day.

“Four days,” he said. “On the night of the thirtieth the Germans left, and on the first of October the Americans drove in, and found the city had already freed itself. The first city in Europe that did.”
“And the boy?” I said.

“There was a boy,” he said, looking out at the bay. “Younger than the others. Six. He didn’t have a gun. He didn’t have a bottle. He walked up the middle of the Via Foria in the morning on the second day, in the middle of the street, in the open, where the men were lying flat behind the overturned trams and shouting at him to get down. A German half-track was coming down the street towards him. That’s a lorry with the back wheels of a tank and a gun on the top. It was coming down slowly, firing at the windows. He walked towards it. He had a grenade in his hand that he’d taken off a dead soldier. He didn’t know how to use it. He walked up to the half-track as if he were walking up to a man selling ice creams, and he stood in front of it, and he looked up at the soldier behind the gun, and the soldier looked down at him.”
He stopped.
“What happened?” I said.

“The soldier didn’t shoot,” he said. “Nobody ever knew why. He just looked at the boy, standing there, so small, not afraid. Not afraid of anything. And then the soldier put his hands over his face. And the boy pulled the cord in the grenade’s handle, the way he’d seen the men do, and dropped it into the half-track, and walked away.”
He drank his coffee.
“There was a man watching,” he said. “From a doorway. A doctor. He saw the whole thing. And he went out into the street after the explosion and took the boy by the hand and took him home.”
The record had come to the end. The needle was going round and round in the last groove, hissing softly, like the sea.
“Did the boy love him?” I said. “The doctor?”
“With his whole body,” said Ferrante.
He put down his cup. He turned from the window and looked at me, and his long, kind face was very still.
“Come to the cave early on Sunday,” he said. “Earlier than usual. I want to show you something.”
I said I would.
I didn’t wait for Sunday. I went on Saturday night.
13. Without the Lift
What happens under stays under.

I went at two in the morning, on foot from Pozzuoli. It’s eight kilometres along the old Roman road and over the shoulder of the Solfatara, where the ground steams in the dark and the air smells of matches and rotten eggs. I passed no one. A fox crossed the road in front of me with something in its mouth. It looked at me. It didn’t hurry.
The racecourse was dark. The old spa was dark, its broken windows full of nothing. I climbed the slope by starlight and unlocked the gate with the key he’d given me for emergencies.

The dog was there. It was lying by the gate in the dark. It got up when I came, in its fluid way, and pushed its nose into my hand. Then it went in ahead of me into the passage, as if it had been waiting.

I’d brought one of his buckets. I’d taken it from the back of the van on Thursday, while he was in the house making coffee. I filled it at the tap on the wall of the spa and carried it up, and set it down inside the gate, by the door of the cave. I lit a candle and put it on the floor. It lay down and went out, and the thread of smoke lay flat on the dark.
Then I went in, five metres, to where the roof comes down, and I knelt.

I’ll tell you something about the end of the passage that I haven’t told you yet. At the very back, where the tunnel stops at the rock face, there is a small square niche cut into the stone at the height of a kneeling child’s head. In the niche, on a little shelf, there’s a tin box like the ones the skulls in Chiaia live in, with a tiny pitched roof and a door. In the box there’s a skull. It’s small, and very old, the colour of strong tea, and its jaw is missing. It’s been there as long as I can remember. When I was small I asked Ferrante whose it was.
“The first,” he said.

That’s all he’s ever said about it. I always took it to mean the first Keeper, the doctor. I thought he’d been put here, at the bottom of his own cave, like a saint under his altar. I was wrong about that. I’ll tell you how I know.

I knelt in the dark, with the dog lying beside me on its side under the invisible surface, and the little tin house a metre in front of my face. I put my own hand on the back of my own neck. And I pushed my face down.
It’s harder than you’d think. Your own hand doesn’t want to. Your own arm knows whose neck it is.
I pushed.
Sour. Battery. Eyes stinging.
Breath. Nothing in it. Breath.
The alarm.
Now.
My heart broke into its run.
And it came, all of it, as it always comes, the bottom of the sea. But this time there was something new under it, and the new thing was this: nobody was going to lift me.

You have to understand what that meant, to a body that had been taught one thing for twenty-eight years. The First Rule: you do not breathe until you are lifted. It wasn’t a rule any more. It wasn’t words. It was built into me, deeper than my bones, the way the nurse’s ragù was built into the walls of her kitchen. My body had learned, every Sunday for twenty-eight years, that you breathe what’s there and you wait, and the hand decides, and when the hand decides, there’s light.
There was no hand. There was my own hand, and it was pressing down, because I’d told it to, and the body didn’t know how to want up without being lifted. It didn’t know there was such a thing.
The lights came. The ring. The tunnel.
Then the voices.
I’ll tell you exactly what I heard, and you can decide what it was. I’ve decided. I won’t tell you what I decided.

The first was a boy, singing. A high, rough voice, very close, in the dark just to my left, where the warmth always is. He was singing a song I didn’t know, in an old Neapolitan so thick I could barely follow it. It was something about a priest and a washerwoman, and it was very rude, and he was laughing as he sang it. I could smell bread. I could smell something under the bread, sweet and rotten, like meat left out in August.
I, said the boy, in the middle of the song, as if he were answering someone. I chose a child.

Then a second voice, a man’s, younger than Ferrante, hoarse, as if he’d been shouting for days. I could smell smoke, wood smoke and something else burning that wasn’t wood. Far off, a lot of people were roaring together, the way a crowd roars at a football match, but wrong. I, he said. I chose a child.

Then a girl’s, a young woman’s, singing too, but a slow song, a lullaby, low, while somewhere water was being poured and poured, and there was the sound of wet cloth being slapped on stone, and a smell like a hospital, of lye and of sickness. I chose a child, she sang, to the tune of the lullaby, as if it were the words.

Then another boy, a small one, six, maybe, breathing fast, and then the scream of tank tracks on cobbles, and a grenade pin, ping, and then a voice I knew. It was younger, so much younger, high and light, but I knew it the way you’d know your own father’s voice on the radio.
I, said the boy who was Ferrante. I chose a child.

And then — fainter, further off, from somewhere ahead of me in the dark, or above, or in a place that wasn’t in the cave at all — more voices. Voices that weren’t dead. A man’s, very calm, very flat, saying something I couldn’t hear, in the ringing quiet after a gunshot. A woman’s voice in a hospital, in a room full of beeping machines, saying clamp. A young man laughing in a glass room full of screens. They didn’t say I chose a child. They said nothing to me. They were just there, a long way off, like lights across the bay. I knew who they were. I’d seen their faces on a laptop.

And last of all, so faint I wasn’t sure, right at the very edge, a little girl’s voice. Small and bright and curious, asking someone a question I couldn’t hear. And then laughing, one high hiccup of a laugh.

The tin house in front of my face wasn’t dark any more. There was a light inside it, a very faint light, coming out through the crack under its little door like a candle in a shrine. And the voice of the boy, the first one, the singer, the one who smelled of bread, came out of the box. Very close. Very kind.
We all say I, it said. Every one of us. We all say I.

My body was screaming. I’d been under longer than I’d ever been under in my life. The lights were going out at the edges, one by one, like the lights of Pozzuoli going on and off in a swarm. The warmth on my left was very close now, so close it was like a mouth against my ear, and the dog was looking at me in the dark with its gold eyes, and it was so easy. It was the easiest thing in the world. All I had to do was what I’d always done: breathe what was there, and wait.
And nobody would come. And I’d never be lifted. And it would be over.
I don’t know where it came from. I’ll tell you that honestly, because it’s the second thing in this story that I’ve never had before, and I don’t know its name.

My hand moved. Not the one on my neck. The other one, the one that was flat on the warm stone, holding me up. It came off the floor, and went up, and found my own hair, at the back of my own head. It took a fistful, and it pulled.

It pulled my head up out of the gas by the hair, the way you’d drag a drowned woman out of a river. It hurt like hell. I felt hairs come out at the roots. My face came up through the surface of the invisible lake into the good air, and my mouth opened, and I breathed.

There was no water. There was no gift. There was no there, there, good girl. It was just air, ordinary night air in a hole in a hill, going into me in great tearing gulps. I knelt with my fist still in my own hair, retching, and the tears came. Not two breaths after. Not on time. All at once, any old how, running down into my mouth with the snot, and I didn’t watch them. I didn’t time them. I just knelt there and let them come, like a dog being sick.

When I could move I crawled out of the cave on my hands and knees into the starlight, and got up, and the bucket was standing where I’d left it by the door. I picked it up and poured the whole thing over my own head.
It was very cold. It was the coldest thing I’d ever felt.
Then I saw him.

He was sitting by the gate on the other bucket, turned upside down, the way old men sit on upturned crates in the Sanità to play cards. He had his coat on and his hat and his grey scarf. His big hands were folded on his knees. Behind him, over the racecourse, the sky was going grey. I don’t know how long he’d been there.
The heavy air around him was up to his chest.

I’d never seen him in so much. Not ever. He was sitting in it as if he were sitting in the sea, up to his heart, and it was perfectly still, and the dawn light came through it as it comes through water.
“You went under without me,” he said.
His voice was very quiet. It wasn’t angry. I don’t know what it was.
I stood in front of him, dripping, with my hair torn and my eyes running and my clothes stuck to me.
“Whose skull is that?” I said. “In the cave. In the box.”
He looked at me for a long time. Then he stood up, slowly, his knees cracking, and picked up the bucket he’d been sitting on, and the one I’d emptied, one in each hand.
“Come home,” he said. “I’ll tell you.”
14. Every Keeper Says I
The voice does not die. Only the throat.

He made me a coffee in the copper pot and gave me a towel and one of his own shirts to put on, a white one, too big, with the sleeves rolled four times. He sat me at the kitchen table by the window, with the bay going from grey to silver to blue below us. Then he went upstairs, climbing through his library one step at a time, and came down again with a book.

It was big and very old, as thick as a loaf of bread, bound in leather gone black and soft as a glove with handling. It had brass corners, one of them missing. When he put it on the table it made a sound like a door closing.
“The Book of Choosing,” he said.

He opened it at the front. The first pages were brown and spotted, and the writing was in an old hand, crabbed and full of loops, in ink gone the colour of rust. The first line was in Italian, the old kind. I could read it, just. The priest had taught me.
Centuries ago I chose a child.

He turned the pages, slowly, so I could see. The writing changed. Every few dozen pages, the hand changed. A new pen, a new ink, a new way of making the letters, sloping one way and then the other, big and then small, careful and then hurried. Seven hands, eight, nine. And every time the hand changed, the new hand began with the same words, at the top of a fresh page.
Centuries ago I chose a child.

“Every Keeper writes his own chapter,” he said. “How he chose. Each in his own hand, so the one who comes after will know that it’s been done before, and that it was necessary.” He laid his big hand flat on the page. “But each one begins the same. The doctor wrote that line to whoever would read his chapter centuries later, and every Keeper since has copied it. And each one says I. As if it were the first.”
“Why?”
“Because it is,” he said. “Every time.”
Then he told me. He told me plainly, simply, without any drama, the way you’d hand someone the keys of a house and show them which key is for which door. I’ll tell it to you the same way.

The first Keeper was the doctor, in 1656. The plague doctor, with the bird mask. He found a boy on a corpse cart in the Sanità, and he held him under in the cave, and the boy loved him for it with his whole body, and became his Hand.
That’s the word for what I am. The Hand. The one the Keeper sends. The one that does what nobody else can do.
When the doctor grew old, the boy became the Keeper.

That’s the whole of it. That’s the secret of the Held, the thing nobody says aloud at the gathering on Sundays. The Keeper isn’t a man the Held choose. He isn’t a priest or a member. He isn’t one of the frightened at all. The Keeper is always the Hand, grown old. The child who was held becomes the one who holds. He chooses a new child of his own, and holds her under, and lifts her out, and she loves him with her whole body. And when he’s old, she takes his place, and chooses, and holds.
Three hundred and seventy years. Fourteen Keepers, counting him, and every one after the first had been a Hand. Each one the same, each one saying I.
“The skull in the cave,” I said.
“Is the boy,” he said. “The first Hand. The one from the cart. When he became Keeper, he asked to be put there, at the end. Where he was first lifted.”
“And the singing?”
He looked at me sharply then, for the first time that morning. Then he looked away.
“Sometimes people hear things,” he said. “Under.”
“And you,” I said.

He was quiet for a while. The sun was up now, coming in through the window across the table, across the book, across his hands. Down below on the water a ferry was going out to Capri, very small and white, trailing a white line.

“I was the Hand of 1943,” he said. “The boy on the Via Foria. The doctor who took him home from the doorway was the Keeper. He held me under for thirty years. He had strong hands.” He touched the back of his neck. “And when he was old, I became the Keeper. And I chose.” He looked at me. “I chose you.”
“And when you’re old,” I said.
“You’ll be the Keeper,” he said. “And you’ll choose. And you’ll write your chapter in this book, in your own hand, and it’ll begin like all the others.”

He turned the pages forward, past all the hands, the rust and the brown and the black, to near the end, where the paper was whiter. There was his hand, which I knew from the Register: upright, careful, in brown ink. Then, after that, a page with nothing on it.
He put his finger at the top of the empty page.
“There,” he said.
And then he cried.

He sat at his kitchen table with his hand on the empty page and his long horse’s face crumpled, and the tears ran down into the lines of it and dripped off his chin onto the old leather. His big shoulders shook. He didn’t make a sound. He cried the way old men cry in church at funerals, as if it had been waiting in him a long time.
I sat across the table from him in his shirt with the sleeves rolled four times, and I watched him.

And I want to tell you what I saw, because you’ll want me to have been moved, and I was something. I don’t know what. I watched him cry, and it was beautiful, the way all of him is beautiful, the way the Bellini was beautiful. The tears came in exactly the right place, at the top of the empty page, at the moment of handing over. They came two breaths after he said there. Not one, not three. Two. They ran down in the right lines on his face. His shoulders shook in the right rhythm. Not too much. Not too little. Exactly enough for a girl in a too-big shirt to see, across a kitchen table, in the morning sun.
I’d never seen anyone cry so well.

The heavy air round his feet hadn’t moved. Not a centimetre. It lay round his good shoes on the kitchen tiles at exactly the depth it had been at when he came down the stairs with the book, a thin film, at the ankle, nothing.
He wiped his face with the back of his big hand, and smiled at me, the saint’s smile, sad and kind.
“Read it,” he said. He pushed the book across the table to me. “All of it. Take it home. Then you’ll know what you’re for.”
I took it home. I read it all that week, at my kitchen table in the Rione Terra, with the ground going up under my chair. I’ll give you some of it, as I go. Not all. Some of it’s not mine to give.
Here’s the chapter from 1799. It’s the ninth hand in the book. Hoarse, the letters jammed together, as if the man who wrote it had been shouting for days.
THE BOOK OF CHOOSING · II — 1799
The mob is a fear that has found its legs.
Centuries ago I chose a child.

I set down first, for the one who comes after, what the city was in that year, because the child cannot be understood without the city. They were made for each other, the way a key is made for a lock.
In the winter of 1798 the King ran away.

He was a big, loud, stupid, well-liked man who liked hunting and fishing and eating macaroni with his fingers in front of the people, and they loved him for it. The French had cut off their own King’s head six years before and made a republic, and now their armies were marching down the length of Italy. Our King ran from them in the night on an English warship, the ship of the Admiral Nelson, with the Queen and the crown jewels and the treasury, to his other kingdom in Sicily. He left his city behind him like a coat on a chair.

The gentlemen of Naples were glad. The lawyers, the young nobles, the professors, the poets, the doctors: they had read the French books and they believed in liberty, in reason, in an end to kings. In January 1799 the French army came to the gates, and the gentlemen opened them.
The lazzari [LAHT-tsah-ree] did not.

I must explain the lazzari, because the one who comes after may live in a time when there are none. They were the poor of Naples. Not a few poor. A whole people of the poor, tens of thousands of them, who had no houses and no trade. They slept on the steps of churches and under the arches of the port, and lived on what they could sell, steal, beg or carry. They wore a shirt and a pair of short trousers and nothing else, summer and winter. They were dark from the sun, loud, quick, devout, and they loved the King, because he was loud and ate with his fingers like them. They hated the gentlemen, because the gentlemen had always hated them.

For three days the lazzari fought the French army in the streets with knives and stones and old muskets. The French had cannon. Thousands of the lazzari died. The French won, and the gentlemen proclaimed a Republic, with a tree of liberty in the square in front of the palace and a red cap on top of it. The lazzari went back to the steps of the churches and waited.
They waited five months.

In those five months the Republic of the gentlemen wrote laws and printed newspapers and argued, and did nothing at all for the lazzari. In the south, in Calabria [kah-LAH-bryah], a cardinal of the Church, a fat, clever, fearless old man, raised an army of peasants and bandits and priests and called it the Army of the Holy Faith. They marched north up the length of the kingdom behind a great banner of the cross, burning every town that had planted a tree of liberty. In June the French army went home to France, because it was needed elsewhere, and the cardinal’s army came to the gates of Naples.
And the lazzari rose.
I set down what I saw, plainly, because the one who comes after must know what a city is when its fear finds its legs.

They went through the streets of Naples for three weeks looking for anyone who had been for the Republic. They looked for anyone who wore short hair in the French fashion, anyone who wore trousers instead of breeches, anyone who could read. They dragged them out of their houses, out of churches, out of the convents where they had run to hide. They killed them in the street with knives and clubs and their hands. They burned them alive in the squares, on bonfires built from their own furniture. And it is true, though I would not believe it if I had not seen it, that some of them roasted the flesh and ate it, there in the squares, and offered it round. The gentlemen had been afraid of the lazzari for a hundred years, and now the lazzari were afraid of nothing at all, because there were so many of them, and because the cardinal had told them God was on their side.

That is the thing I learned in that summer, and I set it down above all. A crowd is the one thing that can do what the fearless do. Every one of them was afraid, alone. Together they were not. Their fear had found its legs, ten thousand of them, and it ran down the streets like water down a hill. I stood in doorways and watched it go past.
I was the Keeper of the Held. I had been the Hand before that, and I knew what the Hand was for.

The Held had clients in that summer as never before. Everyone was afraid of everyone. The gentlemen were afraid of the lazzari, and the lazzari of the French coming back, and the King’s men of the gentlemen’s friends. Brother was afraid of brother over an inheritance, and creditor of debtor, and husband of his wife’s lover. They came up our stairs one after another, white and sweating, and pushed their coins into the houses of our skulls. And they all wanted the same thing: one particular person dead, in a summer when everybody was dying. One more body on one more bonfire.

My Hand was a boy of fourteen, from the wheel, like all of them. I had chosen him at five. He had a scar through one eyebrow and a laugh like a girl’s. He was the best Hand there had been, then. I believe it still.

I sent him out into the burning city every day of those three weeks, and he paid every debt I gave him. A silk merchant on the Toledo, owed money by our client: knifed in his doorway on the night the lazzari came to that street, and they burned his house over him. A notary who had witnessed a will he should not have: thrown from his own balcony into a crowd that had come for his neighbour. A young lieutenant who had got a judge’s daughter with child: found in the morning in the Piazza del Mercato [PYAHT-tsah del mer-KAH-toh], the Market Square by the sea, with his head on a pike among twenty other heads, and nobody asked which hands had put it there. A widow’s brother-in-law. A bishop’s nephew. A man who knew too much about a ship.
Twenty-nine debts in three weeks. The city did the rest. It covered every one of them, as the sea covers a stone.

He went through the slaughter as a boy goes through a summer meadow. I watched him once, from the steps of a church, walk down the middle of the Via Toledo in the middle of the killing. There was a bonfire on the left and a man being beaten to death on the right, and a priest running with his skirts up. The lazzari were roaring like a sea, and the smoke was full of the smell of roasting. He walked straight down the middle of it, eating a peach, at an even pace. He was the only person in the street walking. Everyone else was running towards something or away from it. The lazzari let him pass. They did not even see him. A crowd sees only fear, its own or its prey’s, and he had none of either.
When he came back to me in the evening he knelt at my feet, there in the house, and put his head against my knee, like a dog, and asked when it would be Sunday.

On Sundays he went under longer than any child had. A hundred seconds. A hundred and ten. And when I lifted him and threw the water, he wept, and clung to me, and wept, more beautifully each Sunday than the last.

He obeyed me best on the days the city burned. I set that down here and I underline it, so that the one who comes after will remember it. Of all the times to fear a Hand, I would have said, it is when the world is on fire around him and every lock is broken. But it was in that summer that he loved me most. It was in that summer he came back to me every night, and knelt, and asked for Sunday.
I did not ask myself why. I set that down also.

In August, when it was over, the King came back from Sicily, and the Admiral Nelson with him, and the gentlemen who had not been eaten were tried and hanged in the Piazza del Mercato. They were hanged one by one, on a scaffold in front of the great market church, with the lazzari packed into the square to watch, cheering each one.
I took the boy to see the last of them, because I wished him to see that the law too is only a crowd with a rope.

It was a woman. Her name was Eleonora [eh-leh-oh-NOH-rah]. She was a poet and a scholar, a noblewoman of a Portuguese family, born in Rome, who had lived in Naples since she was a child and had written the newspaper of the Republic. She was forty-seven. They had refused her the axe, which was for nobles, and given her the rope, which was for the common. They had refused her a pair of drawers to wear under her skirt. When she dropped, the lazzari underneath would be able to look up and see her naked, and they had come for that. They were already laughing.

Before she climbed the ladder she asked for a coffee, and they gave it to her, and she drank it. Then she said a line out loud, in Latin, from the old poet Virgil. It is what the hero says to his men after the shipwreck, when they have lost everything and washed up on a strange shore: Perhaps one day it will please us to remember even this.
Then she climbed the ladder.
I was watching her. Everyone was watching her. But I am the Keeper, and I have been taught to watch what nobody watches. So I looked away from the scaffold, into the crowd, and I saw a girl.

She was ten or eleven, a lazzara, one of the lazzari herself, in a ragged shift, barefoot, standing on the base of a column by the church door so she could see over the heads. She was not laughing. She was not cheering. She was not afraid. She was watching the poet on the ladder with her head a little on one side, as you watch a bird on a branch. When the poet dropped and the rope went tight and the poet’s legs kicked and the lazzari roared, the girl did not blink.
Ten thousand people in that square, standing in their fear like water to the waist. And one girl on a stone, dry.
The boy saw her too. I felt him see her. His hand on my sleeve went still.
I looked at him, and he looked at me. Then I nodded, once.
He was back by nightfall. He knelt at my feet and put his head on my knee and asked when it would be Sunday.

I opened the Register at his column, and wrote down the debts of the day, and beside the last one, which had no client, no name, only the girl on the column, Piazza del Mercato, I drew a small circle.
Then I sat for a while by the window, with his head on my knee, and thought about the poet on the ladder. Perhaps one day it will please us to remember even this.
I find, setting it down now, that it does.
III. THE HAND
15. The Trader
A placed child who stops coming on Sundays has not escaped. He has only forgotten what he is for.
The Trader stopped coming in May.

He’d been coming once a month for nine years, on the first Sunday, on the early train from Milan, to kneel in the cave like the rest of us. He’d stand in the sun afterwards in his good blue suit, dripping, his thin face shining, and then he’d catch the afternoon train back. The placed ones all come. Not every week, like me. Once a month, or once a season if they’re far away. But they come. They have to. You can take a fire out of the stove and put it in a lamp, but it still needs its oil.

In May he didn’t come. In June he didn’t come. In July Ferrante called me to his glass office at the Foundation and turned the laptop round to face me. On the screen were lines, green and red, going up and down, like the lines on the hospital machine when I breathed the gas.
“He’s betting against us,” Ferrante said.
