I’ll explain this as simply as he explained it to me, because it’s simple underneath. The Held own things: pieces of companies, buildings, debts, a bank in Switzerland, a port in the north. Most of the money the Trader had made for us in nine years had gone into those things. And there’s a way of betting, in the markets in Milan and London and New York, that the price of a thing will fall. You bet the thing will be worth less tomorrow than today, and if it is, you win. The more it falls, the more you win.

The Trader had made that bet, with all of the fund’s money, every euro, on every company the Held owned a piece of. Then he’d begun to sell pieces of those companies himself, in great slabs, and to whisper in the right ears in Milan that something was wrong with them. And the prices had started to go down.
“How much?” I said.

“Enough,” said Ferrante. “Enough that if it goes on to the end of summer, there won’t be a Foundation. There’ll be a building in Chiaia with a brass plate on it and nothing behind the plate.” He closed the laptop. “He’s not doing it for money. He has money. He’s doing it because he’s stopped coming on Sundays, and he’s found out he doesn’t die.”
“Is that so bad?”
He looked at me for a long time with his kind horse’s face.
“It’s the worst thing that can happen,” he said. “To him. To everyone. A fire that’s found out it doesn’t need the stove.” He put his big hand flat on the laptop lid. “Go to Milan.”

I went on the train. You don’t need papers for a train in Italy, only a ticket. It’s four and a half hours on the fast one, north through the whole length of the country: Rome, the hills of Tuscany going gold, the flat grey plain of the Po [POH], the great river that runs across the top of Italy, and the mist lying on the rice fields. The north is different. The people are paler and quieter and they walk faster, and the heavy air round their feet is a different kind. In Naples it’s a lake, warm and deep and shared, everyone standing in it together. In Milan it’s a thin, cold, private film round each pair of shoes, like frost, separate. Everybody alone with their own.

He worked in a glass tower in the new business district at the north of the city, one of a cluster of towers that went up in the last fifteen years. One is twisted like a wrung cloth. One has trees growing up the outside of it on every balcony, a forest standing on end. His was plain and blue and very tall. From the street you could see the people on his floor through the glass, forty storeys up, small as seeds.
I didn’t go up. I didn’t need to. I sat for two days in a café across the square with a coffee I didn’t drink, and watched.

On the second day the prices fell hard. I didn’t understand it then, and I don’t now. Something happened in New York in the night, and when the markets in Milan opened, the companies he’d bet against began to drop like stones down a well. I could see it happen without a screen, because I could see the tower. Floor by floor, through the glass, as the morning went on, the heavy air came up. On every floor, round every pair of legs, rising, until the people in that tower were standing in it to the knees, and on some floors to the waist. Forty storeys of glass with a lake of fear rising inside every one, like an aquarium filling up.
Except his floor. Except one man on his floor, standing at the window with his hands in his pockets, looking out at the city.
Dry.

He came down at seven. I followed him. He walked through the old streets into a neighbourhood called Brera [BREH-rah], where the painters used to live, all cobbles and ivy, little shops selling expensive paper, bars with tables outside. He sat at a table outside one and ordered a drink.
I sat down at his table.

He looked at me. He didn’t jump. He didn’t stand in anything. He looked at me with his pale, thin, clever face behind its glasses, and I watched him know me, the way Saverio had known me at the gate when I was six, the way a dog knows a dog across a square.
“Domenica,” he said.
He’d seen me at the cave, years ago, once or twice, when our Sundays had crossed. I’d never spoken to him. I’d never spoken to any of them, much, except Saverio.
“Yes,” I said.
“He sent you.”
“Yes.”

He nodded. Then he raised his hand for the waiter and ordered me the same drink he had, without asking, an orange one, bitter, in a short glass with ice and a slice of orange. Then he leaned back in his chair and smiled at me. It was the first smile I’d ever had from someone like me. I want to tell you what it was like, because it was the strangest thing that happened to me that year, until the strange things started.
It was like being looked at by a window.

Everyone else in my whole life, when they looked at me, had something behind their eyes: a little shiver, a little wariness, a little of the heavy air, the knowing of a dog in a yard. Even Ferrante. Especially Ferrante. Everyone who has ever looked at me has been, under it all, a little afraid of me. And it’s in everything, in the eyes, the voice, the way they hold their hands. I’d never once in thirty-four years been looked at by somebody who wasn’t.
He wasn’t.
“How long have you got?” he said. “Before you do it.”
“There’s no hurry.”
“No,” he said. “There never is, for us. Is there.” He drank. “Can I tell you something first?”
“Yes.”
He leaned forward, his elbows on the little table, his thin hands round his glass.

“I stopped,” he said. “In May. I was on the platform at the station in Milan at six in the morning, the first Sunday, waiting for the train to Naples, as I’d done every month for nine years. And I just didn’t get on. I don’t know why. The train came in and the doors opened, and I stood there and watched them close. I thought I was going to die. Do you understand? I thought, the way you’d think it if you stopped breathing, that something would happen. That I’d come apart. I went home and sat on my bed and waited for it.”
“And?”

“And nothing.” He laughed. It was a lovely laugh, surprised, like a boy’s. “Nothing. It’s like giving up cigarettes. You think the want will kill you, and then you find out the want is all it was. There’s nothing under it. It’s not love, Domenica. It was never love. It’s a hole in a hill. It’s gas. It’s the oldest trick there is. They do it to dogs.” He reached across the table, and put his hand on my wrist. His hand was cool and dry and light. “You could stop too. Today. You could get on a different train. We could get on it together.”
I looked at his hand on my wrist.

I’d breathed the gas in the hospital in March. I’d sat on the seawall all night. I’d gone under alone and pulled myself out by my own hair. I knew everything he was telling me. I’d known it for four months. And here was a man like me, the first, holding my wrist in a pretty street in Milan, offering me a train.
I’m going to be honest with you, because there’s no point otherwise. If he had asked me a week after the hospital, I don’t know what I’d have said.
He hadn’t asked me then. He was asking me now.
“Where would we go?” I said.
“Anywhere,” he said. “Anywhere. That’s the thing they never tell you. That’s the word they’re frightened of. Anywhere.”
He finished his drink, and paid, and stood up, and held out his hand to me as if we were going to dance.
“Come and see where I live,” he said. “Then decide.”
We took the tram.

Milan still runs its old trams, the orange ones, built in the 1920s, with wooden benches inside and brass handrails and windows that slide down. They go rattling and swaying through the middle of the city, ringing their bells, as they did a hundred years ago. It was eight in the evening and the tram was packed: people going home from work, a group of students, old women with shopping, a man with a cello in a case. We stood in the middle, holding the brass rail, our shoulders touching, swaying together as it went round the corners. He was telling me about his flat. It had a terrace, he said, with a lemon tree, a small one, in a pot. It reminded him of the south. He was smiling.
I’ll tell you how it happened, in order, because order is what I have.
The knife was a thin one, very thin, with a blade as long as my hand and no wider than a pencil. It’s the kind a fisherman uses to open sea urchins. I’d carried it up my sleeve for two days.

The tram went round the corner by the castle, the big brick castle in the middle of Milan where the dukes lived, and everybody swayed to the left, all together, the way a field of wheat goes over in the wind. He swayed into me. I put my left arm round him, as if to steady him, as if we were lovers. With my right hand I put the knife in under his ribs on the left side, upward, at the angle the pharmacist had shown me when I was thirteen, into the heart.
It took one breath. His.

He didn’t make a sound. He looked down at me, surprised, the way they always look surprised, his face very close to mine. His glasses had gone a little crooked. And then — I’ll give you this, because it’s the truest thing I know about him — he smiled. Not a big smile. A small one, at one corner of his mouth, as if he’d just understood the end of a joke he’d been told a long time ago.

He wasn’t afraid. Not even then. Not one drop. He was the cleanest death I’ve ever given anyone. There was nothing round his feet when he died, nothing at all, not even at the end, when everyone has some. He went out the way a candle goes out in the cave: lay down on its side, small and blue, and was gone.

I took the knife out and held him up against me as the tram straightened, and let him down onto the wooden bench by the window, gently, and sat him there with his head against the glass as though he’d fallen asleep. There was very little blood. With a knife that thin there isn’t, at first. It all goes inside. I took my arm away. I put the knife back up my sleeve.
At the next stop I got off.

I looked back from the pavement as the tram rang its bell and pulled away. A woman sitting across from him had noticed. She’d seen the dark spreading on his blue shirt under his jacket, and she was standing up with her hand over her mouth. As the tram swung away down the street, I saw the heavy air come up inside it, out of everyone, all at once. It filled the old wooden car from the floor to the windows in the time it took the tram to reach the next corner. A tram full of fear to the ceiling, lit orange, swaying and ringing its bell down the street into the dark.
And sitting in the middle of it, with his head against the window, a man who was dry.

I took the night train home. I sat by the window all the way down the length of Italy, and watched the dark go past, and thought about a lemon tree in a pot on a terrace in Milan that nobody was going to water.

I want you to understand that I’d decided. Not on the tram. Before. In the café, watching the tower fill up with fear, I had already decided I was going to do it, and that I was going to do it because he’d asked me to come with him, and not in spite of it. A fearless man who’d found out he didn’t need the hand. Who’d go anywhere. Who’d bring down the Foundation in a summer, from a terrace with a lemon tree, because nothing in the world could stop him. And who, if I’d gone with him, would have needed me for nothing at all.
He was everything I’d been sitting on the seawall wondering whether I was. And I killed him, because there can’t be two.
I didn’t know yet that that was a rule. I thought it was only how I felt.

In Naples, in the morning, Ferrante met me at the station in his van. He didn’t ask anything. He drove me to Chiaia, and up the stairs past the brass plate, to his glass office. He took a big book out of the drawer of his desk, bound in green cloth gone soft at the corners, and put it on the desk in front of me.
“You’ve earned this,” he said.
16. The Register of Breaths and Debts
Write the seconds. Write the debts. Write nothing else. The book is not for feelings. It is for the one who comes after.

There are thirty-one volumes of the Register. They go back to 1656. The old ones are in the cold room behind the cupboard door, on the bottom shelf under the skulls. They’re bound in leather, cracked and powdery, and you’re not allowed to touch them without cotton gloves. The one he gave me was the newest, the green one, started in 1971.
It’s a very simple book. That’s what makes it terrible.
Every page is ruled into columns. At the top of each column is a name, and under the name, in brown ink, run two lists side by side.
On the left: Sundays. A date, and a number. The number is seconds under.
On the right: debts. A date, and a few words. A name, or not. A place. And one word that is always the same: paid.
That’s all. No notes, no thoughts, no feelings. Three hundred and seventy years of children, written down like the takings of a shop.
I found my column.

Domenica. The first entry: April 1998 · 22. I’ve told you about that. Then, Sunday after Sunday, down the page and onto the next page and the next and the next, twenty-eight years of them, in his upright careful hand: 24, 25, 25, 28, 31, 30, 34… The numbers climbed slowly through my childhood like the ground under Pozzuoli. There was a long run of big numbers in the autumn of 2004, after the accountant, 60, 64, 71, and then they eased back down. That was after I learned to cry. Then they began to climb again, steadily, year after year, into the forties, into the fifties. The most recent was the Sunday before I went to Milan: 68.
And on the right, the debts.
Oct 2004 · Via Toledo · paid. That was the accountant.
Mar 2026 · Sanità · paid. That was the onion kitchen.
Mar 2026 · Vomero · paid. The journalist in his bed.

Apr 2026 · Bagnoli · paid. That was the young engineer with the beard, the one with the samples of bad concrete. I haven’t told you about him. There isn’t much to tell. He had a scooter, and a habit of riding it too fast along the coast road at night.
Jul 2026 · Milan · paid.
Forty-one of them, in twenty-two years. I counted. I’m going to tell you about some more of them, as we go. They show things. That’s why I tell them.
But I’ll tell you now, straight, so you’re not waiting for it: ten of them I’m not going to tell you about at all.

Ten of the forty-one have a small circle drawn beside them in brown ink. A perfect little circle, the size of a lentil, drawn with care, in the margin next to the word paid. Like the circle I saw when I was six, next to a name above mine, before he closed the book.
“What are those?” I asked him, there in the glass office, with my finger on one.
“Special,” he said.
That’s what he said. Special. And I said nothing back, because I knew which they were. I had paid them.

So that’s how it’ll be, with those ten, and with any more. When we come to one, I’ll tell you there was a debt, and I’ll tell you it was paid. And that’s all you’ll get. You’ll be annoyed. I’m sorry. Some things are not for telling, not yet, and I’ve decided that these are mine.
I’ve decided. You’ll notice I said that.

I sat in his office for three hours and read the Register, the whole green volume from 1971. He left me alone with it. He went down to the pharmacy, and I heard him through the floor, talking and laughing with the pharmacist.

I read the columns of the others. The Soldier’s, starting in 1990: Sundays, Sundays, then, when he was eighteen, monthly, then seasonal. Debts in places I’d never heard of, in Afghanistan, in Iraq, in Libya, which aren’t debts the Held decided, Ferrante said, but debts the Held were glad of. The Trader’s, which ended in April, with a blank space under it where May should have been, like a missing tooth. The Founder’s, the Surgeon’s. The girl with the red shoes, who’d been placed in Brussels, among the people who write the laws for all of Europe.
Then I went back to the beginning of the volume, to 1971, and read the column at the very front.

It wasn’t a child’s. It was a Keeper’s. Ferrante’s Keeper, the doctor from the doorway on the Via Foria in 1943. He’d kept his own column, as well as his Hand’s, and in it there were no Sundays and no debts. There were just dates, one a year, with a word beside each: well. Well. Tired. Well. Hands, which I didn’t understand. Well. It went down the page in a thin, slanting, old man’s writing, getting thinner and shakier year by year, until 1973.
And in 1973 the last entry wasn’t his.
It was in another hand. It was in Ferrante’s hand, the upright careful one I knew from my own column, though younger, a little bigger, pressing harder into the paper.
Sunday. 4 min.
That’s all. Sunday. 4 min. And then nothing more in that column, ever, all the way down the page to the bottom, ruled empty lines.

I went through the cupboard door into the cold room with a pair of cotton gloves on, and took out the old volumes from the bottom shelf, one after another, the cracked leather ones, and found the Keepers’ columns. I have good eyes and plenty of time.
Every one was the same.

Every Keeper’s column ended in the middle of a page. And every last entry was in a different hand from the rest of the column. It was in the next Hand’s writing. A word, Sunday, and a number, every time. Sunday. 3 min. Sunday. 5 min. Sunday. 6 min.
Thirteen Keepers before him. Thirteen columns. Thirteen last entries, all in the next one’s handwriting.
I put the volumes back exactly as I’d found them, and took off the gloves. Then I stood in the cold room among the sixty-one skulls in their little houses, at fourteen degrees, and looked at them.
I’d always thought there were more skulls than Keepers. Sixty-one, against thirteen. I’d always assumed the others were just old ones, from the Fontanelle, adopted long ago.

I looked at the little houses. Most were wood or tin. Twelve of them, I noticed for the first time, standing there, had something in front of their little doors: a tiny brass plate, the size of a postage stamp. And on each brass plate, a number.
3 min. 5 min. 4 min.
I heard Ferrante coming up from the pharmacy, his slow, heavy, careful tread on the stairs, still laughing at something the pharmacist had said.
I went out to meet him with the green book under my arm, and we drove to the cave, because it was Sunday.
17. The Captain
The dead want only to be remembered. That is why they are so useful.

There’s a debt I want to tell you about properly, because people who read things like this will want to know whether I’m a monster. I’d like to help you decide. I can’t decide it for you. I haven’t got the part.
In August a girl from the Held was raped.

She was the daughter of the man with the car dealerships, the one whose accountant I poisoned when I was twelve. She was nineteen. She’d gone to a party in a villa on the coast, and a man had put something in her drink, and in the morning she’d woken up in a room she didn’t know with her dress torn and no memory, only the bruises and the blood, and a photograph on her phone that someone had sent her, laughing.

The man was twenty-eight, the son of a family that owned half the hotels on the coast. Within a week there were four lawyers. Within a month the case was closed for lack of proof, and the photograph had been deleted from every phone except hers.

Her father came up the stairs on a Sunday, past the brass plate, and stood in the heavy air to his neck. He didn’t sit on a chair. He didn’t take his coat off. He couldn’t speak. He just stood at the front of the room and shook, and pushed a fat envelope into the house of a skull with a tin roof so hard that it split the back.
Ferrante didn’t need eleven words. He said one.
“Yes.”

The man went out every night. He had a red open-topped car he liked people to see. He was easy to find and easy to follow, and easy, in the end, to talk to. He never in his life had been told no by a woman, and he couldn’t imagine one would lead him anywhere he didn’t want to go. I sat down next to him at a bar in Chiaia at midnight. I put my hand on his knee, and I told him I knew a place in the old city where nobody would ever find us.
He thought I meant something else. He was very pleased. The heavy air round his good Italian shoes was nothing, a film. I’d never seen a man less afraid who wasn’t one of us.
I took him to the Fontanelle.

It’s open to visitors now, in the day. The city cleaned it up and put in lights. People come in groups with guides and take photographs. At night it’s locked behind tall iron gates, and I had a key, because one of the forty is on the committee that runs it.
I’ll describe it for you, because there is nothing like it anywhere in the world.

You go in through the gates at the end of a narrow street in the Sanità, at the foot of the hill, and the hill opens in front of you like a mouth. The cave is enormous. It’s not a cave, really; it’s a quarry the Greeks and Romans dug, cutting out the soft yellow stone to build the city, chamber after chamber, deeper into the hill. The roofs are high as a church’s, lost in darkness. And all along the walls and the floor of every chamber, in long low banks, in heaps, in neat rows like loaves on shelves, are the dead.

Skulls, thousands and thousands of skulls. Long bones stacked like firewood. Forty thousand dead, more or less; nobody knows exactly. The ones the city had no room for: the plague dead of 1656, the cholera dead of 1836 and 1884, the poor who couldn’t pay for a grave, all brought here and laid in the dark, and forgotten. And then remembered, by the women of the Sanità, one skull at a time. Here and there among the banks of bones are the little houses: wood, tin, stone, with their tiny roofs and doors, some with lace, some with plastic flowers, some with a rosary hung over the roof, some with coins pushed into the eye sockets. Capuzzelle. The adopted ones. Each one somebody’s.

With a torch, at night, it’s the most beautiful place I know. The light goes across the faces of the skulls, thousands of them, and their eye sockets fill with shadow and empty again as you pass, so it looks as though they’re all turning to watch you go by.
He stopped at the gate when he saw it. The heavy air came up round his ankles, his shins. He tried to laugh.
“What is this?” he said.
“It’s where the city keeps the people it doesn’t want,” I said. “Come on.”

He came. That’s what I want you to notice. He came on, into the dark, among the bones, behind a woman he’d met an hour ago, with a torch. The heavy air was rising round him with every step, past his knees, and he came anyway. You’d think that being afraid would turn people back. It doesn’t, mostly. Mostly it makes them obedient. Fear doesn’t make you run. It makes you follow whoever doesn’t seem afraid.

I talked to him the whole way. Gently. He wasn’t the first man I’d taken down there. I told him about the plague, and the carts, and the boy who sat on the corpses and sang. I told him about the women who came down here in the war, when the bombs fell, to ask the skulls to keep their sons alive. I told him about the archbishop in 1969. I told him the names of the famous ones: the Captain, and Donna Concetta, the head that sweats. I told it to him the way you’d tell a child a story to keep it walking, and he kept walking.

The Captain is at the back of the deepest chamber, on a raised stone in a little shrine of his own, behind a low iron rail. He’s an ordinary skull, the colour of old ivory, with a cross on the stone in front of him and offerings around him: a soldier’s medal, a child’s shoe, a lottery ticket. The story is that a woman of the Sanità used to come and pray to him every day. A young man who was courting her was jealous of the skull, and one day he came down here and poked the Captain in the eye with a stick, and laughed, and asked the skull to come to his wedding. And on the wedding day a stranger came, dressed as a soldier. And when they asked him to take off his hat, he did. Under the hat he was a skeleton, and the bridegroom and the bride both dropped dead of fright on the spot.
He doesn’t sweat. That’s Donna Concetta, in her glass case nearer the entrance; the women touch her and their fingers come away wet. Nobody has ever said it of the Captain.
I stopped in front of the Captain, and turned round with the torch under my chin, the way children do to frighten each other, and looked at the man.
He was standing in it to the chest.
He knew. Not what, but that. He’d known for some minutes. I’d watched him know, and keep walking anyway. His face was white and wet. I could hear his breath, high and short.
“Do you know why you’re here?” I said.
“I didn’t do anything,” he said. “She wanted to. She was drunk. Who sent you? Her father? I’ll pay. I’ll pay you double, I’ll—”
“You put her in a room she didn’t know,” I said. “So I’ve put you in one.”
I’ll tell you what I did, but not all of it, and not because it’s too horrible. It’s because I want you to think about the right part.

I’ll tell you that it took a long time, and that I talked to him the whole time, gently, in the voice you’d use for a frightened animal. I told him about the dead around us, who had died of plague and cholera and hunger, of things they didn’t choose. I told him each of them had been afraid at the end, as he was now. I told him that this was the most honest he had ever been in his life, and that he should notice it. I’ll tell you the heavy air rose until it was over both our heads, until I was standing at the bottom of a lake of his fear at the back of the Fontanelle, among forty thousand skulls, with the torch shining through it like a lamp through dark water. And the skulls were all looking at us, their eyes filling and emptying with the light.

I’ll tell you that at the end I left him lying on the long bank of bones beside the Captain’s shrine, with his face turned to the wall, among the others, the way the city leaves the people it doesn’t want. It’s a big cave. It would be eleven days before a guide noticed him, and then only by the smell.

And I’ll tell you that afterwards I stepped over the iron rail and knelt in front of the Captain, and took a cloth out of my pocket, and cleaned him. I wiped the dust off the top of his head, and out of his eye sockets, and off the stone in front of him, the way the women used to, tenderly, as you’d wash an old man’s face.
He was wet.

The top of his skull, under my cloth, was wet. Cold and wet, beaded, the way a glass of cold water sweats on a summer table. I took the cloth away and looked at it in the torchlight, and it was damp. I touched my finger to his forehead and then to my tongue.
Salt.
Like tears. Like the sea.
Nobody has ever said it of the Captain. He did it for me.
Now, here’s the part I want you to think about.

I’ve told you what he did. I’ve told you what I did. You’re deciding, now, whether it’s justice or murder or both, whether I’m the girl’s avenging angel or a mad woman with a torch. Whether the father was right to come up the stairs. Whether the Held are monsters or the only thing in this city that works.
Go on. Decide.

And then ask yourself this. If I had found a man, one ordinary man, who had raped a girl and walked free, and come to you with him, and said: Here. Tell me to, and I’ll take him into the dark, and nobody will ever know, and nothing will ever happen to you. What would you have said?
And ask yourself whether what you’d have said would have come from your idea of justice, or from the heavy air round your feet.
I walked home through the Sanità at four in the morning. The van was waiting under the bridge, with Ferrante in it, as he always was after the long ones.
“Someone has asked for you,” he said, as I got in. He didn’t start the engine.
“Who?”
“Some people who would like to know,” he said, “what happened to an engineer on a scooter on the coast road in April.”
18. What Torture Is For
Pain is not the instrument. Pain is the oil. The instrument is fear.

They took me on a Tuesday, at the bottom of the steps below the Rione Terra, at eleven in the morning, in the sun, with a white van. Four men. They were quick and good at it. One of them put a cloth bag over my head and another hit me on the back of the skull with something heavy wrapped in a towel. They did it so well that I’d like to have watched.

The engineer on the scooter, it turned out, had been a nephew. The young man with the beard and the serious face and the samples of bad concrete was the son of a sister of the wife of a man who runs a part of the city called Scampia [SKAHM-pyah].

Scampia is in the flat land at the very north of Naples, where the city runs out into fields and motorways. In the 1970s the government built huge blocks of flats there for the poor, out of concrete, in the shape of enormous triangles, like the sails of ships. People called them the Vele [VEH-leh], the Sails. They were going to be the future. Within twenty years they were the biggest drug market in Europe: sixteen floors of broken lifts and dark stairwells and walkways where boys of twelve stood lookout and sold to people who came from all over Italy in cars with the engines running. The clans fought a war over them in the 2000s and left the stairwells full of the dead. The government has knocked most of the Sails down since. One is left standing, painted pale blue, like a ship stranded on a sandbank.
They took me into the cellar of that one.

It was a concrete room with no window, a drain in the middle of the floor, one bulb, a metal chair bolted down, and the smell of old water and older piss. They tied me to the chair with plastic ties at the wrists and ankles, and took off the bag.

There were five of them now. The four from the van, and a fifth, younger, about thirty, in a white shirt with the sleeves rolled up and a very good watch. He was the boss’s son. He sat on an upturned bucket in front of me, like Ferrante at the gate of the cave, with his elbows on his knees, and looked at me.
“Who sent you?” he said.
I’ll tell you what torture is, because I learned it in that room, and because it’s one of the true answers to the question I’m telling you this story to answer.

Most people think torture runs on pain. It doesn’t. Pain is just a tool, the way a hammer is a tool. Torture runs on fear. The pain is there to make the fear, and the fear does the work. It’s not the cigarette that makes a man talk. It’s the second cigarette, the one he can see being lit, the one that hasn’t touched him yet. The fear of the next thing is what opens the mouth. Every torturer in history has known it. The rack, the fire, the pliers: they’re all for showing. Look what’s coming. The body hurts, and the mind runs ahead of the hurt, terrified, into the future, and begs to stop it. You’re not tortured by what’s happening. You’re tortured by what you’re afraid is going to happen next.
Take away the fear, and the machine has no oil.

They started with my hands. One of the van men did it. He was big, with a soft face and a gold cross, and he was good at his work in the way a butcher is. He took the little finger of my left hand in a pair of pliers and broke it, slowly, so I’d hear it. Then the ring finger. Then he lit a cigarette and smoked half of it, and put the burning end on the back of my right hand, and held it there while it hissed.
It hurt. I want to be clear. I’m not made of stone, except in two small places. Pain is pain. I felt every bit of it, like anyone. I sweated and my breath went short and my body jerked in the ties.
But I wasn’t afraid of the next one.

I watched him light the second cigarette with interest. I watched the pliers come towards my middle finger. I looked at the gold cross on his chest, and at the rust on the pliers, and at the stain on the boss’s son’s white cuff, which was wine, I think. I looked at the drain in the floor, and wondered where it went. I was in pain, the way you’re in pain when you’ve hit your thumb with a hammer. I wasn’t anywhere in the future at all. There was no future in me for the fear to run ahead into.
“Who sent you?” said the boss’s son.
“Your cuff’s got wine on it,” I said. “Salt takes it out, if you do it fast.”
He looked at his cuff.
And the heavy air began to come up off them.

Not off me. Off them. Slowly at first, the first hour, a film round their shoes on the wet concrete. They didn’t know why. They’d done this before, I could tell, many times. They knew what was supposed to happen. A person in the chair screams and begs and weeps and pisses and talks, and the men in the room feel big, and strong, and safe, because the fear is all on the other side of the room. Torture is a machine for moving fear from one person into another. It’s a pump. The torturer pumps his own fear out into the one in the chair, and gets bigger as the one in the chair gets smaller.
I had nowhere to put it. So it stayed on their side of the room.

By the end of the first day it was at their knees. The big one with the cross had stopped smoking. He kept wiping his hands on his trousers. One of the others, a thin one, went out and was sick in the corridor; I heard it. The boss’s son sat on his bucket in it up to his waist, and stared at me, and didn’t speak.
Then they found the door.

It was the thin one who found it, coming back from being sick. He was angry, the way frightened men get angry, and he took a towel off the hook by the door and soaked it in the bucket of water in the corner, and said, “Tip her back.”
They tipped the chair back against the wall, and he put the wet towel over my face and poured water on it.

You may know what that is. Armies do it. It’s very old. Armies call it waterboarding. It was used in the Spanish Inquisition, and in the jungles of Asia, and by American interrogators in secret prisons twenty years ago. A wet cloth over the mouth and nose, and water poured on top, slowly, so it soaks through, so that every time you try to breathe in you breathe in water, and the cloth sticks to your face like a second skin, and the body thinks it’s drowning. It isn’t drowning. The body doesn’t know the difference.
It doesn’t go through the watchman. It comes up the other road. The old road, from the lungs, from the blood. The road that’s wide open in me.
It came.

All of it, the bottom of the sea, there in a cellar in Scampia under a wet towel, with five men standing round me. The alarm. Now. My heart broke into its run. My chest heaved and found water. My body screamed and bucked in the plastic ties, so hard that the ties cut into my wrists to the bone. And I was afraid, utterly, purely, as I’m afraid every Sunday. I thrashed. I made the high thin noise the boy in the cave made in 1656.

And they felt it. I heard them: a breath going out of all of them at once, a laugh, the thin one saying there. The machine had found its oil. The pump started working. Their heavy air went down, fast, like a bath draining. I couldn’t see it under the towel, but I could feel it, the room changing. They were big again. They were safe.
Then the thin one pulled the towel off and the chair came forward, and I breathed.
And this is the part I need you to hear, because it’s the worst thing I know about myself, and I’ve never told it to anyone.
For one second, when the towel came off and the air came into me, I loved him.

The thin one, with sick on his breath, holding the wet towel. He was the one who’d lifted me, and the gift came into me, and my body, which had been trained for twenty-eight years, did what it was trained to do. It looked at the face in front of it and loved it. With everything. The way I love Ferrante on Sundays. A great warm flood of it, up from the soles of my feet, for this man in a cellar who’d been sick in a corridor. It lasted one second. It was the most frightening thing that’s ever happened to me, and I can say that because it’s one of the very few.
The body is so stupid. That’s what I learned. You can teach it anything. Teach it that the terror ends when a hand decides, and it will love any hand that ends it. Any hand at all.
The thin one leaned in close. The heavy air round him was down to his ankles now. He was grinning.
“Who sent you?” he said.

And the second passed. The flood went back down to wherever it lives. The gas was gone out of my blood, and the old road closed, and I was dry again, entirely, as if nothing had happened. I sat there in the chair with water running off my face and blood running off my wrists, breathing normally, and looked at him with the same interest as before.
“Can I have a cigarette?” I said. “I don’t smoke. I’d just like to see if you’ll give me one.”
He stepped back.

I watched it hit them, all five, one after the other. They’d seen me afraid. They’d seen it with their own eyes, the thrashing and the noise. They’d felt the machine catch and turn. And then, two breaths later, it was gone, as if it had never been. As if I’d been pretending, or as if I’d been a different woman under the towel and had gone away again.

The heavy air came back up off them in one wave. Past the knees. Past the waist. It came off them faster than it had all day, because now they knew the thing they’d been afraid of was true: there was nothing in me that they could reach. There was one small door, and it led nowhere. Whatever they did to me with the towel, the minute they took it off, I’d be back. They could drown me, and that would be the end of it. But they couldn’t make me tell them anything, because the only fear I had was fear of not breathing. All you can do with that is give the breath back, and when you give it back the fear’s gone.

They tried the towel twice more that night. Each time it went the same way: the terror, the lift, the one-second flood of love for whoever was holding the towel, and then the dry, calm face, asking for things. Each time they came out of it standing deeper. By midnight the thin one wouldn’t touch the towel any more. The big one with the cross had his rosary out.

The boss’s son sat on his bucket in it up to his chest, staring at me, and in the end he got up and went out without a word, and three of them went with him. They left one, the youngest, to watch me. He was a boy of seventeen with a pistol in the back of his tracksuit trousers and a stud in his ear, standing by the door.
He stood in the heavy air to the neck.

I talked to him. Quietly, for about two hours, in the voice I used in the Fontanelle. I told him what was going to happen. I told him who I was, not my name, but what I was. I told him exactly, plainly, in order, what I would do to the other four, one by one, at some point in the next year or the next ten, at a time they didn’t choose and wouldn’t see coming. And I told him that I’d leave him out of it, because he was a boy, and because I didn’t need him.

I told him about the dog in the cave that never gets old. I told him that I’d been afraid on exactly one night in my whole life outside a cave or a hospital, under their towel, for three seconds, three times, and that he’d seen it. He and the four who’d gone upstairs were the only people alive, apart from one old man, who had seen it. It would be very sensible of him to forget he had.
I said it all very kindly.
You remember what I told you in the Fontanelle. Fear doesn’t make people run. It makes them follow whoever doesn’t seem afraid.
At about three in the morning, he came over and cut the ties.

I’ll tell you that the big one with the cross came back at five with coffee, and that I was standing behind the door, and that I didn’t need the pliers. I’ll tell you that the thin one came back at six to take over the watch, and that I’d soaked the towel by then. I won’t tell you more, except that I gave it back to him exactly as he’d given it to me, and I didn’t take it off.

At seven I walked out of the cellar and up the broken stairs and out into the morning, with my two fingers taped together with electrical tape and my wrists wrapped in strips of a tracksuit top. The boy of seventeen was a few steps behind me like a dog.
The boss was outside.

He was sitting on a white plastic chair at the foot of the blue Sail in the early sun, an old man in a vest, with a newspaper and a coffee, as he did every morning. He looked up at me coming out of his cellar. He looked at my hands. He looked past me at the dark doorway, where no one else was coming out.
The heavy air came up round him like a spring coming up out of the ground. Then he put the newspaper down on his knees, and he put both his hands over his face.
I walked past him, close enough to touch. I took the coffee off the little table beside his chair, drank it, and put the cup back.
At the bus stop I told the boy to go home and never come back to Scampia, and he went. I don’t know where. I’ve never looked.

Ferrante was waiting for me in the van, outside the hospital where I went to have my fingers set under the notary’s daughter’s name. He’d been waiting, it turned out, since the night before, in the car park of every hospital in the north of Naples in turn.
The heavy air in the van was up to his neck.

I’d never seen him in that much. Not even at the gate of the cave, after I’d gone under alone. He was sitting at the wheel in his coat and his hat, drowning in it, his big hands on the wheel, white at the knuckles.
“I thought I’d lost you,” he said.
“To them?” I said. I got in and showed him my fingers. “They’re amateurs.”
“No,” he said. He started the van, and didn’t look at me. “Not to them.”
19. San Gennaro
Every Neapolitan waits for something to turn to liquid in a glass.
The nineteenth of September is the feast of San Gennaro [sahn jen-NAH-roh], Saint Januarius, the patron saint of Naples, the one who holds the city in his hands.

He was a bishop, in the old days of Rome, when Christians were still being killed for being Christians. They tried to burn him in a furnace and he walked out of it. They threw him to the bears and the bears lay down at his feet. In the end, in the year 305, they cut off his head. They did it at Pozzuoli, at the edge of the Solfatara, the sulphur crater, about two kilometres from my bed. A woman caught some of his blood in two small glass bottles as it ran out of him, and kept it.

The bottles are still in Naples, in the cathedral, the Duomo [DWOH-moh], in a silver case with glass sides like a little lantern. Inside them the blood is dried, a dark crust, brown-red, like old rust. Three times a year the archbishop takes the case out of the strongroom behind the altar of the saint’s own chapel, a chapel all of gold and silver and marble. He holds it up in front of the people, turns it over in his hands, and prays. And the blood turns to liquid.

That’s the miracle. The dry crust goes soft and red and runs down the inside of the glass like fresh blood. When it happens, the archbishop waves a white handkerchief, and the cathedral roars, and the bells ring all over the city. The scientists have their explanations. I don’t care about them, and neither does Naples.
What Naples cares about is when it doesn’t happen.

Because sometimes it doesn’t. Sometimes the archbishop turns the lantern over and over and prays and the blood stays dry. And the city remembers every time it has. In 1939, before the war. In 1973, the year the cholera came back. In 1980, before the earthquake that killed nearly three thousand people in the hills east of the city. Each time, the blood stayed dry, and each time, the people say, something terrible followed.
I’d never been. Ferrante went every year. That year he asked me to go with him.

The cathedral was full by six in the morning. Ten thousand people, packed so tight inside that the crowd swayed like the tram in Milan when it went round the corner, and more outside in the street, and more on the steps, and television vans, and a man selling plastic statues of the saint, and police. We stood near the front, in the side aisle, against a pillar. Ferrante held his hat in front of him with both hands.
In front of the altar, in the best place, closest to the saint, sat the old women.

They’re called the parenti di San Gennaro [pah-REN-tee dee sahn jen-NAH-roh], the saint’s relatives. They’re old women from the old families of the city who say they’re descended from the woman who caught his blood. They have the right, by long custom, to sit at the front and pray him into it. And they don’t pray the way you’d think. They talk to him. They argue with him. When the blood is slow they shout at him, in Neapolitan, in front of the archbishop and the television cameras and ten thousand people. They call him lazy. They call him faccia gialluta [FAHT-chah jahl-LOO-tah], yellow-face, because of the colour of his golden statue. They tell him they’ve been waiting since dawn and their knees hurt and what kind of saint makes old women wait. They wave their fists at him. It’s the most Neapolitan thing in the world: a whole city that loves its god so much it’s allowed to insult him to his face.
The heavy air in the cathedral was up to the waist.

I’d never seen so much in one place. Ten thousand people standing in it, packed shoulder to shoulder, a lake of fear filling the whole long body of the church to the height of the old women’s chins as they sat. It shimmered in the light from the high windows. It was beautiful. And it was all, every drop of it, the same fear: what if it doesn’t?
The archbishop came out at nine with the silver lantern, and held it up. The old women started.

I watched him turn the lantern over in his hands. I watched the ten thousand watch it. I watched their faces, lifted, every one, towards the little glass bottles in the old man’s hands. Their mouths moved. The heavy air was perfectly still around them, waist-deep, waiting.
And I understood.
It came to me so simply that I nearly laughed out loud in the cathedral, as I’d laughed in the neurologist’s office. I put my hand over my mouth.
They were waiting for the lift.

All of them. Ten thousand of them. Standing in their fear up to the waist, faces up, waiting for an old man’s hands to decide. The whole city. Every year, three times a year, it stood in the dark with its face down in the gas, so to speak, and waited for a hand to lift it out. And when the hand did, when the white handkerchief went up, there’d be the gift. The roar, the bells, the breath let out, the tears running down, there, there. And they’d go home and love their saint with their whole bodies until the next time.
It was the cave. It was the whole city kneeling in the cave.

The Held hadn’t invented anything. The doctor in his bird mask in 1656 had only found a small, private way of doing what this city had always done to itself, at the top of its voice, under a roof of gold.
The archbishop turned the lantern over. And over. And over.
The old women shouted. Yellow-face. Lazy. Come on.
An hour.
Two.

The heavy air was rising. I watched it go up, a centimetre at a time, from the waist towards the chest, through the whole cathedral, like a tide coming into a harbour. People were crying now. Not the gift kind. The other kind. Children were being held up above it on their fathers’ shoulders without anyone knowing why.

At a quarter to twelve the archbishop put the silver lantern down on the altar, very gently, and crossed himself, and said into the microphone, in a tired voice, that the blood had not liquefied, and that they would pray again in the evening, and that the people should be calm.
It didn’t liquefy in the evening either.
I stood against the pillar in the cathedral with the heavy air up to the shoulders of ten thousand people, as dry as a stone at the bottom of a lake.
Ferrante, beside me, was in it to the chest. He was holding his hat so tight that the brim had bent.
“It’s time,” he said. Not to me. To himself. Very quietly.

That night there was a swarm. Two hundred and twelve earthquakes between eleven and four, the biggest a four point one. The ground under Pozzuoli went up two centimetres in one night. In the morning, on the radio, the man from the observatory used the word accelerating.
Ferrante telephoned at seven.
“Come to Chiaia,” he said. “I’ll show you how it ends.”
20. How Keepers Die
The voice passes only through the hand.
He took me into the cold room behind the cupboard door, among the sixty-one skulls at fourteen degrees, and he showed me the twelve brass plates.
“You’ve seen them,” he said.
“Yes.”
“You read the Register.”
“Yes.”

He nodded, as though that was right and proper and he was proud of me for it. He took down one of the little houses from the third shelf, a house of dark carved wood with a roof of green copper and a little door with a brass hinge, and set it on the table in the middle of the room, and opened its door.
The skull inside was big, a man’s, very white, very clean, with all its teeth. On the brass plate in front of the door: 4 min.
“My Keeper,” he said.
He told me. He told me in the same plain voice he’d used for the Four Days, at his kitchen window, and for the Book of Choosing, at his kitchen table. The keys of the house, one by one.
No Keeper of the Held has ever died of old age, or of illness, or in a bed.

When the Keeper is old, and the Hand is ready, and the ground or the city gives the sign, the Hand takes the Keeper to the cave. The sign is a great swarm, or a great sickness, or a saint’s blood that stays dry: something that frightens the whole city at once, so that a death goes by unseen in the crowd of fear. The Hand carries the lake in two buckets. The Keeper takes off his shoes and kneels down in the dust, five metres in, where the roof comes low, with his face to the dark.
And the Hand puts a hand on the back of the Keeper’s neck. And holds him under. And doesn’t lift.

“Four minutes,” he said. He touched the brass plate. “That’s what the plates are. How long each of them took. Some of the old ones, three. One, in 1841, it was seven. He’d been the Hand of the massacre. He was very strong.” He smiled a little. “Mine was four. In 1973. The year of the cholera. The year the blood stayed dry.”
“Why?” I said.
He’d expected that. He sat down on the edge of the table, his big hands folded, and looked at me with great tenderness.

“Because the voice passes only through the hand,” he said. “Think, Domenica. What is a Keeper? A Keeper is a Hand who has been held, all his life, every Sunday, and who loves the hand that held him more than anything in the world. If the Keeper died in his bed, of a cold, the Hand would still be that. A child. A held thing, with no one left to hold her. She’d go mad. Or she’d go loose.” He looked at me. “Like the Trader.”
“And if she holds him under.”

“Then she has done the one thing,” he said, “that can’t be done by a held thing. She’s held him. She has knelt her Keeper down and kept him there, and felt him fight, and not lifted. She has made herself the hand.” He opened his own big hand, palm up, and looked at it as if it belonged to someone else. “And after that there is nothing left in her to be held. There’s only the Book. And the next child.”
“And the scars,” I said.
He touched the back of his neck. The two thin white lines.

“He fought,” he said. “At the end. They all do. Even the ones who’ve asked for it. The body doesn’t know it asked.” He smiled, sad and kind. “He reached back and caught me. Two fingernails. They never healed properly. I was glad.”
I looked at the big white skull in its house with the green copper roof.
“Did you cry?” I said.
He was quiet for a moment.
“Yes,” he said. “The whole time.”
I didn’t ask whether his eyes had been dry. I didn’t need to. I’d read the chapter from 1884 again, the night before, in the Book of Choosing. I’ll give it to you soon.
He closed the little door of the house, gently, and lifted it back onto the shelf among the others. Then he turned round and stood in front of me in the cold room with his hands at his sides.
The heavy air came up round his good shoes. Not a film. More than I’d ever seen on him in that room. Past his ankles. Past his shins.
“And now me,” he said.
21. He Asks
Do not let your Keeper die in his bed.
He asked me properly, the way an old man in Naples asks a girl to marry him: at his own table, after dinner, with the good glasses out.

It was the next evening, at the house on Posillipo. He’d made the ragù again. He’d put Norma on the record player, the prayer to the moon, Casta diva, and turned it low. It was warm still, the end of September, and the window was open on the bay. Through it came the smell of the sea and the lemon trees, and once, far off, the siren of an ambulance going along the coast road towards Pozzuoli, where they’d begun to move people out of the oldest houses in the night.
He waited until I’d finished eating. Then he put both his big hands flat on the table, on either side of his plate, and looked at me.
“At the next big swarm,” he said. “When the gas is high.”
That was all. He didn’t need to say what. He didn’t need eleven words. He’d needed ten.
“How do you know there’ll be one?” I said.
He nodded towards the window. Out there, in the dark, beyond the end of the ridge and the black water, under the lights of Pozzuoli, the ground was going up a centimetre a fortnight.
“There’ll be one,” he said. “Before Christmas. The blood stayed dry.”
Then he told me how long he’d waited.

He’d chosen me when I was four, he said. He’d been watching me through the nurse’s little book since I was a month old, but he’d chosen me at four, when I stood at the open window on the fourth floor with my toes over the sill. He’d been nearly sixty, then, and had already waited for a child like me for twenty years. He’d had others. He’d placed them. None of them had been the one. And then I’d come, on the steps of the Annunziata in a fennel crate, and he’d known.
“Thirty years,” he said. “I’ve been waiting thirty years for you to be ready for this. To be strong enough. To be held enough.” He smiled. “You were ready a long time ago. I wasn’t.”
And then he did the thing that I’ve thought about more than anything else in this whole story.
He was afraid.

Not the film round the shoes. Not the little lift and fall I’d watched all my life at the Foundation and the gate and the cave. Afraid. The heavy air came up off him as he sat there at his own table, up and up, past his knees, past the edge of the table, past his chest, until he sat in it to the collarbone. His big hands were flat on the cloth, and they were shaking. His long face was grey. His eyes were wet. He was eighty-nine years old, and he’d just asked the only person in the world he loved to kneel him down in the dark and hold him there until he stopped. He was terrified. Purely, completely, the way I’m terrified on Sundays, the way you were as a baby in the dark.
I’d never seen anything so beautiful.

You have to understand. Everyone I’d ever known stood in the heavy air. It was the floor of the world to me, like water to a fish. I’d watched it rise and fall round ten thousand people in a cathedral, and round a man in a wardrobe, and round five men in a cellar, the way you’d watch weather. It had never once meant anything to me. Other people’s fear was a thing that happened in rooms, like light.

But this was his. The man who’d lifted me out of the dark three thousand times, whose face was the first thing I’d ever seen worth seeing, whose hand was the only door I’d ever had into feeling anything at all. He was sitting across a table from me, drowning in it, because of me. Because he loved me, and because he was about to ask me to kill him, and because he was a person, and people are afraid to die.
He was the only frightened person I had ever loved.
I sat with that for a while. I’ll let you sit with it too.
Then I thought of other things, quickly, one after another, the way you see things from a train.
I thought of Saverio throwing a knife into a fig tree and giving me one nod.
I thought of the Trader on the tram in Milan, saying anywhere.
I thought of the seawall, and the Roman columns behind me in the dark, and the question I’d asked myself there, the only question I’d ever asked: Have I ever chosen anything?
And I thought of something under a loose tile in the floor of my kitchen in the Rione Terra, which I’m not going to tell you about yet.
“Yes,” I said.
He closed his eyes. The heavy air stayed where it was, up to his collarbone. It didn’t go down. I watched it, to see if it would. It didn’t.
“Thank you,” he said.
“Don’t,” I said. “You asked.”

He laughed. It came out of him all wet and broken, and he put his face in his big hands and laughed into them, and cried, and laughed. I sat and watched him do it, and I couldn’t tell you which was which, and I don’t think he could either.
Norma had come to the end of the prayer to the moon. The needle went round in the last groove, hissing like the sea.
I washed the dishes. He dried. We didn’t talk. It was the nicest evening we’d ever had.

When I left, he walked me to the iron gate that doesn’t shut, and stood in it with his hand on the bars, the bay all lit up behind him. He looked very old, and very tall, and very tired, and he was still standing in it to the chest.
“Sunday,” he said. “As usual.”
“As usual.”
I walked down the hill in the dark towards the sea, and the lights of Pozzuoli, and my bed over the place where the ground rises fastest.
I’d said yes. I’d chosen something. It was the first thing I’d ever chosen in my life. Or at least I thought it was, walking down that hill, and I want you to remember that I thought so.
Nothing in the room had been frightening. That was the problem.
THE BOOK OF CHOOSING · III — 1884
Naples must be gutted.
Centuries ago I chose a child.
I set down first what the cholera is, for the one who comes after, in case by then it is gone from the world and has become a word in old books, like the plague.

It is a sickness of the bowels that lives in dirty water. You drink it, and within a day, sometimes within hours, your body begins to empty itself. It comes out of you as a grey water, like the water rice has been washed in, without end, more than you would think a body could hold. You lose it faster than you can drink. Your blood thickens like syrup. Your skin goes blue and cold and wrinkled, like a washerwoman’s hands at the end of the day. Your eyes sink back into your skull, and your voice goes thin, a whisper, and then the heart stops, because there is nothing left in you to pump. Half of those who take it die. A strong man can be well at breakfast and dead by dark. It is not a slow death. It is not a clean one.
It came to Naples at the end of August 1884, from France, where it had been all summer. By September it was killing hundreds of us a day.

It killed in the low city. It killed in the four old quarters by the port, where two hundred thousand people lived in tall black houses six and seven floors high. The houses were built so close together that the sun had not reached the alleys between them for three hundred years. Whole families lived in a single room on the ground floor, the basso [BAHS-soh], with no window but the door. They lived there with their chickens and their goat, and their dead when the dead could not be moved. There were no sewers. The wells were next to the cesspits. The water they drank had passed through the cemetery.

The King came. I set it down in his favour. Umberto [oom-BEHR-toh], the new King, the King of all Italy now, which had been made one country twenty years before. He was invited to the races in the north that week and refused, and came to Naples instead. He walked through the cholera wards with his hat in his hand, and put his hand on the dying, and did not wash it afterwards. The people loved him for it. They still have his picture in their bassi.

His Prime Minister came with him, and stood in the alleys of the low city with a handkerchief over his face, and said a sentence I will set down because it was the truest thing any government ever said about this city. Bisogna sventrare Napoli [bee-ZON-yah zven-TRAH-reh NAH-poh-lee]. Naples must be gutted. The way you gut a fish.

And so they did. In the years after, they tore out the four old quarters by the port, house by house, alley by alley. They drove a great straight new street through the middle of where they had been, wide and white, with fine buildings on both sides, and named it after the King. They called it all the Risanamento [ree-zah-nah-MEN-toh], the making-healthy.
And the people who had lived in the black houses for three hundred years had to go.

Many did not want to go. They had nowhere to go. Where does a family go who have lived in one room on the ground floor since their great-great-grandfathers? So they stayed, behind their doors, in their bassi, with their goats, and refused. And the men who had bought the land from the city, to build the fine white buildings on it, came to the Held.
I was the Keeper. And my Hand was a girl.

I found her in the cholera hospital, in the September of the worst of it. She was fifteen, a foundling of the Annunziata like all of them, and she worked in the hospital laundry. She washed the sheets of the dying, and when there were too many of the dying for the nuns, she washed the dying themselves, and then the dead. She was small and strong and very dark, with big red hands from the lye, the strong soap they used for the sheets. She sang while she worked. Lullabies, the old ones, from the Sanità. She sang them to the dead as she washed them, very low. She was the only one in that hospital who went near the cholera without a cloth over her face, who put her hands in the grey water without fear of it. She drank from the same cup as the dying. She did not take sick. The nuns said she was a saint.
I knew what she was. I had been one.

I took her to the cave at fifteen, which is very old to begin. I held her under, and she fought, and I lifted her, and she loved me. I have never had such a child. She went under longer than any before her except the Hand of the massacre. She came up out of it every Sunday weeping, beautiful, and put her red hands round my neck and wept into my coat.
And on the other six days I sent her into the low city, to the bassi of the people who would not leave.
I set down what she did as plainly as the Register does, because that is how it should be set down.

The ones who would not leave got the cholera. That is all. In that year, in those streets, nobody counted. A family of seven in a basso by the port, behind a door that would not open for the men from the Risanamento, took the cholera in a night and was found in the morning, all seven, blue and cold. A widow on the fourth floor who had sworn on the Madonna that they would carry her out feet first got her wish. An old man who had been born in his room and said he would die in it did. She went in at night with her laundry basket and her lullabies, and did what she did, and came out. And in the morning the cholera carts came and took them away, and nobody ever asked a question, because hundreds were dying every day, and what were seven.
I will not set down what she put in their water. The one who comes after does not need to know. It is not the method that matters. It is the child.
Forty-three debts, that autumn and the next. The fine white street went through on time.
I set down now the thing that I most wish the one who comes after to read and think about.

She wept every Sunday. I have said so. She wept as no Hand had ever wept, more beautifully than the boy of 1656 who learned on the second Sunday, more beautifully than the Hand of the massacre. When I lifted her, she clung to me and sobbed, and her whole small body shook, and I was undone by it every time. I loved her more than I have loved anything in my life.

One Sunday in the winter of 1886, I lifted her and threw the water, and she wept, and clung to me. And over her shoulder, because I was holding her close, I could see her face in the little hand-mirror I had set on the wall of the passage to see the candle by.
And her eyes, I noticed, were bright and dry.

The tears were running down her face. Her mouth was open and sobbing. Her shoulders were shaking. And her eyes, above it all, were perfectly clear and calm, and looking past my ear at the mirror, at me, watching me be undone.
I did not ask myself what it meant.

I set that down. I did not ask myself. I knew what I had been, at fifteen. I knew what I had learned, on my own second Sunday, in my own Keeper’s arms. And I chose not to ask, because the asking would have taken from me the only thing I had left that I loved. I put my face in her hair and said there, there, good girl, and I let her weep, and I loved her.

She will hold me under. It is the way. When the ground goes up, or the blood stays dry, or the sickness comes back, she will carry the lake up the hill in two buckets, and kneel me down, and keep me there. She will weep over me the whole time. I know it as I know my own name.
I am content.
Do not let your Keeper die in his bed.
Below this, at the foot of the page, in a different hand: small, round, upright, pressed hard into the paper, the hand of a woman who learned to write late.
April 1906. The year the mountain burned. Four minutes and ten seconds.
I wept over him the whole time.
IV. THE FIELDS
22. Red Zone
Count the swarms. Never count the dead.
October came in hot and the ground kept going up.
I’ll tell you what that’s like, from inside it, because you’ll never live in a place like this and you should know.

It’s not like a storm. A storm comes, and does its worst, and goes. This was more like living on the back of an animal that’s slowly waking up. Every week the man from the observatory came on the radio and said a number. Ten millimetres this month. Fifteen. Twenty. Then the word accelerating again, which nobody liked. The earthquakes stopped coming in swarms with quiet weeks in between and simply came, every day, little ones, two and three at a time. Glasses walked across tables. Pictures hung crooked on every wall in Pozzuoli, and people stopped straightening them. Old cracks in the walls of the houses opened a finger’s width, and new ones came. In the Rione Terra a piece of the cathedral’s cornice fell into the square at four in the afternoon and smashed a tourist’s rented scooter, and the tourist stood beside it laughing and taking photographs.

The gas came up too. That’s the part people outside don’t know about. When the ground rises, the volcano breathes harder, and what it breathes is carbon dioxide, the same gas as the cave. It comes up through the soil, through cracks in the roads, through the floors of cellars. The scientists measure it in tonnes. In October they were measuring four or five thousand tonnes a day, coming up out of the ground of the Burning Fields, invisible, heavier than air, filling the low places. They put up signs in Pozzuoli telling people not to sleep in basements and not to let small children play in hollows in the ground. Two dogs were found dead in a dip in a garden in Agnano. Nobody knew why, except me.

The government moved the alert from green to yellow, and then talked on television about orange. They put up maps on the walls of the town halls showing the red zone in red: the ground that would be lost first, half a million people. They showed the roads out, with arrows, and which towns in which other parts of Italy would take the people of which streets, if the time came. Pozzuoli would go to Lombardy, in the north. People laughed at that. They’ll make us eat polenta [poh-LEN-tah], they said. Polenta is cornmeal porridge, the food of the north. Neapolitans think it’s what you’d feed a horse.
And they stayed. Every single one of them. That’s the bargain.

I was the only person in Pozzuoli who slept well. I watched the heavy air in the streets at night come up and go down, come up and go down, with the shocks. The whole town was breathing fear in and out like a sleeper with a bad chest.
On the twelfth of October there was a debt.
I’ll tell you about the place first, because it matters, and because something happened there that you should know about, and it’s not mine.

The Solfatara is a crater on the edge of Pozzuoli, a small one, about seven hundred metres across, flat-bottomed, white and grey and yellow, like the inside of an old cooking pot that’s been left on the flame. Steam comes up out of the ground all over it, in jets and wisps, through holes crusted with yellow sulphur crystals like sugar on a cake. In some places the ground is hot enough to cook an egg. In the middle there’s a pit of grey mud that bubbles and heaves and plops, slowly, like porridge on the stove. The scientists call the holes where the gas comes out fumaroles [FYOO-mah-rohlz], from the Latin for smoke. The biggest one hisses like a train.

For a hundred years people paid to walk on it. There was a campsite at the edge, with pine trees and a swimming pool, and families came from all over the world to stand on the crust of a volcano and breathe the sulphur and take photographs of the steam.

On the twelfth of September 2017, a family from the north, near Venice, were walking there on holiday: a father, a mother, and two boys, eleven and seven. The eleven-year-old went past the fence, into a place where you weren’t supposed to go. The ground was only a crust there. It broke under him, and he fell into a hole full of hot mud and gas. His father went in after him. Then his mother went in after them both. All three died in the hole. The seven-year-old stood at the edge and watched. He was the only one left.

They closed the Solfatara after that. It’s been closed ever since, behind a high fence and locked gates, while the lawyers argue. The steam comes up among the empty pine trees, and the swimming pool at the campsite is dry, with leaves in the bottom.

I’ve thought about that father many times. He went in. He saw his boy go down into the ground and he went in after him, into the hot mud and the gas, knowing, as anyone would have known. He went anyway. And then the mother did the same.
That’s courage. That’s what I was telling you about at the beginning. That’s the thing I haven’t got.
I’ve wondered, sometimes, what I’d have done.
The debt was a boy of nineteen.

His name doesn’t matter. He was a climber of things he wasn’t supposed to climb: cranes, bridges, the outsides of churches, the tops of the empty towers at the edge of the city. He went into places nobody was supposed to go, closed tunnels and fenced-off ruins and the sewers under the old city. He filmed himself doing it with a camera on his chest, and put it on the internet, and a great many people watched him. In the films he never hurried. He never looked down. He walked along the edge of a crane forty storeys up the way you’d walk along a kerb. He talked to the camera the whole time, calmly, about what he could see.
He’d announced that he was going into the Solfatara. Into the closed crater, past the fence, at night, at the worst of the gas, to film the fumaroles from the inside. He’d told his followers when.
He was one of the eleven. One of the circles.
I’m not going to tell you this one.

I’ll tell you that I went over the fence at the Solfatara at two in the morning, in the dark, after him. I’ll tell you that the heavy air from Pozzuoli lay at the foot of the fence like snow against a wall. Then I was over, and inside, and there was none: only the real gas, the volcano’s, which I couldn’t see, and the steam, which I could. It went up all round me in white towers in the moonlight, out of the ground, hissing. It was like walking through the middle of a sleeping army breathing. The ground was warm through my shoes. The mud pit in the middle was heaving and plopping in the dark. I could smell rotten eggs, and something hot and metallic underneath it, like a coin in your mouth.

I’ll tell you that I found him at the big fumarole, the one that hisses like a train, standing at the edge of the steam with his camera on his chest, filming. That he turned round when he heard me and didn’t jump, didn’t start, didn’t stand in anything. He looked at me with interest, the way the boy of 1656 looked at the knife.
I’ll tell you that I walked up to him.
And that’s all you get.

I came back over the fence at four in the morning, alone. The film from his camera was never posted. People who’d followed him waited for it for a week, and then went on to something else, the way people do.
The Register, under my column, in Ferrante’s upright hand: Oct 2026 · Solfatara · paid. And a little circle beside it, the size of a lentil.
Twelve days later Ferrante gave me a letter to deliver to the Soldier.
23. The Soldier
Nobody stops a woman who is not afraid of being stopped.
The letter was in a plain white envelope, sealed, with nothing written on the front. Ferrante gave it to me in the van outside the Foundation, and said only: “Into his hand. Not into anyone else’s.”
I didn’t ask what was in it. I’d never asked what was in anything.

Lago Patria is twenty kilometres north of the city, on the coast, where the land goes flat and sandy and there are pine woods and buffalo farms. The buffalo are the big black water buffalo whose milk makes the real mozzarella, standing in muddy fields with their horns swept back like the hair of old film stars. And there’s the lagoon, wide and shallow and grey, with herons in it. And beside the lagoon, behind three fences, there’s NATO.

NATO is the alliance of the countries of Europe and North America that promised after the Second World War to defend each other. If one is attacked, all of them fight. The base at Lago Patria is one of its big headquarters, the one that watches the south: the Mediterranean, Africa, the Middle East. It’s a town of its own, low white buildings and car parks and flagpoles with twenty-odd flags on them, and satellite dishes, and a gym, and a supermarket that sells American breakfast cereal. Three thousand people work there, from all those countries, in uniform and out of it. You can’t get in without a pass, and a pass needs your papers, your fingerprints, your face on a computer in Brussels.
I don’t have papers.
I’ll tell you how I got in, because it’s funny. It shows something, and that’s the reason I tell you anything.
I walked in.

That’s all. There was a catering van at the side gate at seven in the morning, delivering trays of pastries to the officers’ coffee bar. The driver and his boy were carrying the trays in through a door by the gate, past a guard with a rifle, a young man from the Italian air force, who was checking their passes. I picked up a tray from the back of the van — sfogliatelle, two dozen, still warm — and followed the boy in.

The guard looked at me. I looked back at him. I didn’t smile. I didn’t hurry. I didn’t look at my feet or at the gun or at his face for too long or not long enough. I didn’t do any of the hundred small things that a frightened body does without asking when it’s somewhere it shouldn’t be. A guard’s whole training is in seeing those things. He’s a man paid to stand in a doorway and watch for fear. He looked at me, and there was nothing to see. So, the way a mind does when it sees nothing, his filled in the gap with what it expected: a girl from the catering firm, carrying pastries.
He nodded me through.
The heavy air round his boots, after I’d gone past, came up a little. A few centimetres. He didn’t know why. He’d tell himself later it was the coffee.
Inside, I put the tray down on a table in the coffee bar and took a white catering jacket off a hook in the kitchen and put it on. Then I walked through NATO for two hours.

Nobody stopped me. I want you to understand that it isn’t a trick. There’s no trick. A building like that is made entirely out of fear: the fences, the passes, the cameras, the guards. They all work by making a person who shouldn’t be there feel that she shouldn’t be there, so that she gives herself away. Every lock in the world, the doctor wrote in 1656, is made of fear. A lock you don’t feel is only a door.

I found him in a car park behind a long white building with no windows on the ground floor, leaning on a grey car, smoking. He was in uniform, the plain green one, with a red beret folded under his shoulder strap. I’d last seen him when I was twelve and he was eighteen, standing in the sun at the cave in a new uniform with his hands on his knees.

He was forty now. His head was still shaved. His nose had been broken, more than once, and set badly. He was bigger, wider, heavier in the shoulders, with a scar across the back of one hand like a white worm. And his eyes were still that colour: so pale they were nearly white.

He saw me coming across the car park in a white catering jacket. He didn’t move. He didn’t stand in anything. He watched me come with the same face he’d had watching a six-year-old throw a knife at a fig tree for an hour.
I stopped in front of him and held out the envelope.

He looked at it. Then he looked at me. Then he took it, and opened it with his thumb, and read it. It was one sheet of paper, folded in three, and he read it twice, slowly. Then he folded it back up and put it in the breast pocket of his uniform, and buttoned the pocket.
I don’t know what it said. I still don’t. I’ve thought about it.
“Saverio,” I said.

“Not for a long time,” he said. He had a deep, flat voice, like a stone dropped down a well. He looked at me for a long moment, up and down, the white jacket, my hands with the two fingers that had set crooked after the cellar.
“I heard about Scampia,” he said.
“From who?”
He almost smiled. Then he dropped his cigarette on the tarmac and put it out with his boot.
“Is he well?” he said. “The old man.”
“He’s old.”
“Yes,” he said. “He would be.”

We stood there. Two dry people in a car park in the middle of three thousand others, every one of them, in every building around us, standing in their own small shimmer of heavy air. The guards on the gates. The generals in their offices, planning for wars that hadn’t started. The officers in the coffee bar eating my sfogliatelle. The whole great white town of NATO, built out of fear and run on it, and the two of us standing in the middle of it, dry, like two stones in a riverbed.
He looked at me.
And he nodded. Once.
The way he’d nodded when my knife went into the fig tree. One nod. Small. Nothing in it that anybody else would have seen.
It wasn’t in the letter. I know it wasn’t, because I know Ferrante’s letters, and they don’t have room for nods.

Then he got into his grey car and drove away towards the long white building, and I walked back across NATO, past the guard, out of the side gate, still in the white jacket. I took it off at the bus stop and left it folded on the bench.
That evening Ferrante asked me if I’d put the letter into the Soldier’s hand. I said yes. He asked if the Soldier had said anything.
“He asked if you were well,” I said.
He was pleased. I watched him be pleased.
I didn’t tell him about the nod.
24. The Debt Is Six
A child with no fear is not a child. It is a door left open in the wall of the world.
In the first week of November Ferrante gave me a name with no client.

That had never happened. Every debt in the Register had a client, someone frightened who’d come up the stairs past the brass plate and pushed an envelope into the house of a skull. Even the circles had clients, or something like them. Even the Trader had a client: the Foundation itself, the Held, all forty of them, frightened for their money.
This one came only from his hand.
He gave it to me in his glass office, with the door closed, on a plain card: an address in Pozzuoli, a street I knew, near the station. And clipped to the card, a photograph.

A little girl. Six, maybe. Small, sturdy, brown from the summer, with black hair in two short bunches that stuck out on each side of her head like the handles of a jug.
