She was standing on top of something. You couldn’t see what. She was very high up, against the sky, with her arms out on each side for balance, and she was laughing. She had a gap in her front teeth.
In one of her bunches, holding the hair, there was a clip. Pink plastic, in the shape of a strawberry.
I looked at the photograph for a long time. Then I put the card in my pocket, and said nothing, and went.

The address was a casa famiglia [KAH-zah fah-MEEL-yah], a family house. That’s what they call a children’s home in Italy now. It’s not a big grey orphanage with dormitories, as in the old days, but a flat or a house where six or eight children who have nobody live together with a couple of grown-ups who are paid to look after them. This one was on the first floor of a yellow building next to the railway, with washing on the balcony and a little playground behind it: a slide, two swings, a climbing frame in the shape of a ship, a square of rubber matting.
I sat on a wall across the road and watched for three days.

I learned her name the first afternoon, because the woman who ran the house shouted it out of the window every fifteen minutes. Pia [PEE-ah]! Get down from there. Pia! Leave that boy alone. Pia! Where are your shoes.

She’d been left in a culla per la vita [KOOL-lah per lah VEE-tah], a cradle for life, in February 2020, at the hospital in Pozzuoli. That’s the modern wheel. Some of the big hospitals in Italy have one: a little door in an outside wall, like a cupboard. Behind it is a warm cot that heats itself, and when a baby is put inside and the door is closed, an alarm goes off in the ward, and a nurse comes. The mother can be gone before anyone arrives. Nobody sees her face. It’s the same machine as the ruota at the Annunziata, five hundred years on, with electricity. A woman had put Pia into it in the middle of a February night, wrapped in a hospital towel she must have stolen from somewhere, and gone.
Nobody had adopted her. The adoption lawyer from the Held had seen to that. I found that out later.
She was six. She’d been six since February.

On the first day I watched her climb to the top of the climbing frame, the ship, to the very top of the mast, which is a pole with a little flag on it about three metres off the ground. She stood on the top of it with her arms out, against the sky, laughing, the way she did in the photograph, while the woman screamed from the balcony. She didn’t hold on. She didn’t wobble. She stood up there as if the air were a floor.

On the second day she walked up to a dog on the pavement outside the gate, a big brown guard dog off its lead, which belonged to the man from the bar on the corner. Everyone gave it a wide berth. It growled at her and showed its teeth. She walked straight up to it and put her hand on its nose, flat, and pushed its lip down over its teeth with her thumb, to see what they were like inside. The dog backed away from her with its tail between its legs and went and lay down under a car.

On the third day another child, a boy of nine, pushed her off the swing, and she got up off the rubber matting and looked at him. Just looked at him, with interest. Then she picked up a stone from the edge of the playground, walked back to him, and hit him in the mouth with it, hard, once. She stood and watched with her head on one side while he screamed and the blood came out between his fingers.

Everybody in that playground, every child, every grown-up, the woman on the balcony, the man from the bar who came running, everybody stood in the heavy air. It came up off them in a rush when the boy screamed, until the little playground was flooded with it to the height of the swings.
Pia stood in the middle of it. Dry.
Not a drop. Nothing round her small bare feet on the rubber matting. Nothing at all.

I sat on the wall and looked at her, and I can’t tell you what I felt, because I’d never felt it, and I didn’t have a name. The nearest I can get is this: it was like looking into the mirror in the cave, the little hand-mirror the Keeper of 1884 hung on the wall, and seeing someone in it.
On the fourth day I went over.

I waited until the woman had gone in to answer the telephone, and walked across the road and in at the playground gate, and sat down on the edge of the rubber matting near the climbing frame. Pia was at the top of the mast again. She looked down at me.
“Who are you?” she said.
“Nobody.”
“Everybody’s somebody,” she said. “That’s what Mariella [mah-ree-EL-lah] says.” Mariella was the woman on the balcony.
“Not me.”

She thought about that. Then she climbed down the mast, hand over hand, quick as a monkey, jumped the last metre and a half onto the matting, and came and stood in front of me, close. Too close. Closer than children stand to strangers. Closer than anyone stands to me. Her face was a few centimetres from mine. She smelled of crayons and of dust and of the sweet sticky orange drink they give children.
She looked at me with the face. Interested. Nothing behind it. A window.

I’d never been looked at like that by anyone except Saverio and the Trader. And they were grown men, and I was a grown woman, and we were three stones in a river. This was a child. Six. With a gap in her teeth and a strawberry clip in her hair.
“Your fingers are crooked,” she said.
“Two of them.”
“Does it hurt?”
“Yes.”
“Can I see?”
I held up my left hand. She took it in both of hers, small and hot and sticky, and looked at the two crooked fingers very closely, turning my hand over, the way you’d look at a beetle.
And then she bit me.

She bit the side of my hand, hard, with her small sharp teeth, below the little finger, so hard it broke the skin. And then she let go and looked up at my face to see what I’d do, and laughed. A high hiccup of a laugh. One.

I’d heard it before. In the cave, in the dark, under the gas, in March, without the hand, at the very edge of hearing, after the voices of the dead and the voices of the placed: a little girl laughing, once, a high hiccup.
I laughed.

It came out of me before I could stop it, low and rough, the dog-bark laugh I’d laughed in the neurologist’s office. I sat on the rubber matting with the blood coming out of the side of my hand in little beads, and a six-year-old in front of me with my blood on her teeth, and I laughed, and she laughed back, the two of us, at the same joke. I don’t know what the joke was. I’ve never known. I think it was just that we were both there.
And then I stopped.
Because something in my chest did something.

I don’t know how to tell you what it did. I’m going to try, because I’ve promised to tell you everything I can. It wasn’t the heart running, as it runs in the cave. It wasn’t the flood that comes with the gift. It was smaller than either, and lower, and it hurt. It was as if something under my breastbone, something I’d always had and never noticed, like a muscle you’ve never used, had suddenly tightened. Once. Like a fist closing round a bird.
Then it let go.
“Pia!” The woman was on the balcony, with the telephone in her hand. “Who’s that? Who are you? Pia!”
Pia looked up at the balcony, and then back at me, and then she turned and climbed the mast again, to the very top, and stood there against the sky with her arms out.

I got up and walked out of the gate and down the street to the station, holding my bitten hand against my chest. I didn’t look back. I sat on a bench on the platform for an hour while trains came and went. I pressed my other hand against my breastbone, hard, where the thing had happened, and waited for it to happen again.
It didn’t. Not then.
I told myself it was indigestion.
25. The Circles
There is only ever one leash, and the Held hold it.
“You’ve seen her,” he said.

It was evening, at the house on Posillipo. He wasn’t cooking. We were standing in his kitchen with the light off, and the bay outside the window was full of lights, more lights than usual. All along the coast road towards Pozzuoli there was a slow river of red tail-lights, people driving out of the red zone for the night to sleep at relatives’ houses, in cars, anywhere. There’d been a four point four at six o’clock.
“Yes,” I said.
“And you know what she is.”
“Yes.”
He nodded. He turned and looked out at the bay with his big hands at his sides.
“Then I’ll tell you the seventh rule,” he said. “All of it. You’ve been ready for it for a long time. I told you you’d learn it when you needed it.”
And he told me, in the plain voice, the keys of the house.
There is only ever one leash.
That’s how it begins. The first part of it, There is only ever one, is what I heard in the tunnel when I was nine, before the bang and the horns. And this is the rest:

There is only ever one leash, and the Held hold it. No fearless child may live in the world unless the Held hold her. Every other is a fire with no stove, and every fire with no stove is the end of a house.
“The circles,” I said.

“The circles.” He didn’t turn round. “Three hundred and seventy years. Every child like you who’s ever been born in this city, or come to it, or been found by someone who knows how to look. Every one we didn’t choose. Every one we couldn’t hold. The girl in the next street in 1656. The girl on the column in 1799. The partisan girl of the Four Days. And every one since.” He touched the window glass with one finger, gently, where the lights of Pozzuoli were. “They’re found, and the Hand is sent. And the Register gets a circle.”
“Eleven,” I said.

“Eleven of yours. The geneticist finds them, mostly. In the hospital samples. The gene. Sometimes it’s a doctor who notices something, or a teacher, or the police. Sometimes it’s the internet now: a boy who climbs cranes and films himself.” He breathed in and let it out. “You’ve been the best Hand there has ever been at it. You never once hesitated. Not once in eleven.”
I thought of the eleven. I’m not going to tell you what I thought.
“The Trader,” I said.
“Was as good as a circle,” he said, “when he stopped coming. A held thing that lets go of the hand isn’t held any more. It’s loose. It’s the same as never having been held at all.”
“And Pia.”
“Is the twelfth.”
He turned round then, and looked at me in the dark kitchen. His long face was grey in the light from the window. He looked very old.

“I took her to the cave,” he said. “Once. In March. Before you went to the hospital. I had to know. The geneticist had flagged her at birth, but you can’t be sure from a sample. I had to see. So I took her, one Sunday afternoon, after you’d gone home. And I put her under, as I put you under.” He was quiet a moment. “She’s what you are. She came up out of it screaming and fighting and biting my hand, and the second she could breathe she stopped screaming and asked if the dog minded.”
“She lost a hair clip,” I said.
“Yes.”
“You said it was old.”
“Yes,” he said. “I’m sorry.”
The heavy air was coming up round him in the dark. To his knees. To his waist.
“Why not her?” I said. “Why not keep her? Make her the next Hand. Mine. When I’m Keeper.”

“Because you’ll choose your own child,” he said. “When you’re Keeper. A Keeper never inherits a child. The child must be chosen by the hand that will hold her, from the beginning, before she has words. That’s how it’s always been. Your child will be yours. Not one I found and tested in a cave in March and then left in a home by the railway, unadopted, waiting, for six years.” He shook his head slowly. “She’s been loose for six years, Domenica. She’s never been held. Not once, except that one afternoon. She’s a fire with no stove. You saw her with the stone.”
“I saw her.”
“Then you know what she’ll be, at twelve. At twenty.” He put his big hand flat on the kitchen table. “Anything.”
I didn’t say anything.

“And so,” he said, very gently, “on the night of the swarm, when the gas is high, when you take me to the cave to kneel me down: you’ll bring her. And when it’s done, when I’m gone and the voice has passed to you, the very first thing you’ll do as Keeper, before you’re even up off your knees, is pay her. There. In the same place. In the same air. So that the voice passes clean. So that there’s nothing loose behind you when you begin. Only the one leash, and your hand on it.”
The bay was full of lights. The river of tail-lights went on along the coast road, slowly, towards the north.

“That’s the order of it,” he said. “That’s how my Keeper did it, in 1973. He had a girl too. A loose one, a girl from the Quartieri [kwar-TYEH-ree], the Spanish Quarters, the tight grid of alleys above the Via Toledo. He had me bring her, on the night. That was my first act as Keeper.” He held up his hands, his big workman’s hands, and looked at them in the light from the window. “These have done everything that needed doing.”
His hands were shaking.

I watched them shake. They were shaking badly, an old man’s hands, trembling in the air in front of his face as he held them up, the fingers jittering. The heavy air was at his chest. It was very moving. I’d have been moved, I think, if I’d been someone who could be.
Then he turned back to the window to look out at the bay, and put his hands on the sill.
And I saw his reflection in the glass.

The kitchen was dark and the bay was bright, so the window was a mirror. In it I could see his face, and his hands on the sill, from the front, while he thought I was looking at his back. I could see his hands quite clearly against the black glass, lit from below by the lights of the city.
They were perfectly still.
Not a tremble. Not a flicker. They lay on the sill like two stones, like two hands on a piano before the music, steady as the hands of a surgeon who operates on hearts the size of walnuts.
And the heavy air round him was going down.

I looked from the glass to the real man, his back to me, his shoulders still bowed. Round his legs it was draining away across the tiles like a bath when you pull the plug, past his knees, past his shins, until there was nothing round his good shoes at all. Dry. In the glass, an old man’s dry face looked out at the burning city with eyes that were bright and calm and very, very awake. He thought a back can’t be read.
I looked down at the floor round my own feet, and there was nothing there either, of course. There never is.
I turned away before he could see me looking, and went and filled the copper pot for coffee, as if I’d seen nothing at all.
“You’ll do it,” he said, to the window.
“Yes,” I said.
He let out his breath. In the glass, his still hands lifted off the sill, and as he turned back to face me they began to shake again, and the heavy air came back up round his shoes like a tide.
26. Teaching Pia
Teach the child to breathe before you teach her not to.

He arranged it so that I could take her out. I had to be able to, on the night. A child can’t simply disappear from a children’s home in the middle of an evacuation without someone asking where she went. So the adoption lawyer from the Held sent a letter to the woman on the balcony. The letter said I was a volunteer from a charity, the Fondazione Respiro, which gives days out by the sea to children who have breathing problems. It also said that Pia had been chosen, because of a slight weakness of the chest noted at her last check-up. It was signed and stamped. The name on it was the notary’s daughter’s.

Mariella read it twice and looked at me over the top of it on the doorstep, and the heavy air came up round her slippers. Something about me was wrong, and she couldn’t see what. But the letter was signed and stamped, and she had seven other children and a husband with a bad back. In the end she went and got Pia’s coat.
It was the last warm Saturday in November. I took her to Baia [BAH-yah].

Baia is a small fishing harbour on the far side of Pozzuoli, at the end of the bay, where the land curves round. Two thousand years ago it was the richest place in the world. It was where the Romans went to be wicked. The emperors had their summer palaces there, and the senators, and the millionaires, all along the shore, with hot baths fed by the volcano and fishponds and gardens and statues. Julius Caesar had a villa there. Nero, the emperor who killed his own mother, had her killed there. The poets wrote that a decent man couldn’t spend a night in Baia without losing his decency.
And then the ground went down.

Slowly, over hundreds of years, the slow earthquake, the bradisismo, took the whole of Roman Baia down into the sea. The palaces and baths and gardens and statues went under the water, a little at a time, a few centimetres a year, until the waves were lapping at their doors, and then at their windows, and then over their roofs. Today the town the emperors played in lies five or six metres under the surface of the bay, along the shore, for a kilometre. It’s a park now, under the sea. You can take a boat with a glass bottom out over it, or put on a mask and swim. When you look down, there are the roads, the walls, the doorsteps, the floors of the rooms laid in little coloured stones, the mosaics, with the fish going in and out of the doorways, and the statues standing on the sea floor in the green light with their arms broken off, waiting for someone to come home.
I’d hired a little boat. The man who rented it to me gave us two masks and a lifejacket for Pia. She threw the lifejacket over the side as soon as we were out of the harbour. I let her.
We stopped over a place where the water was very clear, and I put my mask on and showed her how to put hers on, and we went over the side together.

She couldn’t swim. She’d never been in the sea. She went straight down like a stone, and I went down after her and caught her by the back of her T-shirt and pulled her up. She came up spitting and coughing, with her mask full of water, and the first thing she did when she could breathe was laugh.
“Again,” she said.
So I taught her.

I taught her to lie on the water on her front with her face in, with my hand flat under her stomach, and kick. I taught her to turn her head to the side to breathe, and to let it out slowly through her nose under the water, in bubbles. It took her about twenty minutes to be able to do it without my hand. She was very quick. She was quick at everything. She had no fear of the water to fight, so all her strength went into learning.
Then I taught her to hold her breath and go down.
“Big breath,” I said. “All the way. Like a balloon. Then hold it, and go down, and look. When you need to come up, come up. You decide. Nobody holds you. You decide.”
She went down. I went down beside her.

Under us, five metres down in the green light, there was a floor. A Roman floor, the floor of a room in a rich man’s house, made of thousands of tiny squares of black and white stone in a pattern of waves and knots. The sun came down through the water onto it in moving nets of light. A shoal of small silver fish turned over it all at once, flashing. There was a doorway at one end, with its stone step worn in the middle by feet two thousand years ago. Beyond the doorway, standing on a block of stone in the next room, there was a statue: a woman, with her face worn smooth by the sea and one arm gone, and the other arm held out, as if she were offering something to someone who’d just come in.

Pia hung in the water beside me looking down at it. Her bunches floated up on each side of her head like weed. Her eyes behind the mask were very wide. She went down, kicking, a metre, two, towards the floor, towards the woman with her arm out. She went down further than I’d thought she could, and stayed down longer, looking. Then she turned round and kicked for the surface, without hurry, and came up into the air and breathed.

She didn’t panic. Holding your breath isn’t like the cave. You can hold your breath a long time before the gas in your blood rises far enough to sound the alarm, and when you come up by your own choice, the alarm never sounds at all. It’s only when someone else decides when you come up that it turns into the cave.
She came up laughing.
“There’s a lady,” she said. “With no face.”
“She’s been down there a long time.”
“Why?”
“The ground went down,” I said. “Slowly. And the sea came in. Now the ground’s going up again, over in Pozzuoli. One day she’ll be on dry land again.”
“Will we see?”
“No,” I said. “It takes hundreds of years.”
She thought about that, holding the side of the boat with both hands, her legs going behind her in the water like a frog’s.
“Again,” she said.

We did it for two hours. She went down to the faceless woman twelve times, and the twelfth time she touched her outstretched hand, and came up shouting. After that we sat in the boat in the sun and ate bread and mortadella [mor-tah-DEL-lah], the big pink sausage of Bologna, that I’d brought, and peaches, and she got peach juice all down her front and wiped it off with the back of her hand and licked her hand.
Then, with her mouth full of peach, she said, “Does the dog mind?”
I’d been watching the water. I didn’t look at her.
“What dog?”

“The yellow one,” she said. “In the hole. With the man with the buckets.” She swallowed. “He lay down next to me. In the bad air. He didn’t mind. I don’t think he minded.” She considered. “I think he likes it.”
“I think he does,” I said.
“Do you like it?”
The sea moved under the boat. Over by the harbour a fisherman was hosing down his deck, and the sound came to us across the water.
“Yes,” I said. It was true.
She nodded, as if that settled it, and threw her peach stone over the side and watched it sink.
“Are you going to hurt me?” she said.

She said it the way she’d said does the dog mind. Interested. Plainly, without any heavy air at all, round her small bare brown feet on the wet floorboards of the boat. Nothing. A child asking what time it was.

I could have lied. I’ve lied to everyone I’ve ever met. I could have said of course not and smiled. It would have cost me nothing. I can lie better than anyone you’ll ever meet, because there’s nothing in my face that the lie has to get past.
“I don’t know,” I said.
She looked at me for a long moment, with her head on one side.
“Okay,” she said.

And she lay down on her back across the bench in the bottom of the boat, in the sun, with her hands behind her head and her wet hair drying in salty spikes, and went to sleep. Just like that. Between one breath and the next. Fast asleep, in a little boat, in the middle of the sea, a metre from a woman who’d just told her she didn’t know.
I sat and watched her sleep for an hour.

The thing in my chest happened again. Twice. Under the breastbone, low, the fist closing round a bird and opening. The second time it stayed closed for longer, and it hurt more, and I put my hand flat on my chest and pressed, and breathed out slowly through my nose the way I’d taught her.
I told myself it was the mortadella.

I want to tell you what I was thinking, sitting in that boat, and I can’t, because I don’t know. I’ve gone over it a hundred times. I was watching a six-year-old sleep, over a drowned Roman house, on the last warm day of the year. I had a card in my pocket with her address on it, and a debt in the Register that would be paid in four weeks or less, in a cave, in the gas, after I’d killed the only person I’d ever loved. And I’d said yes to all of it. Twice.

And I sat there and watched her breathe. In. And out. And in. Her small chest going up and down under the wet T-shirt with the peach juice on it. And I counted the breaths, for something to do, the way I counted my heartbeats in the wardrobe in the Vomero.
I counted to six hundred and twelve.
Then she woke up and asked if we could go and see the lady with no face again, and I said no, it was time to go back, and she bit me.
27. Monte Nuovo
When the ground goes up, the frightened go out into the streets. The Held go up the mountain.
On the eleventh of December the Held went up the mountain.

That’s something they do. They’ve done it for three hundred years, whenever the ground has gone up hard. They did it in 1970, the year the Rione Terra was emptied, and in 1983, when the earthquakes came in hundreds a day, and they’ll do it again. The Keeper calls them, all forty, at night, and they go up Monte Nuovo [MON-teh NWOH-voh] with candles, and stand on the top, and sing.
I’ll tell you about Monte Nuovo, because it’s the most important hill in the world, and almost nobody outside Pozzuoli has heard of it.
Its name means New Mountain. It’s new because it’s the youngest mountain in Europe. It’s only four hundred and eighty-eight years old.

In 1538 there was a village on that spot called Tripergole [tree-PEHR-goh-leh], on the flat ground between Pozzuoli and the sea, with an inn and a hospital and the old Roman baths. For two years before, the ground there had been going up. Not slowly. Fast. Metres. The sea went back from the shore so far that the people of Pozzuoli walked out onto sand that had been sea-bottom for a thousand years, and picked up the stranded fish in baskets, and took them home and ate them. They thought it was a gift.

Then, on the night of the twenty-ninth of September, the ground opened. Right under the village. Fire and ash and stones came up out of it, roaring, for eight days. The ash fell on Naples, fourteen kilometres away, like black snow. The people of Pozzuoli ran. When it stopped, on the sixth of October, the village of Tripergole was gone, and in its place there was a mountain. A hundred and thirty-three metres high. Grown out of flat ground in eight days, like bread rising.

It’s covered in pine trees now, and broom, and wild herbs, and there are paths up it, and a little nature reserve with a gate. In its top there’s a crater, small and round and green, like a bowl full of trees. From the rim you can see the whole of the Burning Fields laid out below you in the dark: the lights of Pozzuoli, the black crater of the Solfatara, Agnano with the racecourse, the long curve of the bay to Baia, and the sea.

The Held stood on the rim in their good coats with their candles. Forty frightened, respectable people at midnight on a mountain that had grown out of a village. The notary with her short grey hair. The banker. The geneticist. The priest. The pharmacist with his cough sweet. The car dealer whose daughter’s debt I’d paid in the Fontanelle. They stood in a circle round Ferrante, holding their candles in paper cups to keep the wind off, and they sang.
It’s an old hymn, older than the Held, in old Neapolitan, to the Madonna of the Fire. I don’t know the words. It goes up and down slowly, like the ground.
And the heavy air came up off them, all forty, as they sang.

It came up off them more than I’d ever seen it come off the Held, even at the gatherings, even when the clients were weeping. It poured off them, out of them, down the rim of the crater and over the edge into the bowl of trees, and filled it. By the end of the hymn it was up to their waists. They stood in a lake of their own fear on top of a mountain with their candles shining up through it from below, so their faces were lit like the faces of the drowned. And they kept singing. Their voices shook and they kept singing, to an old man in a grey coat who stood in the middle of them in it up to his chest. His big hands, I noticed, were trembling round his candle.
I stood a little way off, on my own, at the edge of the trees, and looked at them.
And I saw them.
I don’t mean I saw them for the first time. I’d seen them all my life. I mean I saw what they were. All at once, the way I’d seen it in the cathedral, waiting for the blood.
They were the city.

Forty people on a mountain, and they were the whole of Naples, the whole three million, made small, like a city built in a bottle. They were frightened of everything: the ground, the gas, the law, the poor, the rich, their own children, their own secrets, each other, death, God. They had always been frightened. They had come up those stairs past the brass plate, one by one, over the years, because they couldn’t stand the fear alone. And they’d found an old man who would decide for them, and a girl who would go where they couldn’t. They’d pushed their envelopes into the houses of skulls, and been grateful, and gone home, and not looked down. They’d made a bargain. We know what you can do to us. We’ll be good. Hold us.
And they’d never once, in three hundred and seventy years, asked who was holding whom.
They thought they were the Held because they held the fearless child on her leash. They thought it was their leash.

I stood at the edge of the pines with the whole of the Burning Fields lit up below me, and the ground, I knew, going up under my feet a millimetre a day. I watched them sing, and I knew whose hand was on whose neck.

When the hymn was finished, Ferrante blew out his candle. Then they all blew theirs out, one by one, round the circle, till they were standing in the dark. He spoke to them, quietly, and I couldn’t hear what he said. The heavy air was still up to their waists, black now without the candles, invisible even to me except where the city lights below caught its surface and shimmered.
I took a phone out of my coat pocket.

Not my phone. I don’t have a phone, not one with a name on it. This one lived under a loose tile in the floor of my kitchen in the Rione Terra, wrapped in a plastic bag. I took it out a few nights a year, never more. I’d taken it out the night before, and charged it. It was a cheap one, the kind you buy at a market stall for thirty euros with no questions. It had eleven numbers in it.
I sent one word to all eleven.
Domenica.
That’s all. One word. You know what it means. It means Sunday. It’s also my name.

Then I turned the phone off and took the back off it and took out the little card inside, and snapped the card in half, and dropped the two halves into the dark under the pines. I put the phone back in my pocket.
I’m not going to explain that. Not yet.

Ferrante came across the rim of the crater towards me in the dark, slowly, an old man on a mountain. The forty were going down the path behind him with their torches, in a long line, like a procession.
“Soon,” he said.
“Yes.”
He looked at me in the dark. I couldn’t see his face. I could see the heavy air round him, up to his chest, lit faintly from below by the lights of Pozzuoli.
“You’re not afraid,” he said. It wasn’t a question.
“Of what?”
He laughed, very softly. Then he put his big hand on the back of my neck, gently, the way he does in the cave, and held it there for a moment, warm and dry and heavy.
It was the first time he’d ever touched me there outside the cave.
My body did what it had been taught. My heart jumped. My breath went short, once, in my chest, waiting to be pushed down into the dark.
He felt it. I felt him feel it.
He took his hand away.
“Good girl,” he said.
28. The Night the Ground Went Up
The mountain does not ask.
It came at fourteen minutes past one in the morning on the eighteenth of December.

I was awake. I was sitting at my kitchen table in the Rione Terra in the dark with a coffee, the photograph of the dog and the strawberry hair clip on the table in front of me. I wasn’t waiting for anything. I just wasn’t asleep.

First the sound. Not a lorry this time. A sound like the whole rock under the Rione Terra being torn, slowly, the way you tear a thick cloth: a long low ripping that came up through the legs of the chair into my spine. The coffee jumped out of the cup. The table walked a hand’s width towards the window. The light that hangs from the ceiling swung and hit the wall. Plaster came down in a sheet, and a crack ran across the ceiling from one corner to the other like a black river on a map. Somewhere below me in the building something heavy fell over and broke.
It went on for eleven seconds. I counted.
Then it stopped. And then, ten seconds later, it came again, almost as big. And again. And again.

The observatory would put the first one at five point two, in the morning, on the radio, in a voice that had had no sleep. The biggest in the Burning Fields since the instruments were put in, and since long before. Six hundred and forty earthquakes between one in the morning and dawn. The ground at the Rione Terra went up eleven centimetres in one night. Eleven centimetres: the length of my hand. The whole town of Pozzuoli lifted by the length of a hand between midnight and breakfast, like a loaf going into a hot oven.
I went to the window.
I’ve told you what Pozzuoli looks like in a swarm. This wasn’t that.

The whole town was coming out of its houses at once. All the lights were on, every window, every street, as if it were noon. The streets were full: people in pyjamas and coats over pyjamas, people with suitcases, people with nothing, carrying children, carrying old women, carrying dogs and televisions and birdcages and the statues of saints from their bedroom shelves. The car alarms were going all over the town, hundreds of them, set off by the shaking, whooping and wailing. And over them, the church bells. Not ringing for anything. Ringing by themselves, swinging in their towers as the towers swung, all the churches of Pozzuoli at once, clanging out of time with each other like a hundred broken clocks.
And the heavy air.

It came up out of the town the way the sea comes into a harbour in a storm. It ran down every street and filled every square. It rose over the cars and the doorsteps and the low walls along the seafront, over the knees and the waists and the chests of the people in the streets. It was up to their shoulders in the square by the town hall, and over the heads of the children, and over the roofs of the cars, so the car alarms seemed to be wailing at the bottom of a lake. The whole of the lower town was under it. Pozzuoli was a town at the bottom of the sea, with all its lights on, and eighty thousand people walking about on the bottom with their arms full, and their mouths open, and their faces turned up, as if looking for the surface.
I looked at it for a long moment. I’ll tell you honestly that it was the most beautiful thing I’ve ever seen.
Then I put on my coat, put the hair clip in my pocket, and went down the broken stairs into it.

The sirens started at a quarter to two. The real ones, the civil defence sirens on the poles, which I’d never heard before except at the tests: a long rising wail, round and round, over the whole of the Burning Fields. Then a voice, through loudspeakers on a car going slowly along the seafront, telling the people of Pozzuoli to go to the gathering points marked on the maps. The buses were coming. Stay calm. Take only what you can carry. Go north.
The Minister in Rome would say on television at six in the morning that the alert was red. The first time in history. Evacuation of the red zone.
In Milan, I read later, when the markets opened, the price of Italy went down like a stone dropped down a well.
I walked through the bottom of the sea to the yellow building by the railway.

It took me forty minutes. The streets were jammed with cars that couldn’t move, their horns going, people getting out and leaving them with the doors open and walking. A woman was sitting on the kerb in her nightdress, praying the rosary out loud very fast. A man was standing on the roof of his car shouting a name. And on the corner by the station, in the middle of all of it, a little old man with a cart was selling taralli [tah-RAHL-lee], the ring-shaped biscuits Neapolitans eat with beer, hard and crumbly and flavoured with black pepper and fennel seeds. He’d come out at two in the morning in a red alert with his cart, and he was selling them. He was doing very good business. People stood in the heavy air up to their necks, buying taralli for a euro a bag, and eating them, crying.
I bought a bag. I’ve never loved Naples more.

The casa famiglia was on the first floor. The building was emptying, people coming down the stairs with their arms full. Mariella was in the courtyard with eight children in their coats and pyjamas holding hands in a line, and a man with a bad back sitting on a suitcase, and a list. She was up to her chin in it. She saw me and her face did something, and she looked at her list, and at me, and at her list.
“The charity,” she said. “You’re the—”
“Yes.”
“They said someone would come. For the chest. For the ones with the chest. There was a call. A lawyer.”
“Yes.”

She looked at the line of children. And at the end of it, at the very end, holding nobody’s hand because she’d let go of it, was Pia, in a red coat too big for her and a pair of yellow rubber boots, looking up at the sky with interest. Her hair was in the two bunches. She had the strawberry clip in one. The other side was held with a rubber band.
Mariella let go of the line.
“Take her,” she said. She was crying. “Take her. Thank you. God bless you. Take her.”
I held out my hand. Pia looked at it, and at me. Then she came, and took it, and held on. Her hand was hot and dry. There was nothing round her yellow boots at all.
“Is it the hole?” she said. “With the dog?”
“Yes.”
“Good,” she said.

Ferrante’s van was waiting where I’d told him, at the end of the street, with the engine running and its lights off. He was at the wheel in his coat and hat. Padre Pio was on the dashboard. In the back there were two steel buckets, full, with lids on, and a bag of sugared almonds on the passenger seat. The van smelled of fennel.
He looked at Pia, climbing in, and at me. He was in it to his collarbone. His hands on the wheel were shaking.
“Good evening,” he said to Pia, very politely.
“You’re the man with the buckets,” she said.
“I am.”
“Can I have one of those?” She meant the almonds.
He gave her the bag.

We drove out of Pozzuoli against the traffic. Everyone else was going north, a river of headlights up the hill towards the motorway and the buses. We went the other way, east, round the shoulder of the Solfatara, where the steam was coming up out of the fenced crater higher than I’d ever seen it, white in the dark, in great slow towers. Then down onto the old road to Agnano.
Nobody stopped us. A police car passed us with its blue lights going and didn’t even slow. Who stops an old man, a woman and a little girl in a van driving towards the volcano?

The racecourse was dark. The old spa was dark. There was nobody. We could hear, from here, the sirens over Pozzuoli behind us, and the bells, very faint. A shock came while we were getting out of the van, a big one, and the ground under our feet moved sideways like the deck of a boat. The fig tree on the roof of the old spa shook all its leaves. Pia held on to my coat and laughed.
Ferrante carried the buckets up the slope, one in each hand, slowly, an old man in the dark, without spilling.
“The lake was drained in 1870,” he said, to Pia. “So we carry the lake.”
“Why?” said Pia.
He didn’t answer.

The dog was at the gate. Yellow in the dark, with the gold in its eyes, its torn ear, its tail curled over its back. It got up as we came, in its one fluid movement like water standing up, and pushed its nose into Ferrante’s hand, and then into mine, and then into Pia’s. Pia put both her arms round its neck and her face in its fur.
Ferrante unlocked the gate.
He took the candle out of his coat and lit it, and bent, with his knees cracking, and put it down on the ground.
Not inside the passage. Outside. On the dust in front of the doorway, a metre from the gate, in the open air.
It went out.

It didn’t lean, and go small and blue, and lie down. It went out the moment it touched the ground, as if a hand had closed on it. The little thread of grey smoke went up, and stopped, and lay flat on nothing.
Not at the floor. Not at the shin, where it had lain every Sunday of my life.

It lay at the height of my waist, across the mouth of the cave. A flat grey line in the dark, perfectly level, perfectly still, running out of the doorway and across the dust towards us like the surface of a black lake that had overflowed its basin. The volcano was breathing out harder than it had in four hundred years, and the cave was full, and spilling.
Pia was standing beside me holding the dog. She looked at the line of smoke.
It lay across the air exactly at the level of her chin.
THE BOOK OF CHOOSING · IV — 1943
The children of this city did not wait to be freed.
Centuries ago I chose a child.
I set down the year first, because the one who comes after should know what it was to be in this city in 1943. There may never be such a year again, God willing.

I was a doctor. I had been the Hand before that, for twenty-six years, and I had been the Keeper for eleven. I was forty-three years old. I had a practice in the Via Foria, two rooms over a shop that sold buttons. I treated the poor for nothing and the rich for a great deal, and I went to the cave on Sundays with my Hand. She was a girl of nineteen, the only one I had had, whom I had chosen the year I became Keeper, when she was eight.
She died in the bombing of the fourth of August.

I set it down plainly. The Americans came over in the morning, four hundred aeroplanes, and dropped their bombs on the port and on everything near it. A bomb came through the roof of the church of Santa Chiara [SAHN-tah KYAH-rah], the great old church of the queens of Naples, and set it burning, and it burned for two days. My Hand was in the street by the port, paying a debt, a man who had been selling the Held’s secrets to the Fascist police, the secret police of Mussolini’s government. The building beside her came down on her and on him together. They found them in the same hole. I like to think that she paid it before the wall came down. I will never know.
I had no Hand. In the middle of a war. And there was no child.

I had been watching, as the Keeper always watches, for years. I had looked at every foundling of the Annunziata, every child in the bombed streets, every orphan the war had made, and the war had made thousands. I had found nothing. It is like this sometimes. Twenty years without a child. Then two in a year.
In September the war came to us on the ground.

The King and his generals made peace with the Americans and the British on the eighth of September, and ran away to the south and left the army without orders, and in a single night the Germans who had been our friends became our masters. They knew the Allies were coming up the coast from Salerno, and that they could not hold the city. And so they decided to leave nothing behind them. They mined the port and blew it up, the cranes, the quays, the ships at their moorings. They blew up the water mains, so there was no water. They blew up the power station. They set fire to the university. They shot people in the street for looking at them. They put up notices ordering every man between eighteen and thirty-three to report for labour in Germany, and everyone knew what that meant.
Thirty thousand were ordered to report. A hundred and fifty went.
On the twenty-seventh of September the city stood up.
I have seen it once in my life, and I set it down because I do not expect to see it again. The whole city, by itself, without anyone telling it to, all at once, stopped being afraid.

It is not quite true. It was afraid. It stood up anyway. I had not understood, until those four days, that this could happen. The Held are built on the fear of the city, the way a house is built on the ground. We had always believed that the fear was the ground and could not be moved. For four days it moved.

The men took the rifles from the abandoned barracks. The women dropped furniture from the windows onto the German lorries, and boiling water, and the stones of their own houses. The priests rang the church bells to call the people, and hid the men in the crypts. And the boys of the streets, the scugnizzi, ten years old, twelve, came up out of the ruins where they lived like rats and ran at the German tanks with bottles of petrol with a burning rag in the neck. One of them, a boy of eleven, threw a grenade under a tank on the third day and was killed by its gun.
And on the second day, the twenty-eighth, I saw a child walk up the middle of the Via Foria.

I was in the doorway of my own practice, the button shop below, flat against the doorframe. In the street outside the men of my district were lying behind two trams they had pushed over on their sides, with their rifles, and bodies were lying in the road between the trams and the end of the street, three of them. And down the street from the end, slowly, came a German half-track, a lorry with a tank’s tracks behind and a machine gun on a ring above the cab. A soldier was behind the gun, firing along the fronts of the houses, at the windows, at anything that moved.
And from the other end, from behind me, up the middle of the street, in the open, in the sun, came a little boy.

He was six. I learned afterwards. A foundling of the Annunziata, whose nurse had died in the August bombing, who had been living in the ruins since, like the scugnizzi. He was barefoot, in short trousers and a vest. He had a grenade in his right hand, a German one, a stick grenade, with a long wooden handle like a potato masher, which he must have taken off a dead soldier. He was holding it by the head, the wrong end.
He was not running. He was not creeping. He was walking up the middle of the Via Foria at an ordinary pace, the way you walk to buy bread.
The men behind the trams were screaming at him to get down. Women were screaming at him from the windows. I was screaming, I believe.
He walked past the trams and past the bodies in the road, past the men who were screaming, towards the half-track. He looked at nothing but the half-track. Interested.

The half-track stopped. The soldier behind the gun stopped firing. He was a young man, I could see his face, younger than my Hand. He looked down at the child walking towards him up the empty street. He swung the gun round. He pointed it at the child.
The child kept walking.

He walked right up to the half-track and stood beside it and looked up at the soldier, and the soldier looked down at him along the barrel of the gun. And I saw the soldier’s face. I have seen the face of every kind of fear there is, I believe, in my life and in my work. I had never seen that one before. It was the face of a man who has pointed a gun at a child, and found that the child does not care.
The soldier took his hands off the gun and put them over his face.

The boy unscrewed the cap at the foot of the handle and pulled the cord inside, the way he had seen the men do it, and reached up on his toes and dropped it over the side of the half-track into the back, where the soldiers were. And he turned round and walked away, down the middle of the street, back the way he had come, at the same pace.
The grenade went off behind him. He did not look round.

I went out into the street. I do not remember deciding to. I went out of the doorway and down the street to the child, and took him by the hand, by the hand that had held the grenade, and walked him back into my house.
He came. He did not ask who I was. He looked up at me as we walked with the same face he had turned on the half-track. Interested. Nothing behind it.

I knew. You know when you know. I had found no second child in eleven years of looking, and I had lost my Hand under a wall in August. And God, or the city, or the ground, sent me a boy walking up the Via Foria with a grenade in the middle of the only four days in three hundred years when the city was not afraid.

The Germans left on the night of the thirtieth. On the first of October the Americans drove in from the south and found the city had freed itself, and gave out cigarettes and chocolate and tins of meat. The bells rang all day.
On the first Sunday after, I took the boy to the cave.
I set down now the thing that the one who comes after must read most carefully of all.
He wept on the first Sunday.
Not the second, as the boy of 1656 did. Not after the third Sunday of the first debt, as so many have, as I did. The first. The very first time.

I knelt him down in the dust, five metres in, and put my hand on his neck, and pushed his face down into the bad air. He fought as they all fight. He made the high thin sound, the kettle sound, that all of them make. I lifted him and threw the water. And he came up out of the dark into the light of the doorway, and looked at me, and his face crumpled, and he wept. He put his arms up round my neck, and sobbed into my coat, and his whole small body shook. And then he said, through his weeping, as I held him, Thank you. Thank you. I love you.
He cried beautifully. I had never seen anyone cry so well. Not in all my years, not any Hand, not myself. It was perfect. It was the most perfect thing I had ever seen.
I was so proud of him that I did not ask myself where he had learned.

A boy of six, who had walked up the Via Foria to a machine gun with a grenade held by the wrong end. Who had never in his life been held. Who had been under the bad air for the first time for twenty seconds. Who did not yet know what Sunday was. He came up out of the cave already knowing exactly what to do with his face, and his arms, and his voice, and the words.
I did not ask.
I set down one more thing, and then I will close this chapter, because I am tired, and it is late, and he is asleep in the next room. He is nine now. He has been the Hand for three years.
There was a girl in the Four Days.

She was nine, a partisan, a girl of the Vomero. In the fighting she carried messages and ammunition between the men behind the barricades, running through the streets under the German guns. Afterwards people told stories about her: that she had walked into a German post by herself and come out with a pistol, that she had laughed when they shot at her. She was a heroine. They put her photograph in the newspaper, with the other children of the Four Days.
I looked at the photograph for a long time. I looked at her eyes.
In the spring of 1946 I sent the boy. He was nine. It was his first circle.

He came back in the evening and knelt at my feet and put his head on my knee, like a dog, and asked when it would be Sunday. When I opened the Register at his column to write it down, I saw that someone had already written it, very neatly, in a careful upright hand, in brown ink. The date, and the place, and paid.
And a small circle, the size of a lentil, perfectly drawn.
He had drawn it himself.
V. THE BREATH
29. Under
You do not breathe until you are lifted.
The cave was full.
I want you to see it as I saw it, because I’ll never see it like that again, and nobody else ever has.

The doorway in the hillside, chest-high, black. The dust in front of it grey in the starlight. And lying across the air in front of the doorway, at the height of my waist, perfectly flat, the line of grey smoke from the candle. It wasn’t hanging there. It was lying, the way oil lies on water, on the surface of something that couldn’t be seen. That something was the gas. It had filled the nine-metre passage from the floor to the roof and come pouring out of the doorway like water over the lip of a bath, and spread across the slope in front of the cave in a low invisible pool, a lake as deep as a woman’s waist. The volcano was breathing out under us.
You couldn’t see it. I couldn’t see it, and I can see fear. It’s not fear. It’s only the earth’s breath, heavier than ours, lying in the hollows.

But you could see what it did. A moth came fluttering across the slope in the dark towards the lamp in Ferrante’s hand, low, and flew into it, into the invisible lake, and dropped. It didn’t flutter. It simply stopped flying, and fell, and lay on the dust.

Behind us, beyond the racecourse, the sirens of Pozzuoli went round and round. The bells were ringing. Every half minute the ground shifted under our feet: a jolt, a sway, a long low groan like a ship’s timbers. Far away, a car alarm started, and stopped.

I lifted Pia up onto the wall by the gate, the old stone wall that runs along the slope there, above the line of the smoke. I sat her on the top of it with her yellow boots hanging down, and put the bag of almonds in her lap.
“Stay up here,” I said. “Don’t get down. Whatever happens. The air down there is bad.”
“The dog’s down there.”
The dog was lying in the gas in front of the doorway, on its side, as it always did, as if it were grass, with its gold eyes open, watching us.
“The dog’s different,” I said.
“Why?”
“Nobody knows. We don’t ask it.”
She thought about that, and ate an almond, and nodded.

Ferrante took off his hat and his coat and his scarf and folded them and laid them on the wall beside Pia, neatly, the scarf on top. Then he sat down on the wall and took off his shoes. He was slow about it. His knees cracked. He set the shoes side by side at the foot of the wall, toes together, as he’d set mine side by side by the gate on my first Sunday when I was six.

Then he stood up in his socks, and in his white shirt with the sleeves rolled down and buttoned, and went down the slope to the doorway of the cave. He stood in the gas to his waist, his head and shoulders up in the good air. He looked like a man standing in the sea.

I took the buckets off their hooks on the wall, where he’d hung them. I carried them down after him. I set one down on the dust at the edge of the lake, outside it, where the air was good. I carried the other in.

I stood beside him in the gas to my own waist. I could feel it. I’d never felt it before, not standing. It was warm, very slightly, like a bath that’s been run and left, and heavy, as if the air there were thicker than air should be. It pressed on my legs.

He looked at me in the starlight. He was standing in it, the heavy air, the other kind, the kind only I can see, up to the chest. In the light from the lamp on the wall it shimmered on top of the invisible lake of the gas, a lake on top of a lake. His hands were shaking.
“I’m ready,” he said.
He knelt.

He knelt down in the dust in front of the doorway, in the lake, slowly, as he’d shown me how to on my first Sunday: back straight, then forward, hands flat on the warm ground on either side. And as he went down onto his knees his head went down too, under the line where the smoke lay, under the surface of the gas, until only the top of his white head and the back of his neck were still up in the good air. Then he bent forward over his hands, and his face was an inch above the dust, and his whole head was under.
I stood over him with the bucket.
The ground jolted. The bucket slopped. On the wall Pia laughed and held on.
He lifted his head, just enough. It came up out of the gas into the air, his long face grey and wet. His eyes were watering from the sour sting of it. He’d been under perhaps four seconds.
“Your hand,” he said.
I put down the bucket.
I put my hand on the back of his neck.

I’d never touched it before. Not like this. I’d been under his hand three thousand times, and I’d never once put mine where his went. His neck was warm, and thin, an old man’s neck, the skin loose over the tendons like cloth over a chair. Under my fingers, just below the hairline, I could feel the two scars, two raised lines, like two strokes of a pen.
My thumb went under one ear and my fingers under the other, the way his always did. My hand knew how. It had always known. It had been learning, the whole time, from underneath.
I could feel his pulse under my thumb.

It was very slow. It was slower than mine. It was the slowest pulse I’d ever felt in a living thing, slower than mine in the wardrobe in the Vomero, sixty a minute, fifty-eight, steady as a clock in an empty house.
The heavy air was up to his chest. And his heart, under my thumb, was walking.
“Now,” he said.
30. Did You Think We Were the Ones Being Held?
The leash runs both ways. Only one end knows it.
He didn’t go under. Not then.
He held his head up just above the line of the gas, an inch from it, his face turned sideways towards me so I could see one eye, wet and bright in the lamplight. With my hand on his neck, he talked.
“I’ll tell you the last thing,” he said. “Then you can do as you like. You always have.”
I didn’t take my hand away.

“You can’t put fear into the fearless,” he said. “That’s the last thing. That’s the thing every Keeper knows and none of them writes down. The doctor in 1656 thought he’d found the lock. He thought he’d found where God hid the key in that boy, in his lungs, and that by turning it every Sunday he could make him afraid, and then make him grateful, and then make him love. It isn’t true. It was never true.”
The ground groaned. He waited for it to pass.

“What happens in the cave isn’t fear,” he said. “Not the fear you see in the streets. It’s panic. It’s the body screaming for air. It comes up the old road from the lungs, and it’s real, God knows it’s real. But it has no object. It’s not afraid of anything. And the moment the breath comes back, it’s gone, completely, as if it never happened. You know that. You’ve known it since you were six. You come up out of the cave and you’re dry again before the water’s stopped running off you.”
“Yes.”

“Panic,” he said, “can be studied. Like weather. Like a tide. You can learn its times. You can learn what it wants. A child with no fear, held down in the dark every week, doesn’t learn to be afraid. She can’t. She learns what the hand wants. She learns what makes the hand gentle, what makes the Sundays shorter, what makes the man in the doorway soft. She learns to cry.” He smiled with half of his mouth, his cheek against the dust. “On the second Sunday. On the third Sunday after the first debt. On the first.”
“You,” I said.

“Me,” he said. “On the first. I’d been living in the ruins for two months. I’d watched women cry over bodies in the street every day of the bombing. I’d watched what it did to the men who saw them. I’d watched what the crying bought. Bread, sometimes. A blanket. A man’s hand on your head. I learned it from watching, like learning a song. And when the doctor lifted me out of the cave and I saw his face, I knew at once what that face wanted, and I gave it to him. I was six.” The eye looked at me. “So were you.”
I didn’t say anything. My hand was on his neck. I could feel his pulse, slow, walking.

“Every one of us,” he said. “Thirteen Hands who became Keepers. Every one of us learned to cry for the hand, and every one of us grew up and became the hand, and held a child under, and watched the child learn to cry for us. And every one of us knew. We knew, because we’d done it. We knew the child was doing it. And we chose to believe the tears. Every Keeper. All of us. Because it was beautiful, and because the alternative was to admit what we were.”
“Which is what?”
He was quiet for a moment. A shock came through the ground, small. On the wall, Pia ate an almond.
“The leash runs the other way, Domenica,” he said. “It always did.”
He let his head sink a little, so his chin touched the line of the gas, and lifted it again.

“Look at them,” he said. “The Held. Forty frightened, respectable people. The notary, the banker, the priest, the judge, the woman with the clinic. They think they hold the fearless child. They think it’s their leash, their fire in their stove. They come up the stairs on Sundays and push their envelopes into the skulls and look at you by the window, and they think you’re their dog.”
“And?”

“And who decides?” he said. “Who stands at the front of the room and says yes in one word, and is never once argued with in three hundred and seventy years? Who chooses which debts are paid, and which chairs are filled, and which of their money goes where? Who has their secrets, all of them, every envelope, every name, every frightened thing they ever pushed into a skull, written down in brown ink in thirty-one volumes in a cold room? Who sends the Trader to Milan and the Soldier to NATO and the Surgeon to Rome and the girl with the red shoes to Brussels, where they write the laws for all of Europe?” He breathed. “A frightened order doesn’t hold the fearless. The fearless hold the frightened. The Keeper is always a Hand grown old, and the Hand is never held. Not for one Sunday. Not for one second. Three hundred and seventy years of the fearless, ruling a city that’s afraid of everything, through forty people who think they’re in charge.”
I looked down at the back of his white head in the starlight. My hand on his neck.
“You stood in it,” I said. “All my life. The heavy air. I’ve watched it on you since I was four. At the gate. In the van. In the kitchen, when you asked. Up to your neck.”

“You can see what fear does to a body,” he said. “That’s what you see. Not what it does to a soul. A soul you can’t see; nobody can. You see the breath go high, and the sweat, and the heart, and the hands. And a body can be taught. I taught mine. For eighty years. Every time I needed you to see me afraid, I made my body do it, the way you make your eyes cry two breaths after the water. I did it so well that even you believed it. I only ever stopped when I thought no one was looking.” The eye looked up at me, very bright. “Even a back can be read, in a window.”
“You saw me see.”
“I’ve been waiting thirty years for you to see.”
The ground jolted. The water in the bucket slopped over its rim and ran away into the dust.
“And the circles,” I said.

“The circles.” His voice was tired now. “You know why. You’ve known since Milan. There can’t be two. Not because a loose fire would burn the city. The city’s been burning for three thousand years and it’s still here. There can’t be two because two fearless people in a city of frightened ones is a war. And one is a king.” He breathed. “Every Keeper has known it. The doctor in 1656 sent his boy to the girl in the next street within a year of finding him. My Keeper sent me to the partisan girl when I was nine. I drew the circle myself. I wanted to. I’ve sent you to eleven.” He closed the eye. “It’s the only rule that was ever true. There is only ever one. Not one leash. One of us.”
“And Pia.”

“Will be the twelfth, after I’m gone, when you’re the one. And you’ll be what I was. Alone, and holding all of them.” He opened the eye again. “I’m not sorry. It’s the best life there is. I’ve had it for fifty-three years.”
“Then why go under?”
He smiled, his chin at the line of the gas.

“Because I’m tired,” he said. “Not of living. Of being the only one. And because I’m eighty-nine, and I’ve never once in my life been afraid of anything except that cave, and I’d like to find out whether I’m afraid of this.” He breathed in, long and slow, at the very edge of the gas. “And because I want it to be you. I chose you. I want to see what you do with it.”
I could feel his pulse under my thumb. Still walking. Fifty-six.
“There was a letter,” I said. “To the Soldier.”
“Yes.”
“What did it say?”

“It said that if you didn’t come back from the cave tonight,” he said, “if you lost your nerve, if you let the child go, if you did anything at all but what the Keeper must do, he should pay you. A circle. The Soldier’s first.” He sighed. “I’m sorry. A Keeper has to be careful. A fire with no stove.”
“He read it twice,” I said.
“He’s very thorough.”
“And then he nodded at me.”
He was quiet.
His eye moved, in the lamplight, up to my face, and stayed there.
31. Eleven
Centuries ago I chose a child.

I’m going to turn round now and talk to you. I’ve been doing it the whole time, but now I’m going to do it properly, because there are things I’ve told you that weren’t true. You’ve been patient. You deserve to have them back.
I told you there were eleven debts I wasn’t going to tell you about. The eleven circles. I told you I’d paid them.
I never paid a single one.

The first was when I was fifteen. A girl in Caserta, a year younger than me, whom the geneticist had flagged in a hospital sample. Ferrante gave me her name and her photograph in the van, and said special, and I went. I found her in a park, sitting on the back of a bench with her feet on the seat, throwing stones at a pigeon, alone. She looked up at me coming, and didn’t move. Dry. A window.
I was fifteen. I’d paid four debts by then and I’d never once hesitated. I’d been held under every Sunday for nine years and I loved the hand with my whole body.

I sat down on the back of the bench beside her, and looked at her, and I thought one thing. I’ve never forgotten it, because it was the first thought I ever had that was mine. Not his. Not the cave’s. Mine.
I thought: I’m not going to be the only one.
So I didn’t.

I took her to the station and put her on a train to the north with all the money I had, and a name I made up on the platform. I went back to Ferrante and said paid, in the van, in my ordinary voice, and he wrote it in the Register. He drew the little circle in brown ink.
He didn’t ask for a body. Nobody ever asks the Hand for a body. That’s what the Hand is for. You say paid, and it’s paid.
That’s the thing about being obeyed. If you obey well enough, for long enough, nobody ever checks.
I did it eleven times. Over nineteen years.

A boy in Salerno. A girl in Bari [BAH-ree], on the other coast. The twins, the boy and the girl from the north who screamed so much in the cave when I was small that Ferrante had to hold them both, one in each hand, and who stopped coming after two Sundays. They had been circled, years later, when the geneticist found they’d grown up loose, and I went to Turin to pay them. A woman in Rome. A young man in Palermo [pah-LEHR-moh]. A boy who climbed cranes. The others.

I didn’t save them. I want to be clear about that. You’ll want me to have saved them, out of pity, or goodness. I haven’t got either. I didn’t save them. I kept them. The way the Held keep skulls. The way the women of the Sanità used to go down into the Fontanelle and choose one, a stranger, nobody’s, and take it home and give it a name and build it a house.

I gave them deaths first. For each of them the notary signed what needed signing, and a doctor who owed me a favour wrote heart, or drowned, or fell. The twins drowned off a beach in Liguria [lee-GOO-ryah], on paper. The boy who climbed cranes fell into a fumarole, on paper; they found his camera at the edge. Ferrante read the notices and drew his circles.

Then I gave them names. The Held have a notary and an adoption lawyer and a woman in the town hall and a man at the passport office. Their whole machine for making the children they place into real people on paper, with real cards and real numbers, I’d watched working for years from my place by the window. I used it. A little at a time. A form here, a stamp there, the notary’s daughter’s name on a letter. I paid for it with the Held’s own money, a little at a time. The Trader had made them so much that nobody noticed. It’s very easy to steal from people who are afraid. They’re always looking somewhere else.
And then I placed them. Exactly as the Held place theirs. In chairs where fear stops other people.

A woman in the Department of Civil Protection in Rome, the office that decides, when the ground goes up, who must leave and when and by which road. She signed the red alert tonight, at a quarter to two. That was the signal, though nobody in Rome knew it. A man at the port authority of Naples. A woman on the risk desk of a bank in Milan, the desk that decides, when the markets open, what the price of Italy is. A young man in the carabinieri [kah-rah-bee-NYEH-ree], the national police who are also soldiers, in the command for the whole of Campania [kahm-PAH-nyah], the region round Naples. A woman in the newsroom of the state television, who decides what the country sees at six in the morning. Others. Eleven chairs.
A week ago, on a mountain, I sent them one word.
Domenica.
It meant: the next great swarm. The night the whole country is standing in its fear up to the neck and looking nowhere else. Tonight.
“While we’ve been standing here,” I said to the back of his white head, “they’ve been working.”
He didn’t move. My hand was on his neck.

In my coat pocket a phone buzzed, twice. Not mine; I don’t have one. It had come in a parcel from the Soldier, addressed to the volunteer from the Fondazione Respiro, and Mariella had pushed it into my hand in the courtyard by the railway with Pia. I took it out with my free hand and read the two messages on it by the light of the lamp, and put it away.

“The cold room in Chiaia is empty,” I said. “The girl from Bari did that, at three o’clock, while the whole of Chiaia was standing in the street. All thirty-one volumes of the Register. Every envelope. Every name, every secret, every frightened thing every judge and minister and banker and bishop ever pushed into a skull. Three hundred and seventy years of it. The skulls too. She took the skulls. I told her to be careful with them.”
The ground jolted. He didn’t move.

“The Foundation’s accounts will be empty by ten o’clock. The woman in Milan will do that when the markets open, when the price of Italy goes down like a stone and nobody is looking at anything else. The bank in Switzerland. The port in the north. The Trader’s money. All of it. It’ll all be ours.”
“Ours,” he said, to the gas.

“Ours. And the morning. That’s the woman at the television. And the roads out of the red zone, and who gets on the buses, and who’s on the trains, and who goes where, and who’s in charge when they get there. That’s the woman at Civil Protection, and the man in the carabinieri, and the man at the port. And the Soldier. He nodded. You wrote to the Soldier.”
He was quiet for a long time.

“You kept one fearless person on a leash,” I said, “for three hundred and seventy years. And all that time the one on the leash was holding it herself. I’ll give you that. That was good. That was very good.” I looked down at my hand on his neck. “I let eleven off. I didn’t need a leash to hold them. They’re like me. They’ll do what they like. They like me.”
And then — I’ll tell you this — he laughed.

He laughed with his face an inch above the gas, his whole body shaking under my hand. It wasn’t a performance. I’d have known. I’ve watched him perform for twenty-eight years. It came up out of him the way the gift comes up out of you after the lift, unasked for. It was the laugh of a man who’s built a house all his life and come home to find someone has built a bigger one on top of it, without him noticing, out of his own bricks.
“Oh,” he said, laughing. “Oh, Domenica. Oh, good girl.”
I want to tell you something now, while he’s laughing, and it’s to you, not to him.

I’ve lied to you. I’ve told you that I loved him, every Sunday, with my whole body, that I said I love you and meant it. That was true. I’ve told you that I sat on the seawall after the hospital and asked myself whether I had ever chosen anything. That was true too. I hadn’t known, until that night, that I had. I’d been doing it for nineteen years and I didn’t have the word for it. The body loved him. The body was trained. The body cried two breaths after the water and meant it.

And underneath the body, the whole time, there was me. Steering. Since I was fifteen on the back of a bench in Caserta. Since before, maybe. Since I was six and cried, or didn’t cry, and watched his face.
Both things were true. I loved him with everything I had, and I was holding the leash.

Every scene I gave you where I did as I was told, I was steering. The wardrobe. The tram. The Fontanelle. The van, the almonds, the cave. Yes. Yes. I love you. Yes. And I steered you too, on these pages, the whole time. I told you what to look at. I told you the debts I wanted you to see, and how to feel about them, and I hid eleven from you. You let me, because I told you I was obedient, and you believed me, because obedience is the most restful thing in the world to watch.
I’m sorry. In the way that I can be.
Go back and read it again some time, if you like. You’ll see me. I’m there, in every chapter, steering.
He’d stopped laughing. He knelt with his chin at the line, breathing, an inch from the gas.
“So,” he said. “What will you do?”
“I don’t know yet,” I said.
It was true. It was the only time that night I didn’t know.
He breathed in, long and slow, the last good air at the very top of the lake.
“Then let me go under,” he said. “I’d like to. Truly. I’m tired. And I want to know if I’m afraid.”
My hand was on his neck.
On the wall behind me, Pia said, “What are you doing?”
32. Pia Under
There is no rule for this.
The ground went up.

Not a jolt. Not a sway. It went up under us all at once, the whole hillside, the way a wave lifts a boat. It went up and then dropped, and there was a sound like the earth itself cracking a knuckle, deep down, enormous. The wall of the old spa down the slope behind us cracked from top to bottom, and the fig tree on its roof leaned over and fell. The observatory would put it at five point six, in the morning. The biggest of the night. The biggest in the history of the Burning Fields.
And the gas came up.

I felt it come. It came up out of the cave in a single pulse, a great slow heave, like a breath let out by something very large lying under the hill. The lake I was standing in to the waist rose in one second to my chest. It came up over the dust, up the slope, up the old wall, in a single swell, invisible, silent, heavy.
Pia was on the wall.

The shock had thrown her. I didn’t see it. I heard the bag of almonds hit the ground. When I turned round, she was gone from the top of the wall, and she was on the slope below it, on her hands and knees in the dust, where she’d landed. She was getting up. She was laughing. She was six years old, and she stood up into the lake that had just risen to my chest.
It was over her head.
I watched her take a breath. I watched it go into her, the stuff that kills dogs, all the way down.
She stopped laughing.

She looked surprised. They always look surprised. She put her hand up to her mouth, as if she’d tasted something sour, a battery, a fizzy drink gone wrong. Her eyes went wide. She took another breath, bigger, the body pulling for air that wasn’t there, and her hands came up in front of her and opened and closed on nothing. And I saw it go into her. I saw it come up the old road. The alarm. Now. The terror, total, the bottom of the sea, the thing I’d been given every Sunday of my life, going into this child in the dark on a hillside. And there was no hand on her neck. There was no hand anywhere.
She went down on one knee, in the dust, in the lake.
Then onto her side.
The yellow dog got up from the doorway of the cave and went to her, through the gas, and lay down beside her, and looked at me with its gold eyes.
And something happened in me.

I’m going to tell it to you as slowly as I can. It’s the only thing in this whole story I’m not sure I can tell, and I want to get every bit of it right. It’s the only thing in my life that I didn’t see coming.

It didn’t come from my lungs. I want you to know that. I was standing in the gas to my chest, but my head was up in the good air, and I was breathing. There was nothing wrong with my blood. The old road, the one from the lungs, the one the cave uses, was shut. I could feel it shut.
And it didn’t come from the two white stones, the almonds. They’re stone. They’ve been stone since I was a child. They don’t pull any cords. The neurologist showed me.

It came from somewhere else. Somewhere I didn’t know I had. It came up from under my breastbone, from the place where the fist had closed round the bird on the rubber matting in the playground and in the little boat over the drowned house. It came up through the middle of me like the ground coming up under Pozzuoli. It was slow and enormous and it could not be stopped. It was cold, and it was hot. It went down into my legs and turned them to water, and up into my throat and closed it, and into my hands. My hands began to shake. Not the way Ferrante’s shook. Truly. On their own. I looked down at them and they were shaking, and I hadn’t told them to.
I looked at the small shape lying on its side in the dust, in a red coat and yellow boots, under the invisible surface of the lake, with a dog lying beside her.
And I was afraid.
Not of the gas. Not of the ground. Not of anything that could happen to me. I’d never been afraid of anything that could happen to me, and I wasn’t now.
I was afraid for her.

Do you understand? I’d seen it all my life, on everyone, the heavy air, rising and falling round their feet, and I’d thought I knew what it was. I’d thought it was one thing. It isn’t. There’s the fear that’s for yourself, which comes in through the eyes, past the almonds, and I’ve never had it, and I never will. And there’s the fear that comes up the old road from the lungs, which the cave gives, which is only panic, which goes when the breath comes back. And there’s a third.

There’s the fear you feel for someone else. And it doesn’t use either road. It doesn’t need the watchman or the lungs. It comes up out of the place where you keep the people you’d die for, and it doesn’t care what you’re made of. It comes anyway.
I’d never had anyone to keep there. That’s all. That’s the only reason I’d never felt it. Not the stones. Not the gene. I’d never had anyone.
I looked down.
Round my feet, in the dust, under the gas, rising, shimmering in the lamplight on the wall, was the heavy air.
Mine.

The first I’d ever had. Coming off me. Pouring off me. Past my ankles, past my knees, filling the hollow in front of the cave, a lake of my own fear on top of the volcano’s lake. I watched it come up off me the way I’d watched it come up off ten thousand people in a cathedral, off a man in a wardrobe, off five men in a cellar. I watched it rise.
It was the most beautiful thing I’d ever seen.
I took my hand off Ferrante’s neck.
33. The Lift
Whoever gives it back is God.

I don’t remember deciding. I want to tell you that, because everything else in my life I’ve decided. In the wardrobe, on the tram, in the cellar, I always knew exactly what I was going to do a long time before I did it, and I watched myself do it from a little way off. Not this time. This time there was nobody watching. There was only the doing.
I took a breath. The biggest I’ve ever taken. All the way down, the way I’d taught her in the boat. Like a balloon.
And I went down into the gas.

It closed over my head. Warm, heavy, silent. It stung my eyes. I kept them open. I could see her, a dark shape in the dust a metre and a half away, in the light of the lamp on the wall, which came down through the invisible lake as moonlight comes down through water. I went to her on my knees, holding my breath, the dust under my hands warm as an animal. The dog lifted its head and watched me come.
I got my arms under her. She was limp, and heavier than she should have been, the way the sleeping are heavy. Her face was against my neck. Her mouth was open. She wasn’t breathing.
I stood up.

I stood up out of the lake with her in my arms, into the good air, my head breaking the surface. And I breathed, and I didn’t stop. I went up the slope with her, past the wall, over the line where the smoke had lain, up and up, three metres, five, until we were well above it, on the bare stony ground above the gate, where the air was night air, ordinary, cold. I knelt down and laid her on her back.
She wasn’t breathing. Her face in the lamplight was grey-blue round the mouth, as the accountant’s was on the Via Toledo when I was twelve.

The bucket. The second bucket, the one I’d left outside the lake. I could see it, at the edge of the slope, standing on the dust. I went down for it and came back up with it, and I knelt over her, and I lifted it, and I poured the whole thing over her. Over her face, her chest, her small body in the red coat.
