The lake, carried, the way it was carried for me every Sunday of my life, cold from the tap at the old spa.
She didn’t move.

I’ll tell you what I did then, because the pharmacist taught me, when I was thirteen, how to stop a heart. If you know how to stop one, you know how to start one. It’s the same knowledge facing the other way.

I tipped her head back, gently, one hand on her forehead and two fingers under her chin. I pinched her nose shut. I put my mouth over hers, over her small cold open mouth that tasted of almonds and of the sour battery taste of the cave, and I breathed into her. Slowly. I watched her chest rise under the red coat. I took my mouth away and watched it fall. I did it again. Then I put the heel of my hand in the middle of her chest, on the breastbone, with my other hand on top, and pushed. Hard. Fast. Thirty times. You count. You’re supposed to count out loud. I counted out loud. My voice was shaking. I’d never heard it shake. Then two more breaths. Then thirty more.

The dog had come up the slope after me. It stood on the other side of her, in the good air, and barked. It had never barked before. Not once in twenty-eight years. It barked and barked into the dark over the racecourse, a hoarse, high bark like a fox’s, over and over, as if it were calling someone.
Thirty. Two breaths. Thirty.
The heavy air was pouring off me. I could see it in the lamplight. It filled the hollow where we knelt, round my knees, round her small body lying on the stones, round the dog’s legs, rising. Mine.
Thirty. Two breaths.
I put my mouth on hers the fourth time and breathed, and under my mouth her mouth moved.

She coughed. Into my mouth. A small, wet, furious cough. And then she turned her head away from me to the side and was sick, almonds and water and the orange drink, all over the stones and my knees. And she pulled in a breath. A great ragged whooping breath, like the first breath a baby takes, the whole of her small body heaving for it.
And then another.
And then she opened her eyes and looked up at me, and her face was wet with the water from the bucket, and her lips were going from blue to pink.
And she said, quite clearly, in a hoarse, cross little voice, “That was horrible.”
And I laughed.

And then I was crying. I’m telling you this as plainly as I’ve told you everything, and you’ll have to take my word for it, because nobody saw it except a six-year-old and a dog. I was crying. Not two breaths after. Not on time. Not for anybody’s face. I knelt on the stones with her head in my lap and I cried, the way you cry when you’re a child and you didn’t know yet that there were such things as mornings. And I didn’t watch it. I didn’t time it. For the first time in my life I didn’t count.
She lay in my lap and looked up at me crying, with interest.
“Why are you doing that?” she said.
“I don’t know,” I said.
“Okay,” she said. And she took my hand, the bitten one, and held it against her chest, where I could feel her breathing.
In. And out. And in.
The dog had stopped barking. It lay down beside her, its head on its paws, and looked at me.
Then I looked down the slope, at the cave.

The lake had sunk back a little, after the surge. The smoke from the candle was gone, but I could see where the line was by the dust on the slope: below it, everything was still. No moth would fly there. In the lamplight from the wall, the doorway of the cave was a black mouth in the hill, and in front of it, in the dust, inside the lake, Ferrante was kneeling.

He hadn’t got up. When I’d taken my hand off his neck and gone down into the gas for her, he could have stood. He could have lifted his own head an inch and breathed. He had all the time in the world. He was eighty-nine and he was fearless and his heart walked at fifty-six beats a minute, and nobody was holding him.

He was kneeling as he’d shown me on my first Sunday. Back straight, then forward. Hands flat on the warm ground on either side. Head bowed. His whole white head under the surface of the lake, his face an inch above the dust, his back to me.
He wasn’t moving.
I don’t know how long he’d been there. I hadn’t counted. For the first time in three hundred and seventy years, nobody had counted.
I had two hands. One of them was holding a child’s hand against her chest so I could feel her breathe. The other was on her wet hair.

I could have gone down. It was ten metres. I could have put the child down on the stones, and gone down the slope into the gas, and put my hand on the back of his neck, and lifted him out into the good air, and poured the water over him, if there’d been any water left. I’d used it all on her. And breathed into him. And said there, there. And he’d have opened his eyes and looked up at me, and seen my face, and then I’d have had to decide what to do with him for the rest of his life.
I didn’t go down.
I sat on the slope with the child in my lap and her hand in mine, and I watched him kneel there in the dark, in the lake, until I was sure. And then for a long time after.

I’ll tell you I don’t know what it was. I’ve thought about it every day since and I still don’t. Whether it was murder, because I could have lifted him and didn’t. Whether it was mercy, because he’d asked, because he was tired, because he wanted to know if he was afraid. Whether it was love: the only kind I had for him, the kind he’d built in me himself, Sunday after Sunday, which was the kind that holds you under and doesn’t lift. Whether it was the first thing I ever did that he hadn’t taught me, or the last.
I’ll tell you what I do know. The heavy air was coming off me the whole time I watched him. It was rising round me and Pia and the dog, on the slope, in the lamplight. I was afraid.
I was afraid for him too.
I just wasn’t afraid enough to let go of her hand.
34. Morning in the Red Zone
The ground has no memory. The stone does.
At dawn the swarm went quiet.

It didn’t stop. It never stops. But the big ones stopped coming, and the little ones came further and further apart, and the ground under the Burning Fields settled. It didn’t go down. It just stopped going up, for now, like an animal that’s stood up in the night and walked round in a circle and lain down again in a slightly different place. Eleven centimetres at the Rione Terra. Fourteen at the old harbour. The observatory said so on the radio at six o’clock.

At six o’clock, on the state television, a woman in a grey suit read the morning news to the whole of Italy. She said the evacuation of the red zone had been carried out in exemplary order. She said the authorities were in full control. She said the country should be calm. She was very good. She was perfectly calm herself, and everyone who watched her believed her, because she didn’t stand in anything at all.

At nine o’clock, when the markets in Milan opened, the price of Italy went down, and then, quite suddenly, at about half past nine, it came back up. Nobody could explain why. Someone, the newspapers said the next day, had been buying.
At ten o’clock the Soldier telephoned me, on the phone from his parcel.
“It’s done,” he said, in his deep flat voice. “All of it. All eleven. Nobody’s hurt who wasn’t supposed to be.”
“Was anybody supposed to be?”
He was quiet for a moment.
“Two,” he said. “I’ll tell you about them. Not on the phone.”
“All right.”
“Is he—”
“Yes.”
He was quiet again, longer this time.

“I’m sorry,” he said. And I think, as far as Saverio can be, he was. I think he had been to the cave too, every Sunday until he was eighteen, and knelt, and been lifted, and loved the hand. And I think that, like me, he’d never once been held.
My hand, holding the phone, was shaking. I looked at it. It went on shaking.

I didn’t know why. Then I did. Pia was asleep in the van behind me, across the back seat, under Ferrante’s coat, with the dog lying on the floor beside her. Every few minutes I turned round to make sure she was still breathing.
At noon the Held came to Chiaia.

Not to the Foundation. The building had been evacuated. There’d been some damage in the night to the old houses along the sea, cracks and fallen cornices, and the police had put red tape across the door with the brass plate. They came to the pharmacy downstairs, because the pharmacist had a key, and because they didn’t know where else to go.
Thirty-eight of them. Two didn’t come. I’ve been told about the two. I’ll tell you another time.

They stood in the old pharmacy among the wooden shelves and the two hundred painted jars, in their good coats over yesterday’s clothes, grey-faced, unshaven, with no sleep. And they were in the heavy air to the chest, all of them, the whole room flooded with it to the height of the counter. Some of them had been up to the Foundation before they came down. They’d found the cold room empty. The shelves were bare. The skulls were gone. The Register was gone. Thirty-one volumes, three hundred and seventy years of every frightened thing they’d ever done, gone in the night.

The notary saw me first, when I came in. Then the banker. Then all of them, turning round one by one. They looked at me, standing in the doorway of the pharmacy in my coat with the dust of the cave on it, and the dried sick of a six-year-old on the knees of my trousers. I watched them understand.
Not all of it. They’ll never understand all of it. But enough.
Where was he? they wanted to know. What had happened? Who had taken the books? What would happen to them? What would happen to them? What would happen to them?
They’re the frightened. They didn’t want to be saved. They wanted someone to decide.
I stood at the front of the pharmacy, behind the old counter, where he’d always stood behind the desk upstairs. I didn’t sit down.
“He’s gone,” I said.
The heavy air rose. Past their chests. Up to their chins.
“The books are safe,” I said. “The skulls are safe. They’re with people I trust. Nobody will ever read them who shouldn’t.”
It went down a little. I watched it go.
“Everything will go on,” I said. “The way it always has. The Foundation. The gatherings. The clients. The debts.” I looked at them, one after the other, all thirty-eight. “Sundays.”

The notary began to cry. Then the pharmacist, with his cough sweet. Then the banker. I watched them cry. It was very moving. I’d have been moved, I think, if I’d been looking at anything but the heavy air going down round their legs like a tide going out, as they understood that someone was going to decide for them. That they were held.
The priest from the Vomero came forward, wading in it, and knelt on the floor of the pharmacy in front of me, and took my hand, and kissed it.
I let him.

I want to be honest with you, to the end. I didn’t give it back. Any of it. The Register, the money, the skulls, the chairs, the thirty-eight frightened people kneeling in a pharmacy in Chiaia. I didn’t burn the books or open the cold room or call the police or set anybody free. I kept it all. I’m a fearless woman with eleven people like me in eleven chairs that matter, and a soldier, and thirty-one volumes of the secrets of every frightened powerful person in this country. Of course I kept it. What did you think I’d do? I’ve told you what I am.

The next Sunday a client came up the stairs to the pharmacy, a woman, and pushed an envelope into the house of a skull the pharmacist had found for her, a borrowed one, with a tin roof. And I decided. One word.
And that week I paid it.

But I didn’t draw a circle beside it. And I never will. Nobody will ever draw a circle in the Register again. I’ve told the eleven that, and they’ve told me what they think of it, and they’re staying anyway. They like me.

I went back to the cave on the afternoon after the swarm, alone, before the police or the scientists came to measure the gas. I took him out of the lake by his shoulders and laid him on his back in the dust in the sun, outside it, and closed his eyes, and put his coat over him, and his hat on his chest, and his shoes side by side at his feet, toes together.

His face was calm. I looked at it for a long time. I’d like to tell you there was something in it, at the end: that he’d found out, that he’d been afraid. There wasn’t. Or if there was, it had gone, the way it goes when the breath comes back.
There was nothing round him on the dust. No heavy air at all.
There was round me.
The dog was lying in the doorway of the cave, in the gas, on its side, with its gold eyes open.

I didn’t count. I never wrote down how long. On his column in the Register, when the books came back to me, at the bottom, under the last of his years, there’s an entry in my hand. It doesn’t have a number. It has one word.
Domenica.
35. Centuries Ago I Chose a Child
So this is it.

It’s night. I’m in his house on Posillipo. I suppose it’s my house now. The lawyer will see to it. Somebody has to live in it, and I couldn’t go back to the Rione Terra: it’s in the red zone, and they’ve closed it, and they say it’ll be months. The ground’s still going up there, under my bed, a millimetre a day. I’ll go back one day. I’d like to.

The books are on the stairs, one pile on each step. The ragù pot is on the stove, washed. Norma is in its sleeve on the shelf by the record player. I haven’t played it. I don’t think I will for a while.
Pia’s asleep in the big bed upstairs, in the room that faces the sea.

I’m sitting beside her, on a chair I’ve pulled up to the side of the bed, in the dark. The window’s open a little, and I can hear the sea down on the rocks at the bottom of the lemon terraces, going in and out, and very far away, round the bay, the sirens still going over Pozzuoli. They’ve been going for a week.

She’s asleep on her back with her arms flung out and her mouth open, the way children sleep, as if they’d been dropped from a height onto the bed and stayed where they landed. She has a strawberry hair clip in each bunch. I gave her the one from my coat pocket, the one I found in the cave in March, the one he said was old. She was very pleased. She said it was hers. She knew it by a scratch on one of the green leaves.
I’ve got my hand an inch from her mouth.

I’ve had it there for three hours tonight. I can feel her breath on my palm: warm, slow, damp. In. And out. And in. Every time it goes out against my hand, something under my breastbone, in the place where the fist closes round the bird, lets go. And every time there’s a pause between one breath and the next, a long one, the way there is in children’s sleep, the fist closes, hard, and the heavy air comes up off me, round the legs of the chair, across the floorboards, under the bed. And I wait. And the breath comes. And the fist lets go.

I’ve been doing this every night for a week. I don’t sleep. I can’t. I’ve never not been able to sleep in my life, and I can’t. If I take my hand away I can’t feel her breathe, and if I can’t feel her breathe I have to put it back.
So this is it.

This is what you’ve all been living with. All of you. The whole time. The notary and the pharmacist and the priest and the man in the duck tie and the father in the Solfatara who went in after his boy. The woman screaming one name at a window in 1656 and the mother in the cradle-for-life who walked away into a February night. Ten thousand people in a cathedral with their faces turned up, waiting. This. A hand an inch from a mouth in the dark, waiting for the next breath. All night, every night, for the rest of your life, the heavy air coming up off you whenever the breath is slow. And nothing you can do about it. Nothing you can decide. No hand to lift you. Just this.
I don’t know how you bear it.

I used to watch you stand in it, all my life, and wonder why you didn’t just step out. I thought it was weakness. I thought you could just walk out of it the way I walk out of a room, dry. I didn’t know it was this. I didn’t know it was holding.

I’m never going to take her to the cave. I want to tell you that clearly, so it’s written down. Not once. Not ever. Not to see. I’ve had the gate welded shut. The Soldier did it, with a torch, the day after, while I watched. The dog lay in the sun beside us while he did it, and watched too, and when it was done it got up and walked through the bars as if they weren’t there. It went into the dark and lay down in the gas, and closed its eyes.
We don’t ask it questions.

I’m never going to hold her under. And I’m never going to let go of her either. Both of those are true. I’ve worked out that I’ll be doing this for the rest of my life: sitting beside a bed in the dark with my hand an inch from her mouth. I’ll do it when she’s six and when she’s twelve and when she’s thirty and climbs cranes and walks up to men with guns and bites people and laughs. When she stands at the top of the mast against the sky with her arms out and doesn’t hold on. Whatever she does. She’ll do anything. She’s like me. And I’ll be standing at the bottom in the heavy air up to my neck, holding.
That was the question, wasn’t it. The one I said at the beginning you’d asked without knowing.
What is a person with no fear capable of?

I’ve told you. I’ve shown you all I can. She can walk into any room. She can stand in a wardrobe for nine hours. She can kill a man on a crowded tram in one breath and walk off at the next stop. She can sit in a cellar while five men do their worst, and walk out past their boss and drink his coffee. She can walk into NATO with a tray of pastries. She can hold the leash of a whole city from the end everyone thinks is the collar. She can steal three hundred and seventy years of secrets in a single night and keep them. She can let an old man she loves kneel in the dark until he stops, and watch, and not go down.
Anything. That was the answer. He was right. It’s the most frightening word there is.
But there was one thing she couldn’t do. She couldn’t be held. Not for one Sunday. Not for one second. Not by the cave, not by the hand, not by the man who built her. Nobody could put a leash on her.
So she put one on herself.

That’s the last thing a fearless person is capable of. It’s the only thing that’s ever stopped one. Not God. Not the law. Not the Held. She has to choose it. She has to find someone small enough and loud enough and loose enough to be worth it, and put her own hand on her own neck, and keep it there.
Pia’s breathing has gone slow again. A long pause.
The fist closes.
I wait.
The breath comes, warm, against my palm.
In.
And out.
THE BOOK OF CHOOSING · V — 2026
Do not let your Keeper die in his bed.
Centuries ago I chose a child.

That’s how it begins. Every one of us has written it, fourteen hands in three hundred and seventy years, each in our own ink. Centuries ago I chose a child. As though it were the first time. As though it were us who did the choosing.

I’m the fifteenth. I’m writing this at his kitchen table on Posillipo, in his book, with his pen, in brown ink, because there’s no other ink in the house. It’s three in the morning. There’s an earthquake every few minutes, small ones, and the pen jumps. You’ll be able to tell, if anyone ever reads this, which words were written during a shock. They wander.
I’m not going to write how I chose her, because I didn’t.

I sat on a wall by a railway for three days and watched her stand at the top of a mast against the sky. Then I sat down on a rubber mat, and she came down the mast to me, hand over hand, and walked up close, too close, and looked at me with nothing behind her eyes. And she bit me. And she laughed. And something in my chest that I’d had all my life and never used closed, once, like a fist round a bird.
That’s all. That’s the whole of it.
Centuries ago I chose a child.
This time the child chose me.

Below the old line inside the back cover — Do not let your Keeper die in his bed — in a hand that is new to the book: small, upright, steady, written during an earthquake so that the last word wanders:
Let her.
And at the very foot of the page:
24 December 2026. The ground at the Rione Terra went up one more millimetre tonight, under an empty bed.
The Keeper of the Held is awake. She is afraid.
She’s holding.

GLOSSARY
Agnano [ahn-YAH-noh] — An old volcanic crater west of Naples that once held a round lake, drained in 1870 and now a racecourse. The Cave of the Dog lies behind its ruined spa.
amygdala [ah-MIG-dah-lah] — Greek for almond. One of two small almond-shaped parts deep in the brain, one on each side, that act as a watchman: they notice danger and set off fear. In
Domenica they have turned to stone. Plural: amygdalae.
Annunziata [ah-noon-TSYAH-tah] — The Annunciation. An old church and foundling hospital near the port of Naples, where unwanted babies were left in the wheel for five hundred years.
Arenella [ah-reh-NEL-lah] — The hilltop neighbourhood of Naples where the Cardarelli hospital stands.
Bagnoli [bahn-YOH-lee] — A seaside district of western Naples, inside the Burning Fields.

Baia [BAH-yah] — A fishing harbour west of Pozzuoli. In Roman times it was the luxury resort of emperors; the slow earthquake has since sunk its villas five or six metres under the sea, where they can still be seen.
Bari [BAH-ree] — A port city on Italy’s Adriatic coast, across the country from Naples.
basso [BAHS-soh] — Low. A one-room home on the ground floor of an old Naples building, opening straight onto the street, with no window but the door. Plural bassi.
Bellini, Vincenzo [bel-LEE-nee] — Sicilian composer of operas
(1801–1835). Ferrante’s favourite, above all Norma.
Bisogna sventrare Napoli [bee-ZON-yah zven-TRAH-reh
NAH-poh-lee] — Naples must be gutted. The Prime Minister’s words after the cholera of 1884, which led to the tearing-down of the old port quarters.
bradisismo [brah-dee-SEEZ-moh] — Slow earthquake, in English bradyseism. The slow rising and sinking of the ground in the
Burning Fields as the volcano pushes from below.
Brera [BREH-rah] — An old artists’ quarter of Milan, all cobbles, ivy and small bars.
Calabria [kah-LAH-bryah] — The southernmost region of mainland
Italy, the toe of the boot.
caldera [kahl-DEH-rah] — Old Italian for cooking pot. The huge bowl left when a volcano collapses into itself after a great eruption.
Camorra [kah-MOR-rah] — The old criminal clans of Naples.
Campania [kahm-PAH-nyah] — The region of southern Italy round
Naples.
Campi Flegrei [KAHM-pee fleh-GREH-ee] — The Burning Fields.
The sleeping supervolcano under the western half of Naples and
Pozzuoli, half of it under the sea.
Capodimonte [kah-poh-dee-MON-teh] — Top of the mountain. The hill and royal palace above the Sanità.
Capri [KAH-pree] — The island at the mouth of the Bay of Naples.
the Captain — The most famous skull in the Fontanelle, said to have come to a jealous man’s wedding as a skeleton in a soldier’s coat.
capuzzelle [kah-poot-TSEL-leh] — Neapolitan for little heads.
Nameless skulls from the Fontanelle that local women adopted, cleaned, housed and asked for favours, until the Church banned the practice in 1969.
carabinieri [kah-rah-bee-NYEH-ree] — Italy’s national police, who are also part of the armed forces.

carbon dioxide — The gas every person breathes out. It is half as heavy again as ordinary air, so it sinks and pools in low places, like the floor of the Cave of the Dog. Breathed in large amounts it causes air hunger and panic.
Cardarelli [kar-dah-REL-lee] — The largest hospital in southern
Italy, on the hill above Naples.
casa famiglia [KAH-zah fah-MEEL-yah] — Family house. A small modern children’s home where a few children with no family live with paid carers.
Caserta [kah-ZEHR-tah] — A city north of Naples.
Chiaia [KYAH-yah] — The elegant seafront quarter of Naples, full of palaces and expensive shops. The Fondazione Respiro stands there.
cholera — A disease spread by dirty water that drains the body of fluid within hours. It killed some seven thousand people in
Naples in 1884.
Civil Protection — The Italian government department that handles disasters and decides on evacuations.
Col Moschin [kol mos-KEEN] — The 9th Parachute Assault
Regiment, the oldest of Italy’s special-forces units, named after a mountain its first men stormed in 1918.
comune [koh-MOO-neh] — The Italian town or city council, which keeps the register of every person born there.

culla per la vita [KOOL-lah per lah VEE-tah] — Cradle for life. A modern baby hatch: a small heated cot behind a door in a hospital’s outside wall, where a mother can leave a newborn safely and unseen. An alarm calls a nurse.
Depretis, Agostino [ah-goh-STEE-noh deh-PREH-tees] — Prime
Minister of Italy at the time of the 1884 cholera.
Domenica [doh-MEH-nee-kah] — Sunday, from the Latin dominus, lord, master. The narrator’s given name.
Donna Concetta [DON-nah kon-CHET-tah] — A skull in the
Fontanelle known as the head that sweats.
Dumas, Alexandre [ah-lek-SAHN-druh dew-MAH] — French novelist (1802–1870), author of The Three Musketeers, who visited the Cave of the Dog.
Duomo [DWOH-moh] — The cathedral of Naples, where the blood of San Gennaro is kept.
ECM1 — The single gene whose broken copies, one from each parent, cause Urbach-Wiethe disease.
Eleonora [eh-leh-oh-NOH-rah] — Poet and journalist of the
Neapolitan Republic of 1799, hanged in the Market Square that
August.
Esposito [es-POH-zee-toh] — Exposed, set out. The surname given to every foundling left at the Annunziata, and now the most common surname in Naples.
faccia gialluta [FAHT-chah jahl-LOO-tah] — Neapolitan for yellow-face: what the saint’s ‘relatives’ shout at San Gennaro, after the colour of his golden statue, when his blood is slow to turn liquid.
fearless dominance — A measure psychologists use for how calm, bold and at ease a person stays in the face of danger. High levels turn up in leaders, heroes and psychopaths alike.
Ferrante [fer-RAHN-teh] — The Keeper of the Held.
Fondazione Respiro [fon-dah-TSYOH-neh reh-SPEE-roh] — The
Breath Foundation. The charity in Chiaia that serves as the
Held’s public face.
Fontanelle [fon-tah-NEL-leh] — The little fountains. A vast old quarry in the Sanità where the city’s unclaimed dead were laid for three centuries.
fumarole [FYOO-mah-rohl], plural fumaroles [FYOO-mah-rohlz] —
From the Latin for smoke. A hole in volcanic ground through which steam and gas escape.
funicular — A short railway that climbs a steep hillside, its cars pulled up and down by a cable.
Gennarino [jen-nah-REE-noh] — An eleven-year-old boy killed fighting a German tank during the Four Days of Naples in 1943, later awarded Italy’s highest medal for bravery.
Goethe, Johann Wolfgang von [GUR-tuh] — The great German poet (1749–1832), who visited the Cave of the Dog in 1787.
Grotta del Cane [GROT-tah del KAH-neh] — The Cave of the Dog.
A short man-made passage near Agnano where volcanic carbon dioxide pools on the floor. For centuries guides suffocated dogs there for tourists and revived them in the lake.
Lago Patria [LAH-goh PAH-tree-ah] — A coastal lagoon north of
Naples, home to a large NATO military headquarters.
lazzari [LAHT-tsah-ree] — The great class of the homeless poor of old Naples, who fought for the King in 1799. Singular lazzaro; a woman, lazzara.
Liguria [lee-GOO-ryah] — The coastal region of north-west Italy, around Genoa.
Mariella [mah-ree-EL-lah] — The woman who runs Pia’s children’s home.
moka [MOH-kah] — The small eight-sided stovetop coffee pot found in every Italian kitchen.

Monte Nuovo [MON-teh NWOH-voh] — New Mountain. A volcanic hill 133 metres high that grew out of flat ground near Pozzuoli in eight days in 1538, burying the village of Tripergole. The youngest mountain in Europe.
mortadella [mor-tah-DEL-lah] — The large, pink, mildly spiced pork sausage of Bologna.
NATO — The military alliance of the countries of Europe and North
America, which promise to defend one another. One of its large headquarters is at Lago Patria.

Norma — Bellini’s opera about a priestess who prays to the moon for peace while hiding a secret love, and at the end walks into the fire. Her prayer, Casta diva [KAH-stah DEE-vah], means chaste goddess.
Padre Pio [PAH-dreh PEE-oh] — A twentieth-century monk from southern Italy, said to bear the wounds of Christ in his hands, now a saint loved across the south.
Palermo [pah-LEHR-moh] — The capital of Sicily.
parenti di San Gennaro [pah-REN-tee dee sahn jen-NAH-roh] —
The relatives of San Gennaro: old women who claim descent from the woman who caught his blood and sit at the front of the cathedral to pray, and shout, the miracle into happening.
Pia [PEE-ah] — The fearless six-year-old left in a cradle for life at the hospital in Pozzuoli in 2020.
Piazza del Mercato [PYAHT-tsah del mer-KAH-toh] — The Market
Square, by the sea in Naples, where public executions were held.
Po [POH] — The great river that runs across the top of Italy through a wide, flat plain.
polenta [poh-LEN-tah] — Porridge of cornmeal, a traditional food of northern Italy.
Posillipo [poh-ZEEL-lee-poh] — From Greek, rest from pain. The ridge on the western edge of Naples where rich Romans built summer villas. Ferrante lives there.
Pozzuoli [pot-TSWOH-lee] — The old port town at the heart of the
Burning Fields, where the ground rises fastest.
Quartieri [kwar-TYEH-ree] — The Spanish Quarters: a tight grid of narrow alleys above the Via Toledo, built for Spanish soldiers in the 1500s.
ragù [rah-GOO] — The Neapolitan Saturday sauce: meat cooked slowly in tomato for six hours, eaten on Sunday.
Rione Terra [ree-OH-neh TEHR-rah] — The oldest quarter of
Pozzuoli, on a rock over the harbour, emptied in a single day in
1970 when the ground rose. Domenica lives there.
Risanamento [ree-zah-nah-MEN-toh] — The making-healthy. The rebuilding of central Naples after 1884, which tore down the old port quarters and drove a wide new street through them.
ruota [RWOH-tah] — The wheel. A turning wooden drum set into the wall of the Annunziata, in which mothers left babies they could not keep. Closed in 1875.
Salerno [sah-LEHR-noh] — A city on the coast south of Naples.
San Gennaro [sahn jen-NAH-roh] — Saint Januarius, patron of
Naples, beheaded at Pozzuoli in 305. Dried blood said to be his turns to liquid three times a year; when it does not, the city fears disaster.
San Giovanni [sahn joh-VAHN-nee] — An old factory district on the east side of Naples, now home to a university technology campus.
Sanità [sah-nee-TAH] — A poor old quarter of Naples built in a valley over ancient catacombs, crossed by a bridge so the kings could pass above it.
Santa Chiara [SAHN-tah KYAH-rah] — A great medieval church in
Naples, burial place of its queens, gutted by fire after the bombing of 4 August 1943.
Saverio [sah-VEH-ryoh] — The boy who later becomes the Soldier.
Scampia [SKAHM-pyah] — A district on the northern edge of
Naples, long known for its drug market and clan wars.
scugnizzi [skoon-YEET-tsee] — The street boys of Naples, famous for fighting in the Four Days of 1943.
Serapis [seh-RAH-pis] — An Egyptian god. The ruined Roman market in Pozzuoli, whose columns show the ground sinking under the sea and rising again, was long called his temple.
sfogliatella [sfol-yah-TEL-lah] — A Neapolitan pastry shaped like a shell, made of many thin crisp layers around sweet ricotta.
Solfatara [sol-fah-TAH-rah] — The sulphur place. A steaming crater on the edge of Pozzuoli.
Spaccanapoli [spahk-kah-NAH-poh-lee] — Split-Naples. The long straight Greek street that cuts the old city in two.
taralli [tah-RAHL-lee] — Small ring-shaped Neapolitan biscuits, hard and crumbly, flavoured with black pepper and fennel seed.
Tripergole [tree-PEHR-goh-leh] — A village near Pozzuoli buried when Monte Nuovo was born in 1538.
Umberto [oom-BEHR-toh] — King of Italy, who walked through the cholera wards of Naples in 1884.

Urbach-Wiethe [OOR-bahk VEE-teh] — A very rare inherited illness, first described in Vienna in 1929, that causes a hoarse voice, tiny bead-like bumps on the eyelids, and sometimes the hardening of both amygdalae into calcium, leaving a person without fear.
Vele [VEH-leh] — The Sails. Huge triangular blocks of flats built in
Scampia in the 1970s, later a drug market; most have been demolished.
Via Foria [VEE-ah FOH-ryah] — A long, busy road running below the Sanità.
Via Toledo [VEE-ah toh-LEH-doh] — The main shopping street of
Naples.
Vomero [VOH-meh-roh] — The respectable middle-class quarter on the hill above Chiaia.
waterboarding — A torture in which water is poured over a cloth on a person’s face so that the body believes it is drowning.
THE WORDS OF THE HELD
the Held — The secret order behind the Fondazione Respiro: about forty frightened, respectable people, held together by their fears.
the Keeper — The head of the Held, who chooses the fearless child and holds her under. Always a former Hand, grown old, except the first.
the Hand — The fearless child the Keeper forges and sends where no one else can go.
going under (also to go under) — Kneeling in the Cave of the Dog while the Keeper’s hand holds the face down in the gas.
the lift — The moment the Keeper pulls the child’s head up out of the gas.
the gift — The first breath after the lift.
a debt — A killing asked for by a client and decided by the Keeper.
To pay a debt is to carry it out.
the Register of Breaths and Debts — The Keeper’s ledger, kept in brown ink, recording each Sunday’s seconds under and each debt paid.
the Book of Choosing — The leather book in which each Keeper, in their own hand, writes how they chose their child.
the heavy air — Domenica’s name for the fear she sees coming off people as a colourless gas that pools at their feet.
